NEWS IN BRIEF 


Bindley opens North Carolina DC 


INDIANAPOLIS — Calling it the “new Atlanta” of the 
Southeast, Bindley Western Industries is moving into the 
Charlotte, N.C., market with a new 20,000-square-foot 
distribution center. 

The facility is set to open in late December and will be 
operating by early January, C. Richard Zartman, presi- 
dent of Bindley Western Drug Co., told Drug Store News. 

“We think Charlotte offers great growth opportuni- 
ties,” Zartman said. Sales and distribution functions will 
be handled from the new center, the drug wholesaler’s 
10th division. 

Zartman estimated start-up costs at between $2 million 
and $3 million. He predicted that the new division will 
eventually generate more than $200 million in sales and 
employ about 20 people. 

Stanley L. Neal has been named the general manager 
for the Charlotte facility, reporting to Zartman. Neal was 
previously director of the company’s Prime Vendor Pur- 
chasing Program and assistant general manager of the 
Mid-South Division in Atlanta. 

The Indianapolis-based company operates distribution 
centers in Orlando, Fla.; Houston, Phoenix, Dallas, Los 
Angeles, Atlanta and Indianapolis, and wholly-owned 
subsidiaries in Stamford, Conn., and Brockton, Mass. 
Bindley Western is one of the largest drug wholesalers in 
the country, with sales to exceed $1 billion in 1987, accord- 
ing to the company. 


Boys’ earthquake loss reported 


LOS ANGELES — Financial losses from the Oct. 1 
earthquake here are starting to appear on company earn- 
ings results. The Boys Markets, a chain of one drug store 
and 54 supermarkets, posted an extraordinary charge of 
$449,000 in the third quarter resulting from the quake, 
which registered 6.1 on the Richter scale. 

While 30 to 40 of the stores only sustained minimal dam- 
age of about $100, approximately 10 stores each recorded 
$20,000 or more in damage, according to George Golleher, 
Boys senior vp. 

Golleher said the damage was “predominantly product” 
with few structural problems. “We basically were very 
lucky.” 

The extraordinary charge impaired earnings growth in 
the quarter ended Oct. 4, to $2.62 million on sales of $174 
million. In the previous year, the company posted third 
quarter net income of $2.20 million on sales of $149 million. 

For the first nine months of the year, Boys reported 
sales of $408 million and income of $7.06 million. These fig- 
ures cannot be compared to the previous year, since Boys 
operated under a different company during the first quar- 
ter of fiscal 1986. 


Adams takes post at Revco 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Revco D.S. has named [an J. 
Adams director of strategic computing, responsible for all 
data base, end-user computing and decision support sys- 
tems. 

Adams, 40, a native of Britain, was previously with 
Firestone Tire and Rubber Co., where he served as man- 
ager of decision support, microcomputing and office ser- 
vices.

DRUG STORE NEWS, November 9, 1987 


se drive launched 


Chain now at eight units; 100 targeted within five years 


MEMPHIS, Tenn. — Su- 
perD has launched a major 
franchise program that under- 
scores parent Malone & 
Hyde’s commitment to the 
drug business, company offi- 
cials said. 

The effort will expand a cur- 
rent roster of eight drug 
stores te 100 in five years, as 
the franchise growth rate out- 
strips that of corporate-owned 
stores, which number 101 to- 
day, Bob Billings, drug divi- 
sion president, told Drug 
Store News. 

The program signals a re- 
commitment to the drug retail 
and wholesale side, two years 
after M&H, primarily a food 
wholesaler, had sought pur- 
chase bids for its SuperD drug 
business. 

The $3 billion company had 
sought to sell the stores dur- 
ing a period when drug chains 
were selling at high multiples, 
but failed to receive an ade- 
quate offer when a buyers’ 
market began to prevail, Bill- 
ings recalled. 

The drug division now plans 
to use franchising as the best 
way to achieve M&H’s high re- 
turn on investment goals, and 
meet tighter cash flow re- 
quirements imposed by its 
Sept. 1984 $585 million man- 
agement leveraged buyout, 
Billings said. 

“We don’t have to spend 
$350,000 to open a new store,” 
said Billings, noting that fran- 
chise developement requires 
little asset investment. 

Billings said one-year-old 
M&H Franchising Inc., a re- 
organized franchising opera- 
tion, has started marketing 
aggressively to independents 
within SuperD’s ADIs within 
a 300-mile radius of Memphis. 

“We have an awful lot of in- 
terest from independents in 
small towns, where we can’t 
go with corporate stores,” 
said Billings. 

Independents have become 
more receptive. “There is a 
real dilution occurring in most 
markets, because most of the 
large supermarkets feel they 
need a pharmacy, and they’re 
taking a big slice of the H&BA 
pie,” Billings said. 

The 200 independent phar- 
macies supplied by M&H are 


i e? ‘ aA 
5 " a r gS . 7 2 : 
id an %: A ‘ q i" 


Interior of a Super? franchise in Memphis, Tenn. 


candidates. 

Corporate units are being 
targeted for sites that can 
promise a fast payback. “We 
plan to take all of the sites that 
we project will hit our five- 
year hurdle rate. We’re man- 
aging cash, and we don’t want 
to take locations that don’t 
have a pretty quick payoff,” 
Billings said. 

M&H had bought back its 15 
outstanding franchise con- 
tracts two years ago when it 
attempted to sell the SuperD 
stores and leave the drug busi- 
ness. At one time SuperD had 
about 35 franchise stores. 

After a year without fran- 
chising, the franchise pro- 
gram was reorganized last 
year, using a separate staff to 
allow a tighter focus on fran- 
chise marketing and support. 
Franchises under the old pro- 
gram were sometimes slight- 
ed in favor of corporate stores, 
when district managers had 
responsibility for both, offi- 
cials said. 

Ron Lewis, a former district 
manager and SuperD franchise 
owner, is director of franchis- 
ing, with a beefed-up 10-person 
staff that may expand to 13 this 
year, Billings said. 

Billings said at least 12 more 
franchises will open in fiscal 
1988, ending Sept. 1, making 
over 20 by year’s end. Expan- 
sion will continue at the pace 
of 20 te 25 a year. 

“I’m confident that we will 
make that, and I suspect we 


will exceed it significantly,” 
said Billings. 

Lewis said the growth is on 
target after stores number 
seven and eight were signed in 
Memphis and Jackson, Miss., 
last month. 

“We're offering the phar- 
macist the ultimate goal of 
owning his own store. It’s one 
of the strongest recruiting 
tools we have,” said Lewis. 

SuperD looks for strong in- 
dependents, with growth po- 
tential. The average new fran- 
chise builds sales 30 percent in 
the first year, Lewis said. 

Stores range from 3,500 
square feet to 7,200 square 
feet and sport the chainwide 
black, red and gray decor. 
Their format is based on the 
convenience-oriented layout 
of SuperD corporate stores. 
That includes gondolas slant- 
ed toward a center aisle which 
channels shoppers from the 
front entrance to the rear-of- 
store pharmacy. 

Franchises also receive cus- 
tom pricing, rebate incentives 
for buying merchandise from 
M&H, the Hyde Park and Pro- 
fessional Touch private label 
products, free accounting ser- 
vices and third-party bill pro- 
cessing. 

Besides an upfront inven- 
tory investment that varies, 
the independent pays a 3 per- 
cent of sales royalty, and an 
added 1% percent for adver- 
tising, including regular circu- 
lars and coupon books. 


M & H to begin licensing 


‘Consumer’s’ apothecaries 


MEMPHIS, Tenn. — Ma- 
lone & Hyde’s drug division 
will begin franchising apothe- 
cary-sized stores under the 
“Consumer’s” banner. 

“We feel this will have a lot 
of appeal for pharmacists who 
want to get into business for 
themselves, but don’t want 
the front end,” drug division 
ey Bob Billings told 

rug Store News. 

The program will be devel- 
oped under the drug division’s 
one-year-old franchising 
arm—M&H Franchising 
Inc.—to set up stores in mar- 
kets where the drug division 
currently operates. 

It offers the same potential 
for high return on funds in- 
vested as does the division’s 


current push for franchising 


its conventional-sized SuperD 
drug stores, Billings said. 

The franchises will assume 
the name of the 38-store Con- 
sumer’s chain of 1,800-square- 
foot to 2,800-square-foot 
stores in Arkansas, Oklaho- 
ma, Wisconsin and Missouri 
that will be retained as corpo- 
rate stores. 

M&H also owns and oper- 
ates the chain of bantam Petty 
stores based in Little Rock, 
Ark., and the Pay Rite chain 
in Springfield, Mo. Billings 
said southern Missouri fran- 
chise stores might be offered 
the Pay Rite label, since the 
Consumer’s logo isn’t avail- 
able for M&H to use in that 
state. 

Consumer’s’ pharmacies 
typically account for 85 per- 


cent of sales, with the remain- 
der from a front-end of cherry- 
picked OTC and cosmetics 
products. 

A Consumer’s franchise 
would be one of asmall handful 
of chains of franchised apothe- 
cary stores in the country. Be- 
sides Medicine Shoppe, the 
coast-to-coast 700-unit fran- 
chisor, only the the 63-store 
Medicap Pharmacies Inc. of 
Des Moines, Iowa, uses the 
concept. 

Billings said first-time own- 
ers won't be the only pros- 
pects for a franchise. The 
crush of competition—partic- 
ularly from Wal-Mart, which 
is putting pharmacies into its 
small town market stores—is 
pressuring independents to 
seek out survival routes.

Household supplies promos help buyers clean up 


rug chains have acti- 
vated household 
chemicals’ traffic and 
rofit benefits through regu- 
ar promotions priced within 
pennies of the competition, 
chain merchandisers say. 
Household cleaners and 
fresheners are strong traffic 
builders when stores are will- 
ing to go to the mat on price 
and keep updated assort- 
ments of the task-specific new 
brands shoppers want, said 
buyers. 
any buyers said they pro- 
mote at or slightly above cost, 
using vendors’ payments fo” 
shipped merchandise to subsi- 
dize advertising or insure the 
category creates a net profit. 
Some chains then recover 
margins through everyday de- 
partments that capture the 
convenience buy, often at con- 
venience store prices. 
Douglas Drug of Rhode Is- 
land posts strong sales when it 
promotes such items as liquid 


dishwashing detergent and 
laundry detergent, said a 
chain merchandiser. 

“We’re very fast to react to 
new products. We jump on it, 
give it distribution, and sched- 
ule it for an ad, and we enjoy 
tremendous sales at full price 
[spurred by vendor coupons],” 
he said. 

Douglas then typically fol- 
lows up with an ad feature of 
its own with cents off the ev- 
eryday price. 

“‘We’ve found when we tie a 
promotion in with manufac- 
turer couponing, we get phe- 
nomenal sales,” he said. 

Douglas reserves in-and- 
out promotions for merchan- 
dise that is bought on deal (off- 
label, bonus packs). It carries 
a 36-foot everyday section of 
detergents and cleaners that 
produces “a fair margin.” “It’s 
an added sale that helps us 
create a one-stop shopping im- 
age,” he said. 

Harco generates 20 percent 


margins from a 24-foot every- 
day section, though most of its 
sales come from in-and-out 
center-aisle stackouts pro- 
moted at cost, said Keith Con- 
nell, director of merchandis- 
ing. Top movers have been 
Texize’s Yes, Liquid Tide, and 
Procter & Gamble’s new Dash 
in introductory promotions. 

To keep up with new SKUs 
that consumers want, Harco 
may expand footage. Compet- 
itors, including Revco and 
Eckerd, feature 48 feet. 

Connell isn’t alone in feeling 
pressure to expand assort- 
memts. Vendors’ steady un- 
veiling of new brands is fuel- 
ing strong category growth, 
as consumers respond to more 
task-specific products. 

“The name brand guys are 
pushing quality, and it 
works,” ‘ail Chris Anthony, a 
merchandiser with Pay ’n 
Save. Where an all-in-one 
cleaner once sufficed, for ex- 
ample, shoppers. now look for 


cleaners targeted for specific 
surfaces, such as tile, bath- 
room, vinyl, and formica, An- 
thony noted. 

While seeking quality, 
shoppers are also more at- 
tuned to value, possibly a re- 
sult of the influence of the 
price clubs on the West Coast. 
The result has been closer 
shopping of larger sizes at the 
Seattle chain, says Anthony. 

‘“‘The more competitive 
prices seem to be falling on the 
larger sizes. People are will- 
ing to buy in quantity to save” 
and stock up, Anthony said. 

Pay ’n Save combines a reg- 
ular 48-foot planogram cap- 
turing the convenience pur- 
chase demand, with 
promotions at or near cost. 

Chemicals accounted for 
three of six items featured ina 
September Pay ’n Save “Su- 
per Six” sale newspaper ad, 
with a 1-gallon Clorox bottle 
at 89¢, Tide (72 ounces) at 40 
percent off at $2.99, a one- 


third-off $1.39 value for a 22- 
ounce Windex. 

Since price competitiveness 
is critical in this high replen- 
ishment category, small 
chains can be hampered if they 
can’t receive buying efficien- 
cies to battle supermarkets 
and mass merchandisers. 

Eleven-store Birch Drug 
has limited its exposure be- 
cause the local DeMoulas su- 
permarket chain is able to sell 
chemicals at retail more 
cheaply than Birch can buy 
them from vendors, said Andy 
Chiras, Birch’s director of 
merchandising. 

Receiving shipments of up 
to 10,000 cases at a time, De- 
Moulas has sold half-gallons of 
Wisk at $1.89. The vendor’s 
deal price to Birch is $1.94, 
Chiras said. 

Birch keeps an 8-foot conve- 
nience section, and will pro- 
mote pre-price items, such as 
a recent $1.19 Lux offer, and 
Pledge at 99¢.

® The Twinsburg, Ohio-

@ Revco has not met its goal

12 percent as part of its plan to

expense control is better, 
Sells said, and the “board is

meeting overall goals. 


Chilling effect 


Sells’ reticence about possi- 
ble store selloffs or market re- 
treats is understandable. As 
an acknowledged “people ori- 
ented” executive (the descrip- 
tion of Jeffrey A. Cole, chief 
executive of Cole National 
Corp., the billion-dollar spe- 
cialty retailer where Sells 
earned his business spurs), 
Sells knows that a ceo’s loose 
talk about strategic market 
changes can have a chilling ef- 
fect on soldiers in the trenches. 

So while outsiders say that 
Revco has a number of mar- 
kets that can’t be defended 


and the company will have to 
trade stores and trim its scope 
in its efforts to regain lost 
strength, Sells will talk only in 
very general terms about the 
long-term scenario for his 
chain. 

There are, he says, at least 
two basic changes that he is 
eager to make. First, he wants 
to introduce an “organized 
presentation” of merchandise 
at store level to make it easier 
for customers to shop. Sec- 
ond, he wants to take the com- 
plexity out of running the 
stores by eliminating much of 
the grinding paperwork. 

Both goals are interrelated 
and both are driven by the de- 
sire to serve customers bet- 
ter. They also strike at the 
heart of Revco’s recent opera- 
tional headaches. 

Sells, sensitive to the effect 
of his words on people in the 
field, is careful to blame Rev- 
co’s well publicized past prob- 
lems on “inadequate systems” 
that have failed to deal with 
the complexity of running a 
huge, farflung chain of more 
than 2,000 stores, rather than 
on the “very dedicated, very 
hard-working people” who are 
“eager to get on with it.” 

At another point, Sells 
says, “The stores have to be 
simplified,” adding that the 
complexity has to be returned 
to headquarters and the dis- 
tribution center. “The people 
in the stores have to be able to 
spend their time with custom- 


prices which do not reflect the 
company’s full worth is an ex- 
cellent investment opportuni- 


ty,” said Henry Panasci, Jr. 
Fay’s chairman, after the 
board authorized the purchase 
of up to one million shares. 
“This action will. . . en- 
hance shareholder value, and 
reaffirms the (board’s) confi- 


dence. . . inthe company’s fu- 
ture,’ ’ Panasci announced Oct. 
21.

of its market value from Aug. 
25 to Oct. 26, sliding from 
$9.125 to $6. 125.

day,” Oct. 19, the total value 


of the retail and wholesale 
stocks tracked by Drug Store 


News continued to slide into 


the following week. Retail and 
wholesale stocks hit their lows 
on Monday, Oct. 26.

expected to see a rebound in 
their stock prices, and most

Shkolnik joins Perry Drug’s Auto Works 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Alan L. (Larry) Shkolnik has been 
named senior vp-marketing of Perry Drug Stores’ Auto 
Works division. The announcement was made by Peter T. 
Murray, who himself was elevated only last month to pres- 
ident of the division, which operates 243 discount stores in 
eight states. 

hkolnik, 46, was most recently president and ceo of 
Lucky Stores’ automotive division and had previously 
served as president of Nationwise of Columbus, Ohio. 
Earlier, he founded and was president of Benny’s Car 
Parts, also in Columbus. 

“Larry is a very talented executive with years of experi- 
ence in this business,” Murray commented. “His entire 
background reflects a history of running auto parts stores, 
with an emphasis on marketing, advertising and merchan- 
dising.” 


Spielfogel named new exec vp at Austin 


NEW YORK — Gary Paul Spielfogel, the 32-year-old 
son of Interstate Cigar Chairman Sidney Spielfogel, has 
been tapped for the newly-created position of executive vp 
at Austin Drugs, which 1s owned by Interstate. 

The younger Spielfogel, who said he reports to Law- 
rence é Aaronson, Interstate’s president and ceo, de- 
scribed his new responsibilities as “100 percent directed 
toward the profitability of Austin and the development of 
a better image for our stores.” Currently, he said, he is fa- 
miliarizing himself with the nine-store chain’s operations 
and working with Austin President Gary Lefferts. 

The new executive vp joined Interstate in 1977 and was 
involved in purchasing and special international assign- 
ments there before his appointment at Austin.

Perry Drug consolidates, 


realigns staff to cut costs 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores has 
completed a consolidation and realignment 
pro that included the reduction or reas- 
signment of about 60 administrative and office 
staff people and the shrinking of some depart- 
ments to cut costs. 

In line with those reductions, the chain has 
also delayed indefinitely its previous plan for a 
new corporate headquarters building in down- 
town Pontiac. The chain’s current facilities, 
which are housed in scattered sites around the 
Pontiac area, are now “more than adequate to 
serve the company’s requirements,” according 
to Perry Chairman Jack Robinson. 

The consolidation pro included merging 
the operations of two older warehouses into a 
newer, highly automated distribution center in 
Dayton, Ohio, and the gradual integration of 
Perry’s acquisitions of retail auto parts chains 
into a unified Auto Works division. Perry 
closed two warehouses—in Muncie, Ind. and 
Columbus, Ohio—and moved their inventory 


ministrative staffs,” said David Schwartz, Per- 
ry’s new president and coo. “This consolidation 
will make us more efficient and productive.” 
Under the realignment program, Perry’s 
core drug store business was divided into four 
ups headed by veteran Perry officers (see 
Peas Store News, Sept. 28). The realignment 
also saw the departure or reassignment of 
some department heads and the promotion of 
others, including Myron Winkelman to head of 
pharmacy operations, and Keith Cunningham, 
director of advertising. They and other depart- 
ment heads now report directly to Schwartz 
under the new corporate plan.

Imasco reports higher sales, earnings 


MONTREAL—Imasco Ltd., parent of Peoples Drug 
Stores and Shoppers Drug Mart, reported increases in 
sales and earnings for the second quarter and six months 
ended Sept. 30. 

Revenues in the second quarter edged up to $1.23 billion 
Canadian, from $1.15 billion Canadian in the comparable 
period a year ago. Net income rose to $77.03 million Cana- 
dian, or 61 cents per share, compared with $55.61 million 
Canadian, or 44 cents per share, in the same period last 
year. 

Six-months revenues reached $2.4 billion Canadian, 
against $2.2 billion Canadian in the comparable year-earli- 
er period. Net income also rose, to $147.2 million Canadi- 
an, or $1.17 per share, from $108.5 million Canadian, or 92 
cents per share, in the same period last year. 


Wellby parent’s net, sales up 


SCARBOROUGH, Me.—Hannaford Bros., which op- 
erates Wellby Super Drug Stores, announced increases in 
= “‘. net income for the 13- and 39-week periods ended 

ct. 3. 

Revenues for the 13 weeks hit $267.3 million, up from 
$234.9 million in the comparable period a year ago. Net in- 
come rose to $6.8 million, or 74 cents per share, compared 
with $5.9 million, or 64 cents per share, in the year-earlier 
period. 

For the 39 weeks, revenues were $763.3 million, versus 
$655.2 million in the period last year. Net income jumped 
to $18.6 million, or $2.03 per share, in the period, from 
$14.4 million, or $1.57 per share, the previous year. 


Melville boosts sales, net income 


HARRISON, N.Y. — The Melville Corp., owner of 
CVS Stores and Freddy’s Deep Discount, reported sales 
and net income boosts for the third quarter and nine 
months ended Sept. 26. 

Sales rose to $1.4 billion for the third quarter, from $1.3 
billion in the comparable period last year. Net income hit 
$51.7 million, or 95 cents per share, up from $47.3 million, 
or 67 cents per share, in the third quarter a year ago. 

Nine-month sales were $3.9 billion, against $3.5 billion 
the previous year. Net income for the nine months was 
$123.5 million, or $2.27 a share, up from $104.6 million, or 
$1.93 a share, in the comparable period last year. 


Quarterly figures up for Medicare-Glaser 


ST. LOUIS—Medicare-Glaser announced increases in 
net sales and earnings for the second quarter and six 
months ended Sept. 30, as wellas plans to repurchase up to 
250,000 shares of its common stock. 

For the quarter, net sales rose 18 percent, to $25.7 mil- 
lion, from $21.8 million in the comparable period in fiscal 
1987. Net earnings increased to $196,000, or 6 cents per 
share, from $128,000, or 4 cents per share, in the year-ago 
period. 

For the first six months, the company reported net sales 
of $51.5 million, an 18.6 percent increase over last year’s 
$43.4 million. Net earnings also rose, to $223,000, or 7 
cents per share, from $132,000, or 4 cents per share, in the 
comparable six months a year ago. 

The corporation’s board of directors authorized the pur- 
chase by Medicare-Glaser of up to 250,000 shares of its 
common stock, 50 cents par value, in open market transac- 
tions. The company currently has 3,040,524 shares of com- 
mon stock issued and outstanding. 

Commenting on the repurchase, president and ceo Har- 
lan Steinbaum said, “It is our belief that the acquisition by 
the company of its common stock at prices which do not re- 
flect the company’s full worth is an excellent investment 
opportunity. This action will serve to enhance shareholder 
value and reaffirms the confidence of the Medicare-Glaser 
board of directors in the company’s future.” 

Steinbaum added that the firm plans to open one full- 
line drug store in the third quarter and another in the 
fourth quarter of this fiscal year. Medicare-Glaser closed

Thrifty Corp. chosen by PLMA to 
receive its ‘Salute to Excellence’ 


CHICAGO—Thrifty Corp., which 
redoubled its efforts in private label 
marketing since 1984, was chosen to 
receive a “Salute to Excellence” 
award by the Private Label Manufac- 
turers Assoc. 

At presstime, Thrift 
honored Nov. 16 at the PLMA Store 
Brands Supershow at the Hyatt Re- 
gency O’Hare. The chain was cited 

or its efforts to improve private label 
sales and Thrifty brand penetration. 

The Los Angeles-based drug chain 
expanded its efforts in private label 
to boost overall store sales and profit- 
ability, according to Ken Crosby, se- 
nior vp and director of buying and 
merchandising. “We needed a cham- 

ion, a focus for our efforts, and 
hrifty brand products provided it,” 
Crosby noted in a talk to Associated 
Chain Drug Stores members last 
year. “We kicked off two major ad 
ahs agen re pharmacy and private 
bel—and set up a separate buyin 
department for our private label 
products beginning in 1984.” 
Thrifty also overhauled its private 


was to be 


label packaging and adopted more ag. 
gressive in-store promotional poli- 
cles, with compare-and-save shelf 
talkers and a unique guarantee. “We 
advertised that if anyone was dissat- 
isfied with any of our private label 
items, they would get the national 
brand for free,” Crosby said. 

The chain launched its program with 
an extensive market survey, to gauge 
the attitudes of Thrifty customers to- 
ward ifty-label products. It re- 
sponded with a new, stricter set of 
standards for private label items, in- 
cluding a provision that they offer 
minimum savings of at least 20 per- 
cent, high quality and “superior gross 
profit ins.” The chain now uses 
two independent testing labs to screen 
all house brand items, and offers them 
at price reductions ing as low as 50 
percent below the price of nationally 
advertised brands, Crosby said. 

The result of Thrifty’s efforts: pri- 
vate label sales doubled in two years. 
“We're very satisfied with the pro- 

ress we've made,” Crosby told 

CDS members.

By Susan Ball 

NEWORLEANS 
— James J. Le Blanc, 
a veteran of 30 years 
with K & B Inc., has 
been named president 
and chief operations 
officer of the 148- 
store chain, according 
to Sydney Besthoff 
III, who will keep the posi- 
tions of chairman and ceo. 

Le Blanc brings to the posi- 
tion “his broad experience and 
calm, guiding hand,” Besthoff 
said, adding that the appoint- 
ment will mean “a lessening of 
my responsibilities and opera- 
tions over the long term.” 

Le Blanc, 52, who had been 
vp and operations director 
since 1984, told Drug Store 
News he plans to continue mov- 
ing the chain in the direction it 
has followed for the past three 
years: “Cost-cutting, concen- 
trating on keeping our custom- 
er base, and hopefully, continu- 
ing slow growth ahead.” 

“Three years ago,” Le 
Blanc said, “we saw what was 
happening in the Gulf South— 
the economy was weakening 
oecause of changes in the oil 
industry—and we began mak- 
ing changes. We became more 
conservative, maintaining our 
sales base and giving up some 
growth to maintain that 
base.” Any chain who didn’t 
anticipate the regional down- 
turn “probably isn’t around 
anymore,” he added. 

Besthoff noted that two 
states in which K & B oper- 
ates, Texas and Louisiana, 
have been especially hard-hit

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Austin promotes Lerner, Owen 


EAST MEADOW, N.Y. — Austin Drugs has promoted 
two, as part of a general reorganization at the nine-store 
chain, according to Gary Spielfogel, whose appointment to 
the new position of executive vp was recently announced. 

Eugene Lerner will be director of _ and How- 
ard Owen will be vp-marketing and finance. Lerner, who 
has been with Austin for about eight years, was a super- 
vising store manager. Owen previously was vp-opera- 
tions. 


Arbor arrives in Grosse Pointe 


GROSSE POINTE, Mich. — Maintaining an acceler- 
ated growth pace, Arbor Drugs opened its 76th drug store 
in this well-heeled bedroom community outside Detroit 
Nov. 16. The opening marks the halfway point in Arbor’s 
expansion program for fiscal 1988, which calls for another 
five new stores in metropolitan Detroit by next August. 

The newest Arbor was designed to complement Grosse 
Pointe’s upscale, Early American architectural style, with 
a brick facade and wood bay display windows. It also fea- 
tures a new interior design and color package which will 
serve as a prototype for future stores. The package in- 
cludes earth-tone colors and a new signage system. 

Arbor will open at least 10 new units a year for the fore- 
seeable future, many of them in parts of Michigan north 
and west of its current marketing area in greater Detroit. 

In other developments: 

@ The chain announced two recent promotions, naming 
Eric Bolokofsky and Dennis Wozniak vice presidents. Bo- 
lokofsky, 35, was named vp-merchandising after serving 
as director of that department. He is an 11-year Arbor vet- 
eran. Wozniak, 32, was promoted to vp-purchasing, and 
will head all buying activities. He began his career at Ar- 
bor in 1978 as an assistant buyer, serving as senior buyer 
of electronic appliances, sundries and general promotional 
merchandise for the last four years. 


Pay ’n Save grows in Alaska 


SEATTLE — Pay ’n Save recently added its 11th Alas- 
ka store, with the purchase Nov. 25 of Nugget Super Rex- 
all in Juneau for an undisclosed amount. 

This raises the chainwide total to 107. Pay ’n Save plans 
to remodel the store in January. The chain said further it 
will retain the store manager for the 22,000-square-foot 
site, in addition to employing another 24 people. 


Dot warehousing with parent 


BENTONVILLE, Ark. — Twelve-store Dot Discount 
Drug Stores is now using parent company Wai-Mart’s 
harmacy warehouse, instead of outside wholesalers. 
owever, it will use FoxMeyer as a secondary source, ac- 
cording to Terry Files, buyer and new store coordinator 
for Dot. 

Files said Dot store managers will continue to do the 
majority of the buying for the remaining products—a con- 
cept Files said allows the stores to react quicker and make 
better deals. 

Wal-Mart also recently announced former executive 
vice president of special divisions, Paul Carter, has been 
promoted to executive vp-finance. In his prior position 
Carter oversaw the Dot division, a duty that is now being 
passed on to Westley Wright, former vp-personnel. 

Dot anticipates adding another three to nine stores in 
1988—“depending on what we find,” Files said.

MIDDLEBURG, Ohio — 
Marc Glassman, whose Marbal 
Drug chain owns the highest 
grossing individual deep dis- 
count drug stores in the nation, 
is preparing to open new com- 
pany stores in his hometown 
market of Cleveland. 

According to _ reliable 
sources, Glassman is prepared 
to double the number of his 
company-owned stores before 
the end of next year. 

Since May, Glassman has al- 
ready opened two more Marc’s 
deep discount drug stores for a 
total of seven Marc’s in West 
Cleveland. He has also opened 
one more Bernie Shulman’s 
deep discount store in East 
Cleveland for a total of three. 

According to informed 
sources, three more Marc’s will 
open before the end of this 
year, plus another three Marc’s 
and one more Bernie Shulman’s 
by spring 1988. 

Marbal Drug also has a fran- 
chise division, which currently 
operates several deep discount 
drug stores under the name 
Texas Drug Warehouse in the 
Dallas market. 

Because Glassman has a poli- 
cy of not elaborating on upcom- 
ing events, he would not con- 
firm exactly how many new 
Marc’s and Bernie Shulman’s 
will open in 1988, but he did ac- 
knowledge that more new 
stores are in the works.

knowledgeable sources in

planned to more than double

DrSNliaunches SAMI/Burke 


tracking of H&BA products 


With this issue, Drug Store News launches 
the first in a series of periodic reports on the 
comparative sales volume of 57 health and 
beauty aid products sold in drug stores and 
food stores, The nationally projected figures, 
supplied by SAMI/Burke, are based on ware- 
house withdrawal information from 54 major 
markets tracked by the marketing research 
company. 

The figures show very strong penetration by 
drug stores in the categories In which drug 
stores tend to have greater breadth, including 
over-the-counter medications like cold rem?- 


dies, antacids, synthetic vitamins, cou hreme- 
dies and laxatives. Food stores, on the other 
hands, hold commanding shares in categories 
that depend on heavy traffic and frequent ex- 
posure, such as disposable diapers, toothpaste 
and shampoos. 

In a category like internal analgesics, drug 
and food retailers both do well, with the catego- 
ry heading the list of H&BA’s in drug stores 
and number two (next to diapers) in food 
stores. But food stores do better in total sales in 
the category because of their strength in shop- 
per count. 


Kroger lists 16-, 40-week results 


CINCINNATI —_ The 
Kroger Co. posted results for 
the 16- and 40-week periods 
ended Oct. 10. . 

Sales for the 16 weeks in- 
creased to $5.2 billion, from 
$4.9 billion in the comparable 
period last year. Income from 
continuing operations was 


$45.3 million, compared with a 
loss of $39.4 million in the 
year-ago period, which includ- 
ed a charge of $82.3 million re- 
lated to the restructuring of 
certain operations. 

The loss from discontinued 
operations in the 1986 eriod 
was $11.8 million, according to 


the food chain. 

For the 40-week period, the 
company reported sales of 
$13.3 billion, against $12.8 bil- 
lion in the comparable period 
last year. Net income reached 
$135.9 million for the period, 
against $32.6 million a year 
ago.

@ PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores omitted its 
common stock dividend for the first time in 47 consecutive 
quarters, and reported a $4.6 million loss for its fourth 
quarter ended Oct. 31. The loss included a $400,000 charge 
against operations, a one-time $3.5 million charge to cover

struction planning costs. In the comparable 1986 quarter, 
the chain earned $315,000. Quarterly sales increased 9.2 
percent, to $189 million, from $173 million last year.

Bergen sells medical supply unit 


ORANGE, Calif. — Bergen Brunswig Corp. announced 
it has signed a definitive agreement to sell Bergen Bruns- 
wig Medical Supply, a wholly-owned subsidiary, for ap- 
proximately $40 million. 

The board of directors fixed Nov. 20 as the record date for 
determining holders of its 7% percent convertible subordi- 
nated debentures, due 2010. These holders will be requested 
to consent to the proposed sale of the subsidiary. 

The corporation is one of the nation’s largest distribu- 
tors of products sold to pharmacies, a major distributor of 
medical and surgical supplies, and the largest national dis- 
tributor of prerecorded videocassettes. 


O&M picks up Stotter’s assets 


RICHMOND, Va. — Owens & Minor said it has signed 
a letter of intent to buy certain assets of Leon Stotter, 
Inc., a Bridgeton, N.J. medical surgical distributor ser- 
vicing the New Jersey, Delaware, and Eastern Pennsy]l- 
vania markets, including Philadelphia. Stotter sales were 
projected at $50 million for 1987. 

The buy will move O&M—a wholesaler and packager of 
pharmaceuticals, as well as a medical and surgical supply 
distributor—into new markets, and furthers a recent com- 
pany trend of growth through acquisitions of medical and 
surgical firms. 

. Gil Minor III, president and ceo, said the buy will nat- 
urally extend O&M’s current trading area, since Stotter’s 
markets abut O&M’s northern most zones in Washington 
and Baltimore. 


Amfac bidding aloha to mainland 


FOLSOM, Calif. — Amfac Inc. announced it will sell 
Amfac Health Care and its other mainland businesses and 
concentrate on its core Hawaii operations as part of a com- 
prehensive restructuring plan. 

A company spokesman said no firm offers have been 
made yet for Amfac Health Care, the nation’s sixth largest 
publicly held distributor of ethical pharmaceuticals. The 
restructuring process and sale of non-Hawaiian business- 
es “is expected to take some time,” said Melburn G. Whit- 
mire, president of Amfac Health Care. At present, “it will 
be business as usual.” 

Amfac’s investment bankers estimated that the sale of 
Amfac’s distribution, food and mainland resort operations 
together could bring approximately $600 million to $750 
million. Amfac Health Care’s 1986 revenues were $567 
million. Sales in the first nine months of 1987 were $532 
million, compared with $402 million in the 1986 period. 


Nichols named Revco regional veep 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Revco has named Clarence D. 
Nichols as regional vp for its Carolina region based in Char- 
lotte. Nichols will be responsible for all store operations in a 
440-unit region that includes North and South Carolina and 
parts of Virginia. A 13-year Revco employee, Nichols was 
most recently a regional merchandise manager for stores in 
Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, and Arizona. He succeeds 
Darrell Patton, who resigned to pursue other interests. 

Also, former district manager Robert Thompson was pro- 
moted as regional merchandise manager for the Carolina re- 
gion reporting to Nichols. Thompson will be res nsible for 
ordering and distribution of merchandise, and p g and 
implementing merchandise and promotional programs.

Fay’s 1st med center unit 


unveiled in Syracuse, N. Y. 


Convenience should capture Rx business 


SYRACUSE, N.Y. — Fay’s Drug has 
opened its first pharmacy in a medical center 
building as part of a plan to expand its pharma- 
cy services. 

The Liverpool, N. Y.-based chain opened a 
Fay’s Pharmacy on Dec. 10 in the new Madi- 
son-Irving Medical center here, which includes 
doctors’ offices, and an outpatient surgery cen- 
ter for a local hospital. 

“We feel that we can capture that prescrip- 
tion business as a matter of convenience, - 
and. . . perhaps transfer it to another of our 
stores in the Syracuse area,” said John Kogut, 
Fay’s senior vp-operations. 

“We are trying to teke advantage of new op- 

ortunities within pharmacy,” Kogut added. 

e said Fay’s plans to open a second such unit 
in the first half of 1988 in Watertown, N. Y. 

Fay’s is also using the med center unit to 
launch it’s first service offering prepared intra- 
venous medication. Specially-trained pharma- 


_Kogut said the chain plans to roll out the de- 
vice and medication program into three of 
Fay’s conventionally-sized and sited stores 
that serve nursing homes in Albany, Roches- 
ter, and Buffalo. 

The Syracuse unit, under 2,000 square feet, 
offers full pharmacy services, plus OTC items 
and small selections of drug categories such as 
tea cards, candy, and “a very limited 

&BA,” Kogut said. 

Hours will coincide with the hours of the doc- 
tors’ offices. Offices include practices in ophthal- 
mology, dermatology, plastic surgery, psycholo- 
gy, obstetrics, gynecology, family practice, 
optometry, psychiatry, and oral surgery. 

As part of it’s move into new pharmacy ave- 
nues, Fay’s also has added a new dimention to 
its nursing home services by locating a pharma- 
cy within a nursing home. The unit was recent- 
ly installed in the St. Camillus Health Center, 
in Camillus, which is just west of Syracuse.

Medicaid plan under attack; 
NACDS predicts defections 


Attorneys: payback scheme is unlawful 


WASHINGTON — Law- 
yers for the chain drug indus- 
try intensified their attack on 
the government’s new Medic- 
aid drug reimbursement 
rules, predicting mass defec- 
tions from the program by 
pharmacies unless the courts 
overturn the present system. 

In a brief filed with the fed- 
eral District Court here, at- 
torneys for the National Asso- 
ciation of Chain Drug Stores 
asked for a “summary judg- 
ment” ruling declaring the 
new Medicaid reimbursement 
scheme unlawful on grounds 
that it fails to ensure a reason- 
able profit for participating 
drug stores. 

Those new Medicaid rules, 
which were issued by the 
Health Care Financing Ad- 
ministration late last year, 
abandoned the existing 
“MAC/EAC” system for reim- 
bursing pharmacies in favor of 
a new approach under which 
state Medicaid administrators 
were ted broad authority 
to design their own systems to 
pay for Rx drugs. Under the 
new regulations, states may 
adopt any reimbursment ap- 
proach they choose as long as 
their “aggregate” payments 
for Medicaid Rx drugs do not 
exceed a dollar ceiling set by 
the HCFA. 


Raising the ante 


NACDS filed suit late last 
fall challenging those rules, 
arguing that HCFA’s new 
rules are invalid because the 

ency failed to require state 
Medicaid officials to ensure 
that participating drug stores 
have the opportunity to earn a 
reasonable profit on third-par- 
ty Rxs. 

In its latest court filing for 
summary judgment, the chain 
drug group raised the ante by 


suggesting that retail phar- 
macies may abandon Medicaid 
unless the new reimburse- 
ment rules are withdrawn. 
The key to NACDS’ case is 
the association’s argument 


ment rates allow for the recov- 
ery of costs and a reasonable 
profit,” NACDS argued. 
HCFA’s new rule “provides 
no guarantee that states will 
adequately compensate pri- 


But in order to achieve this objec- 
tive, it is ‘indispensable’ that phar- 
macy ‘reimbursement rates allow 
for the recovery of costs and a 


reasonable profit, 


NACDS argued. 


that, at least indirectly, the 
Medicaid law requires HCFA 
to ensure that Rx reimburse- 
ment levels are set high 
enough to enable drug stores 
to realize a reasonable profit. 
Although the Medicaid Act 
does not state that explicitly, 
it does require states to spend 
sufficient funds to avoid any 
“lowering [of] the amount, du- 
ration, scope, or quality of 
care” to Medicaid recipients. 
“Consequently,” NACDS 
told the court, ‘HCFA is 
obliged to ensure participa- 
tion of a sufficient number of 
private providers so that Med- 
icaid beneficiaries can receive 
medicai services to the extent 
these services are available to 
the general population.” 
“Unless an adequate num- 
ber of neighborhood pharma- 
cies are willing to participate 
in the Medicaid program, the 
access of Medicaid patients to 
pres drug services will 
hindered,” the association 
added. 
But in order to achieve this 
objective it is “indispensible” 
that pharmacy “reimburse- 


vate pharmacies,” the associa- 
tion said. “Indeed, it does not 
even require states to consid- 
er whether reimbursement is 
adequate and poses no obsta- 
cle to setting reimbursement 
levels below costs.” 

As a result, “some drug 
stores will be forced to leave 
the program because of their 
inability to expend large 
amounts of time and resources 
on a venture which cannot 
generate enough income to 
make their business viable,” 
NACDS warned the court. 

This, in turn, renders 
HCFA’s rule “defective” be- 
cause the Medicaid law re- 
quires that pharmacists “earn 
a reasonable profit so as to en- 
courage their continued par- 
ticipation” in the drug pro- 
gram, the chain group said. 

The next move is up to 
HCFA, which has not yet an- 
swered the NACDS charges. 
Lawyers at the agency are 
preparing a response tot e as- 
sociation’s request for summa- 
HF Ra spicy and that HCFA 

ing 1s to surface 
within the next few weeks.

DRUG STORE NEWS, January 4, 1988 _- 


This category has proven to be an explosive segment for drug chains; 


but success requires retailers to stock enough copies of the latest rental hits 


ith VCRs now 
found in more than 
50 percent of all 


American households, the 
home video revolution has 
reached a high-water mark, 
with a remarkable level of 
penetration in just a few short 
years as an industry. 

The attainment of such re- 
markable household penetra- 
tion in such a short time, and 
the multibillion-dollar market 
for tape sales and rentals it has 
spawned, have made video an 
explosive growth segment for 
~drug chains, but one fraught 
with perils as well. 

Those perils have been well- 
documented. The fast growth 
has caused problems. Price- 
cutting and the scramble for 
enough copies of the hottest 
new releases has already put 
some smaller, less-capitalized 
operators out of business, and 
forced new levels of discipline 
on drug chains that devote 
space to rentals. 

“The rental business is 
evolving rapidly, «and for a 
business that’s only eight or 
nine years old, it’s starting to 
look pretty mature,” said 
Gene Fink of WIN records and 
video, a New York-area dis- 
tributor. 

“I think the shakeout will 
really accelerate in the next 
year or two, with a lot of mom 
and pops closing up. The mom 
and pops don’t have the capital 
for enough copies to satisfy 
enough customers, and the 
renting public is becoming 
more disenchanted with those 
kinds of stores,” Fink said. 

He added: “They’ve already 
been through all the older 
movies, and they want the 
hottest new selections or 
they’ll take their business to 
one of the bigger shops.” 

Both factors—the growing 
competition from big video 
chains with huge selections, 
and the expense and difficulty 
in obtaining enough copies of 
the most popular titles—have 
been enough to keep some 
drug chains out of the rental 
business. 

The president of one of the 
Midwest’s fastest-growing 
drug chains noted: “We don’t 
plan to get into the rental busi- 
ness, because there are com- 
petitors on every corner and 
you have to spend a fortune to 
get the hot tapes. Then, in six 
weeks, the public wants some 
other movie, and you’re stuck 
with a dozen copies of an $80 
item that nobody wants.” 

“We don’t plan to get into 
it,” added another chain exec- 
utive in Michigan. “There are 
already too many competi- 
tors, and the margins don’t 
justify the effort and ROI for 
us.” 

Many other drug chains, 
however, have shrugged off 
those challenges pn waded 
into what can be a profitable, 
traffic-boosting category. 

Among newer entrants are 
CVS, Walgreens and Long Is- 


Pay ’n Save offers an extensive video rental department, and hanging signs tout the chain’s very low 


price of 99 cents per title per day. 


land’s Austin Drug, which tied 
in a successful Christmas pro- 
motion using Walt Disney’s 
newly-released video of Lady 
and the Tramp. 

Another recent entry into 
video rental is the fast-grow- 
ing Phar-Mor deep discount 
drug chain. Phar-Mor dazzled 
the video rental market in Chi- 
cagoland with a new, high-vol- 
ume video rental business cen- 
tered in a brightly-lit kiosk at 
the front of the store. 

By offering its rentals at 69 
cents a night—the lowest 
— in town—Phar-Mor has 

uilt a high-volume business 


in a few short months, and re- 
cently developed a much larg- 
er video center for its newest 
Chicago-area store, according 
to spokesperson Carol Robin- 
son. 

To avoid the pitfalls plagu- 
ing many mom and pops, how- 
ever, most drug chains which 
have gotten into the business 
rely on outside expertise—in- 
cluding full-service wholesale 
distributors, rack jobbers and 
even leased vending machines 
stocked by others—to handle 
many facets of the business. 

“There are now about 400 to 
500 new releases a month, and 
we have to boil that down for 
our retail customers,” Fink 


said. ““‘With tapes costing 
them $60 at wholesale, we 
can’t afford to recommend bad 
titles.” 

In terms of blank videotape, 
the industry’s rapid maturity 
means a slowdown in new 
sales growth, and a scalin 
back to single-digit pare 
os in the number of 

CRs and blank video tapes 
sold in future years. 

The original Electronics In- 
dustry Association forecast 
for 13.7 million VCRs and 340 
million blank videocassettes 
sold to retailers this year has 
now been reduced to 13.5 mil- 
lion VCRs and 310 million 
pieces of blank tape, due to an 
overall flatness in the market 
in the first half of the year. 

In terms of blank tape, not- 
ed one industry executive, 
“We are now dealing with a 
market which can be consid- 
ered mature, and this trans- 
lates to more conservative 
growth rates. 

“We will no longer see the 
dramatic double-digit annual 
growth experienced during 
the period 1983 through 1986 
because household penetra- 
tion has soared from less than 
20 percent to a substantial 50 
percent level,” said general 
manager R. Stanton Bauer of 
Fuji Photo Film USA’s Mag- 
netic Products Division. 

Bauer was quick to add, 
however, that “single-digit 
growth on an immense base is 
still impressive growth.” 

Together with supermar- 
kets, in fact, drug stores have 
done most in recent months to 
capitalize on the continuing 
demand for blank videotape. 

“Over the last 12 to 18 
months, the food and drug 
channels have enjoyed the 
most growth, and now consti- 
tute 11 percent of total video- 
cassette sales,” Bauer noted 


in a recent report. “We believe 
that these two channels, in 
articular, will continue on a 
ast growth curve throughout 
the balance of the ’80s.” 

One reason: the growing im- 
portance of female buyers in a 
once-male dominated catego- 
ry. Women—who dominate 
the drug store and supermar- 
ket shopping environment— 
now make up about half the 
market for blank videotape, 
according to Bauer, and their 
importance continues to grow. 
As it does, it is shifting the bal- 
ance in favor of drug and su- 
permarket chains.

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Sells and Fantle named to NACDS board 


NEW YORK — Boake A. Sells, chairman and ceo of 
Revco D.S., and Sheldon W. “Bud” Fantle, chairman and 
ceo of Dart Drug Stores, were elected to the NACDS 
board of directors. They are filling the unexpired terms of 
the late H Levin, founder of Happy Harry’s in Dela- 
ware, and Sidney Dworkin, former Revco chairman. The 
terms expire April 15, when board elections will be held 
for three-year terms. 

Sells, former president and chief operations officer of 
Dayton Hudson Corp., joined Revco in October. Fantle, 
who served as NACDS chairman in 1980-1981 and on the 
association’s board from 1975 to 1987, purchased Dart 
Drug Stores in November, after resigning his position as 
chairman of Peoples Drug Stores. 


Fay’s names four board members 


LIVERPOOL, N.Y. — Fay’s board of directors has 
elected four top Fay’s Drug officers as members, filling va- 
cancies. 

Elected are Lawrence Rose, president and chief opera- 
tions officer, John Kogut, senior perations, Daniel 
O’Leary, vp-finance and cfo, and Warren Wolfson, vp- 
general counsel and secretary. 

The assignments fill out a 13-member board, including 
Chairman Henry Panasci, Jr. 


Co-op advertising takes the forefront 


NEW YORK — Co-operative advertising will outpace 
other ad forms in 1988, according to Pinpoint Marketing, 
Inc., acompany that develops cost-shared ad programs in- 
velving manufacturers and retailers. & 

Co-op ad spending will grow 11 percent to $8.88 billion, 
compared with 8.9 percent growth of all media used in lo- 
cal advertising, according to Arnold Ferber, Pinpoint’s 
president. 

An uncertain economy promotes co-op fund use, Ferber 
argues, and the number of vendors with co-op ad pro- 

should increase to 5,000 this year, compared with 
,500 in 1985.

Control Data acquires SAMI/Burke 


MINNEAPOLIS — Control Data Corp., the $3.3 bil- 
lion computer manufacturer, has purchased SAMI/Burke, 
the Cincinnati-based market research o ization, from 
Time, Inc. Terms called for an initial $60 million cash pay- 
ment, and additional payouts based on SAMI/Burke’s rev- 
enue growth. 

SAMI/Burke offers a wide range of data bases and mar- 
ket research services, including product tracking, market 
modeling, and custom surveys.

Cullum buys 


DALLAS — Cullum Cos. has acquired 
Safeway Stores’ former distribution center in 
Garland, ‘Texas, marking the end of Safeway’s 
presence in the Dallas market. Purchase price 
was not disclosed. 

The huge, 1.2-million-square-foot center 
served several hundred Safeways in Dallas, El 
Paso and other markets, prior to the supermar- 
ket chain’s departure from Texas. Cullum, par- 
ent company of Tom Thumb supermarkets and 
Page Drug, also purchased 10 former Safeway 
stores in Dallas last spring when Safeway 
pulled out of that market, converting them to 
supermarkets and food/drug combos. 

ith the purchase, Cullum nearly doubles 
its warehouse capacity and provides a solid 
platform for what managers say will be a major 
expansion drive in future years. 

The chain will continue to occupy its current 

eneral offices and distribution center in North 
allas, but six satellite warehouses now in use 
will be phased out and consolidated at the Gar-

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Medicine Shoppe gets larger quarters 


ST. LOUIS — To accommodate its rapid growth as the 
nation’s bi = drug store franchisor, Medicine se In- 
ternatio moved to a new, larger corporate headq 
ters in office space formerly occupied by Monsanto Co. The 
move more than doubles the com s headquarters space 
to 36,000 square feet, and gives the the rights to lease 
the rest of the building for a total of 54,000 square feet. 

Medicine Shoppe ended fiscal 1987 with 698 franchised 

harmacies, and plans to have 1,000 in operation by 1991. 

e chain, which opened 57 new outlets last year, achieved 
net earnings of $4.4 million on sales of $316 million in fiscal 
1987. Same-store sales were up a brisk 15 percent. 


Owens & Minor seeks listing on NYSE 


RICHMOND, Va. — Owens & Minor, the pharmaceuti- 
cals and medical/surgical supplier, expects to move its com- 
mon shares listings to the New York Stock Exchange by ear- 
ly February. The company shares are listed on OTC- 
NASDAQ under the symbol OBOD. 

The company has also elected Hue Thomas III, 48, to the 
post of istribution. He has served since 1985 as assistant 
vp, and earlier was vp-medical ve an division and manag- 
er of the Atlanta medical/surgical branch. 


year company veteran who served as chief operations officer 
and most recently senior executive vp and a director, has re- 
signed to pursue other opportunities. 


Maxidrug names Kirk to replace Neville 


WEST SPRINGFIELD, Mass. — Maxidrug, the U. S. 
division of Canada’s Jean Coutu Group, has named Mat- 
thew Kirk as director of merchandising, according to Max- 
idrug president Michel Coutu. 

Kirk was formerly a merchandising executive with 
Heartland Drug, a deep-discount operation now owned b 
CVS. At Maxidrug, he replaces George Neville, who le 
last summer. 

“He will be a big plus for our company,” Coutu said, cit- 
ing his 19 years of experience in a deep-discount environ- 
ment. “He knows that type of organization. Deep dis- 
counters are more aggressive and demand more 
Seat: meacagne gs behavior,” Coutu said, indicating that 
Maxidrug will become “more aggressive.” 


Harry Evans, Bartell Drug vet, dies Dec.17 


SEATTLE — Harry Evans, a 27-year veteran of Bartell 
Drug, died suddenly Dec. 17. He was a buyer of promotional 
and seasonal merchandise, and supervised the chain’s photo- 
finishing efforts. 

Senior vp Val B. Storrs called Evans “responsible for 
many new and innovative programs which helped our com- 


pany grow and prosper.” 


Pay Less NW targets Kent, Wash., site 


KENT, Wash. — Pay Less NW has signed a lease to open 
a 23,707-square-foot store here, with a Super Safeway as a 
co-anchor. Population here is to by 75 percent 
by the year 2000, predominantly in y households.

: fragranced lotion to be a prob- 
em. 

Curel is marketed as a thera-

work requires them to wash 
their hands frequently. Curel 
has been formulated to end the

skin problems.

will be available in 6-ounce

Lucky Stores names new concept store 


DUBLIN, Calif. — Lucky Stores has dubbed its new con- 
cept store, which will debut in San Diego next month, Ad- 
vantage. The 482-store chain delayed the opening one month 
because of remodeling delays at a former Gemco location. 


Ralphs could go on the auction block 


COMPTON, Calif. — Ralphs Grocery could be placed on 
the auction block as a result of an unfriendly bid for its par- 
ent company Federated Department Stores. Campeau 
Corp. made a hostile $4.2 billion bid for Federated last 
month, and disclosed in a SEC gy, Mee if successful, it 
might sell off the Ralphs division. The 129-store grocery 
chain does not have in-store pharmacies, but does lease 
space in several of its Giant locations to Thrifty drug 
stores’ Jr. concept. 


New Arbor store boasts earthy decor 


WEST BLOOMFIELD, Mich. — Arbor Drug’s new de- 
cor, ne earthtones and new ne was unveiled in 
the chain’s 75th store, opened Jan. 20. The 9,450-square- 
foot unit is the fifth of 10 stores planned for the Detroit 
metro area in fiscal 1988.

New era begins at Peoples; 
broad repositioning in store 


ALEXANDRIA, Va. — After more than a 
year of reorganization, Peoples Drug Stores is 
raising the curtain on what its management hopes 
will be a long-running hit show. 

The 819-store chain, plagued by operating diffi- 
culties and losses in 1986, made a major effort last 
year to recast its marketing strategy and restruc- 
ture its management and ag nme: earan 

Peoples’ new marketing thrust will center on 
customer convenience and service, a new lower 
price image, better in-stock positions, clean and 
uncluttered stores, and a product mix emphasiz- 
ing the core drug store categories of pharma- 
cy/OTC, cosmetics and H&BA. 

Peoples has adopted a new slogan to sum up 
what it hopes will be its new image with consum- 
ers: “The convenience you want—The savings 
you deserve.” 

The changes are the result of consumer re- 
search carried out in the first part of 1987, which 
showed that what drug store customers wanted 
most was convenient shopping, including shorter 
checkout lines, easier-to-find merchandise, a bet- 
ter in-stock performance and friendlier service. 
The research also found that consumers consid- 
ered Peoples to be a high-priced store.

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Albertson’s to purchase 8 Farmer Jacks 


BOISE, Idaho — Albertson’s said it is buying eight 
Farmer Jack supermarkets from the Detroit-based Bor- 
man’s Inc. supermarket chain. 

All of the purchased stores contain pharmacies, Dave 
rg vp and treasurer of Albertson’s, told Drug Store 

ews. 

Three stores are in Salt Lake City, with one each in 
Caldwell and Mountain Home, Idaho, Jackson, Wyo., and 
Tooele and Richfield, Utah. 

All stores, but the one in Jackson, were to be trans- 
ferred March 7, in a purchase that adds “several new 
towns” to Albertson’s roster, and enhances presence in 
other markets. 


Harco opens Ala. stores; count up to 75 


NORTHPORT, Ala. — Harco Drug is moving ahead 
with store openings, with the latest two units, both for- 
merly owned by Eckerd, being unveiled in Huntsville 
and Selma in February, bringing its store count to 75. A 
new store is set to open this month in Hueytown, and 
construction on a Harco in Auburn should be completed 
in April. 

Harco also recently gave three executives vp titles: 
Jim Harrison III, who is assistant to the president; 
Frank Gable, director of sales; and David Fuhrman, in 
charge of diversified operations. 


Medi-Save opens three new stores 


BATON ROUGE, La. — Medi-Save Pharmacies Inc. 
has opened three of the 11 new stores it plans to in 
1988, according to executive vp Carl Napoli. Two leased 
units opened last month in Wal-Mart stores in Mt. Sterling 
and Morehead, Ky. A third opened last month in a Super 1 
Foods store in Monroe, La. 

The chain also opened its second freestanding Medi- 
Save Discount Optical outlet in February in Metairie, La. 


Progar named a vp at Thrift Drugs 


PITTSBURGH, Pa— Ralph Progar, Thrift Drugs’ for- 
mer manager of store coordination and productivity, has 
been named to the newly-created post of vp-stores admin- 
istration, Thrift president Robert Hannan said. 

Progar will take responsibility for developing and ad- 
ministering store programs, and will serve on Thrift’s 
Management Council. 

In addition, Progar has been elected chairman of the 
nine-member Pennsylvania State Board of Pharmacy. He 
will direct board activities in all areas relating to pharma- 
cy ag ne 

e joined Thrift in 1968 as a student pharmacist. 


Solomon joins La Salle 10 International 


PARAMUS, N. J. —Jeanhette Solomon, who recently 
retired from K&B Drugs where she was the cosmetics 
buyer for many years, has joined La Salle 10 Internation- 
al, the cosmetics and perfume vendor. 

Solomon will be sales director for the Southeast and 
Southwest regions, as well as a consultant, said Terry Au- 
genbraun, senior vp-marketing. 

“She will be calling on woe | of the accounts that know 
her. She has a plenty of knowledge, and is welcome addi- 
tion,” said Augenbraun.

LOS ANGELES — Costco 
membership warehouse club 
will install seven pharmacies a 
year, while warehouse club in- 
novator Price Club is still test- 
ing its initial site.

its first pharmacy in 1986, and 
opened 14 in quick succession 
during fiscal 1987. Currently, 
the company operates 16 
pharmacies in its West Coast 
warehouses, Charles Burnett, 
vice president of pharmacy, 
told Store News.

pace slowed down from last 
year, largely because the com- 
pany is trying to keep a limit 
on its headquarters person- 
nel. For this same reason, 
Burnett said the company is 
initially opening pharmacies 
close to home.

the wages Costco is cur- 
rently operating two optical 
centers and leasing one. Bur- 
nett said the pharmacy and o 
tical departments, are set side 
by side in the warehouses, 
take up about 2,000 square 
feet, and share the same ser- 
vice personnel.

continued to open optical de- 
partments, operating 11 cur- 
rently, but the chain has yet to 
move beyond the initial phar- 
macy it opened last May at its 
original warehouse in San Die- 


Eckerd to close La. DC July 1 


HAMMOND, La.— Eckerd will close its 
228,000-square-foot distribution center here 
July 1 in a move it said will improve efficiency. 
The closing of the DC, which primarily serves 
Lousiana and Mississippi markets, will leave 
the company with six such centers. The 165 
stores in those markets will be served by DCs 
in Atlanta, Houston and Dallas.

Rx to OTC switches 


The increased cost of health 
eare will further be reduced as 
consumers increasingly gai 
OTC access to drugs which 
formerly required a prescrip- 
tion. 

“According to a recent in- 
dustry survey, four times as 
many common health prob- 
lems are being treated by OTC 
products as are taken to physi- 
cians,” said Young. He attri- 
butes the increased use of 
OTC products to switches. 

“In the last ten years, al- 
most all of the successful OTC 
products were Rx to OTC 
switches,” said Young. 

Many OTC products are of- 
fering more than symptomatic 
relief of minor conditions, ac- 
cording to Young. Some cure, 
some prevent, others help 
manage disease. The trend 
will continue; the OTC market 
will be e , he added. 

Self-medication using OTC 
products is not only a boon to 
consumers interested in tak- 
ing a more active role in their 
own care, but an economic 
benefit to society, according 
o ns Charles re of Kline 

mpany, a marketing con- 
— firm. a 

“For every dollar spent in re- 
tail OTC,” said Kline, “the con- 
sumer gets $1.79 in health care 
benefits.” The study shows 
that OTC medications saved 
the U.S. economy $23.8 billion 
in 1987 in lost time from work, 
visits to doctors, prescription 
drugs, insurance services, 
travel and home remedies.

health decisions. But consum- 
ers must fully understand pow- 
erful drugs. Selling medication 
directly to the public carries a 
heavy legal and ethical bur- 
den. 

Perhaps the counseling role 
will ultimately fall to the phar- 
macist as the health care mar- 
ketplace continues to evolve. 

e pharmacist is the per- 
son who can answer whether a 
new blood testing kit can tell a 
consumer what he needs to 
know,” said George Harris, 
editor-in-chief of American 
Health ine. 

Arthur White, president 
and ceo of WSY Consulting 
Group, thinks the pharmacist 
will ultimately become the in- 
formation source. 

“The American people are 
asking their doctors to tell 
them that medication is safe,” 
he said, “but it’s the pharma-. 
cist that knows that informa- 
tion. The family pharmacist 
has retreated to a distant area 
of the pharmacy so that he or 
she is not as accessible. That 
role as information giver 
should be reestablished. The 
American people are rece 
tive to self-care and self-medi- 
cation, but they won't go it 
alone. They are counting on 
complex partnerships with 
health care professionals, doc- 
tors and pharmacists.”

Revco suffers $17.4M loss in 3rd qtr. 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Despite operating profits of $29.7 
million before depreciation and amortization, Revco D.S. 
suffered a net loss of $17.4 million on sales of $600.3 million in 
the third ended Feb. 6. This compares with third- 
quarter results last year of $579.4 million in sales, o j 
profits of $38.6 million and a net loss of $11.8 million. 

Year-to-date sales are up 4.8 percent over last year, to 
$1.66 billion, with a net loss of $50.9 million on operating 


profits of $92.2 million. 
riod inched ahead 1.4 per- 


Same-store sales for the 

cent, up 2.8 percent for the first 36 weeks of the fiscal year. 

Prescription drugs accounted for most of the increase. 
Revco chairman Boake Sells blamed much of the “be- 


low-plan performance” on high out-of-stocks during the 


Christmas season, but said the problem is being corrected. 


Sells added that Revco’s new management team, as well 
as a 3.6 percent gain in prescriptions filled at Revco this 
year, should also improve operating results. 

On another front, Revco’s divestiture program is con- 
—e with the remaining divisions e to be sold 
by mid-year ahead of schedule, said executive vp and chief 
financial officer Vito Cardace.

EUGENE, Ore. — Tiffany-Davis’ new owner Dale Engel 
said he plans to keep the former family-run operation true to 
its friendly and convenient neighborhood drug store image.

. The acquisition gave Engel the comgeny Six

DRUG STORE NEWS/INSIDE PHARMACY, March 28, 1988 


IP25 


By Barbara White 

It’s no secret that checkstands are 
heavily merchandised, crammed full of 
the items retailers hope will create 

uick turns, impulse purchases and ul- 
timately, big profits in a small space. 

Merchandising the pharmacy check- 
stand area is quite another matter. 

Many drug chains minimize the im- 
pulse items at their pharmacy check- 
stands in favor of a clean, health-ori- 
ented image, opting not to take full 
advantage of merchandising in this 
heavy traffic area. 

“Merchandising the pharmacy area 
hasn’t been a priority for Drug Empo- 
rium,” said Steve Denovchek, director 
of pharmacy at the prominent deep- 
discounter. Denovchek said that the 
“supermarket mentality” that governs 
the checkout area at the front of the 
store has been avoided in the pharma- 
cy area. 

“The pharmacy is a service-oriented 
area where prescriptions are filled pro- 
fessionally. We are not trying to create 
extra sales by placing impulse items 
there to the extent that we merchan- 
dise checkout at the front of the store,” 
he said. 

Proximity to the pharmacist plays 
heavily in tailoring the merchandise 
mix at other chains. At Perry Drugs, 
the area behind the pharmacy check- 
stand—the area that customers see 
from the other side of the counter—is 
reserved for products that pharma- 
cists wish to recommend to customers, 
according to Mike Winkleman, assis- 
tant vp of pharmacy services. 

“When a busy pharmacist is tring to 
fill 200 prescriptions a day, it’s work to 
have to walk down the aisle to recom- 
mend products,” said Winkleman. 
“Pharmacists are the most highly 
trusted professionals and their recom- 
mendations are important.” That’s 
why the chain leaves the selection of 
the most frequently recommended 
products to be placed behind the 
counter to pharmacists at individual 
stores. In nearly every case, the prod- 
ucts placed there are private label, ac- 
cording to Winkleman. 

A recent Lebhar-Friedman Re- 
search survey of pharmacy checkstand 
merchandising revealed that chains 
are creating a specialized product mix 


Rx checkstands aim 
for clean look: study 


for the area, one that invites some im- 
pulse purchases but also provides con- 
sumers with information and eases- 
consultation with the pharmacist. 


Lip protection tops list 


When asked which three items are 
the most desirable year-round prod- 
ucts for placement at the pharmacy 
checkstand, chain headquarters and 
store management personnel respon- 
sible for those decisions showed one fa- 
vorite item. The darlings of the phar- 
macy checkout area were lip 
protection products, chosen by 53 per- 
cent of respondents. 

Lip protection products are quick 
turnovers generating high sales per 
square foot. Factors, such as these, 
play an important part in the decision 
of which products occupy the prime 
real estate of the checkout counter. 

Quick turnover was the most impor- 
tant factor contributing to that choice. 
Eighty percent of the pharmacy super- 
visors, general merchandise manag- 
ers, store managers 
and others surveyed 
cited quick turnover 
as the most important 
factor for consider- 
ation when choosing 
which items get the 
coveted space. 

Sales per square 
foot fi d heavily as 
a consideration as did 
a product’s impulse 
buying potential. 
Broad customer ap- 
peal was cited by 63 
percent of the respon- 
dents as a factor in se- 
lecting items to occu- 
py space near the 
checkout area. 


Testing customer 
appeal 


Customer appeal 
fi s heavily into decisions about 
what is merchandised near the phar- 
macy checkout counter at MediSave, 
according to Bob Miller, MediSave’s 
director of advertising. 

Miller said that MediSave’s pharma- 
cy checkout area, although not heavily 
merchandised, serves as a test site for

new products which are often given

into the store’s product mix.

quick read of how a product will be ac-

If it goes well, then 
we integrate the item 
into regular buying 
patterns and place the 
item in the appropri-

Other chains 
agreed; 17 percent of 
the respondents cited 
health and beauty tri-

wanted at pharmacy 
checkout areas.

at Kerr, said that a 
range of trial sizes 
priced from 15 to 39 
cents, can usually be 
found at the chain’s 
pharmacy checkout. 

Items enjoying a 
surge of creed can get some unex- 
pected checkout space—at least for a 
while. 

Diagnostic kits and vitamins were 
the items retailers added most fre- 
quently to their pharmacy checkstand 
areas this past year. 

Fish oil capsules, at the height of 
popularity this year after a study indi- 
cated that the supplements lowered 
cholesterol, patbssay § their moment in 
the sun this year at the pharmacy 
checkstands at MediSave. 

After subsequent studies ques- 
tioned the effectiveness of fish oil, Me- 
diSave transported the tablets back to 
the vitamin area. Checkstand status 
can sometimes be short-lived and elu- 
sive. 


Reliable Turns 


Although 53 percent of the survey’s 
respondents said that they had placed 
products at the pharmacy checkout 
counter over the past year that had 
never been tried there before, the old 
faithful performers get the coveted 
space year after year at many chains. 

The products that chain decision 
makers want most at the pharmacy 
checkstand, after lip balm, are vita- 
mins, named by 40 percent as one of 
the three most desirable items. 

_ “Vitamins are a good profit 
item,” explained Steve Bishop, vice 
tga of Bill’s, a California chain. 
ith an 8-foot counter area and virtu-

ditional items to be merchandised 
around the pharmacy checkout 
counter. 

The chain has devoted shelving on 
the bottom area of the pharmacy 
checkstand to eyecare and a diabetic 
section, according to Bishop. 

“The diabetic products are expen- 
sive, and keeping them near the phar- 
— allows better surveillance,” he 
said. 

Drug Emporium’s diabetic products 
are placed at the pharmacy checkout 
counter as well, but for different rea- 
sons. 

“Diabetic products would do well 
anywhere,” said Steve Denovchek, 
“but customers have questions and we 
want to make the pharmacist available 
to answer them. Our decisions on what 
to place at the pharmacy checkstand 
are customer driven.” 

Eye care has been given checkout 
status at MediSave. “We went from 4 
feet to 8 feet in two and a half years in 
eye care,” said Miller.

Rudden named vp-merchandising at Dart 


LANDOVER, Md. — Jon Rudden, most recently vp- 
marketing at the Rea and Derick division of Peoples, has 
been named vp-merchandising at Dart Drug Stores. 

Rudden joins a line of former Peoples executives who 
have followed Sheldon “Bud” Fantle to Dart, after Fantle 
bought an interest in the chain and became chairman last 

ear. 
: Rudden will report to Louis Schechter, senior vp-mar- 
keting, and also formerly of Peoples. Fred Edwards was 
named Dart’s senior executive vp earlier this year after 
leaving Peoples. 

Rudden was part of a Northumberland, Pa.-based man- 
agement team that oversaw 90 Rea and Derick units. 


Klawitter retires early from NACDS post 


ALEXANDRIA, Va. — Harold J. Klawitter has taken 
early retirement from his post as vp-pharmacy affairs of 
the National Association of Chain Drug Stores, and Bruce 
Briggs has been named to head the pharmacy affairs de- 
partment. 

Klawitter, in his early 60s, led NACDS’ team of profes- 
sional relations specialists for about 42 years. His depar- 
ture is the latest of several changes in top and middle man- 
agement at NACDS since the retirement of Bob Bolger 
and the appointment of Ron Ziegler as president of the as- 
sociation. 

Briggs, who has been with NACDS for five years, was 
pharmacy affairs director before his promotion. 

In announcing Klawitter’s departure, Ziegler ex-

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 11, 1988 


Arbor puts new DC on line, 


lays groundwo 


NOVI, Mich. — Arbor Drug Stores has nearly 
completed a transfer of warehousing operations 
to a newly constructed, automated faci ty, vast- 
ly up ing its distribution capacity and laying 
the groundwork for a doubling in store count. 

At 234,000 square feet, the new center offers 
Arbor five times the storage capacity of its old- 
er warehouse. The new facility includes auto- 
mated sortation devices, tri-level picking and 
rack systems, and a total of 22 receiving and 
outgoing trucking bays. 

“With this we can handle the future,” said 
Arbor president and chief operations officer 
Markus (Max) Ernst during a tour of the new 
facility. “We can easily handle 150 stores with 
this warehouse, and we have the capacity to 
double the existing space later.” 

Arbor began shipping merchandise out of the 
new center early this year, and is near full utili- 
zation. The center will allow the chain to boost 
its ratio of centrally controlled inventory from 
about 65 percent to 75 or 80 percent, “resulting 
in significant cost savings and improved ser- 
vice in restocking our stores,” according to a 
company report.

60 years ago 

WASHINGTON, D.C., 1928 — 
The so-called “drug store ownershi 
law” passed in Pennsylvania in 1 
has been declared unconstitutional 
by the United States Supreme 
Court. This law, which was formed to check 
the growth of drug chains, although its object 
is not directly revealed in the law itself, pro- 
vided in effect that no one but a licensed phar- 
macist legally own a drug store. In the case of 
a partnership or corporation, it required each 
partner and each stockholder to be a licensed 
pharmacist.

in an effective educational window at the Owl 
me | Store, 19th and Broadway, Oakland,

ed with the new. For instance, insulin was 
shown Ame with viper’s tongues—the 
old method of treating diabetes. :

30 years ago 

ARDEN GROVE, Calif., 1958 
— The new Garden Grove, Calif. , 
Sav-on unit, 20th in the self-service 
chain, is the first to dispense with 
display windows. Outside of glass 
entrance doors, the 11-foot wall to 
the left of the entrance contains the only glass 
area: four foot panels designed to protect inte- 
rior lighting to shoppers. Chain heads felt 
outside displays were unneccessary in this 
particular shopping center location.

HICAGO, Iil., 1968 — Smiles all around 
are indeed in order as Waigreen president 
A.A. Borg and board chairman C.R. Wal- 
n Jr. receive a mortar and pestle trophy 
rom Dennis Fill, president of E.R. Squi b, 
commemorating the filling of the chain's 200 
millionth prescription. It took the Chicago- 
based chain 67 years to reach this milestone 
since its founding in 1901: but the real mea- 
sure of the chain’s recent growth in the pre- 
scription area is the fact that the 100 million 
mark was passed only six years ago.

A regional viewpoint 


One of the industry’s major 
regional chains reports that 
treatment sales are up “a little 
over last year,” which its fran- 
chised treatment buyer inter- 
prets “as a good sign because 
the economy is so bad.” 

Franchised treatments in 
this chain are merchandised in 
the cosmetics department in 
family sets. 

This chain has not changed 
its merchandising of treat- 
ee in a long time, 
basically because the buyer 
sees no need to aggressively 
emphasize treatments in this — 
market. 

“Only asmall segment of the 
market uses treatments,” the 
buyer says, “and that segment 
doesn’t seem to be growing. 
Manufacturers need to do 
more to educate customers. 

“Treatment manufacturers 
really have to presell their 
customers. Just running a 
coupon in one of our books or 
in an ad doesn’t do much. The 
manufacturers have to con- 
vince the customers before 
they get to our stores that 
they want a treatment prod- 
uct and they want it to achieve 
some specific effect. When 
that happens on a broader 
scale, you'll see more growth 
in this category.”

ease, and friendly service. 

Many chains also made strides in 
honing their operating efficiencies at 
headquarters and in stores, and in up- 
grading their distribution capabilities 
with new automated warehouse sys- 
tems. 


Most growth on hold 


A few chains, such as Rite Aid and 
Hook-SupeRx, pursued aggressive 

owth in 1987, but the majority held 
cack. preferring instead to seek a high- 
er return on existing assets through 
store remodels and upgrades. 

A parallel development was the vig- 
orous effort by many chains to tighten 
their grasp on their primary markets 
and to abandon areas where their in- 
vestment had failed to pay off in a 
greater share of sales. 

Thus, chains like Osco and Longs en- 
gaged in a mutual sale of stores in Ari- 
zona, northern California and Colora- 
do, and both came out of the deal in a 
much stronger position. 

Although the overall sales trend was 
upward, several of the largest chains 
in the business stumbled badly in 1987. 
They included such once-successful 
companies as Revco, Dart, Pay ’n Save 
and Perry, all of whom dipped into the 
red inkwell in order to report the 
year’s results. All four chains, howev- 
er, were engaged in turnaround efforts 
that included selling major non-drug 
store assets and 


began the job of creating a lean opera- 
tion responsive to customer needs. 

At Perry, president David Schwartz 
consolidated the reins of power 
through an executive reorganization 
while the chain sold its retail auto parts 
business, which soured in 1987. At 
Dart Drug, Bud Fantle and his son Jeff 
headed an investment — that took

month later in Topeka, Kan., and two 
others were on the drawing boards.

permarket, including the partnership 
of K mart and Bruno's vt French op-
