Major executive shifts 


Difficulties experienced by a num- 
ber of chains resulted in executive 
shifts at the highest levels. At Revco, 
for example, Boake Sells, the former 
abet og of Dayton Hudson, was 

rought in to breath new life into the 
faltering chain. Sells totally redrew 
the chain’s reorganization chart and 


emerged in 1987 to 
challenge chain drug operators. In 
Dallas, for example, Wal. art teamed 
with the Cullum Cos. to open an Amer- 
ican version of the European hyper- 
market. Wal-Mart, which had already 
made powerful incursions into the 
drug store market with its discount 
stores and Dot deep discount outlets, 
and Cullum, a major combination store 
operator in Dallas, opened the first 

ypermart USA, a 222,000-square- 
foot superstore selling everything 
from food, soft goods, and tires to 


sparkle and punch into their own 
stores. The year saw the entry of sev- 
eral dramatic new drug stores, includ- 
ing Longs’ Horton Plaza unit in down- 
town San Diego, Peoples’ ‘‘Boss’”’ 
prototype in the Washington market, 
and SupeRx Corp.’s racetrack store in 
Phoenix. | 

All of the new store models strived 
for an ambiance of comfort and conve- 
nience for women shoppers and for an 
image as preeminent merchants of 
health care and beauty products. 


Technology advances 


In the area of technology, several 
chains began to invest more heavily in 
sophisticated point of sale systems at 
the cash register, including Wal- 
greens, Longs, Eckerd, and the indus- 
try leader in POS, Rite Aid. (See com- 
puterization article, p. 75.) 

But while these companies were 
moving ahead in their efforts to 
achieve greater checkout efficiency 
and at the same time to capture real 
product movement on a timely basis, 
most chains remained well behind the 
leaders. The industry as a whole 
lagged at least five years and as much 
as 10 behind the supermarket field in 
POS technology.

Rite Aid (right) nabbed 356 Gray Drug Fair units in 1987, taking industry honors for the biggest acquisition of the year. F & M (left) helped its growth by buying 10 Pathmark 
Super Drug Stores in Maryland, New York and Virginia. F & M wants to operate at least 100 off-price drug and H&BA stores by 1990. 


Many takeovers mark ’87, but few were 


erger and acquisition activity 

heated up during the year, al- 

though the size of most trans- 
actions failed to match some of the pre- 
vious year’s megadeals. 

One exception, of course, was Rite 
Aid’s purchase of Gray Drug Fair, the 
troubled Cleveland-based chain, from 
Sherwin-Williams for what was con- 
sidered a bargain-basement price of 
$115 million in cash. 

In completing the purchase of Gray 
Drug Fair’s 356 stores in nine states 
and the District of Columbia, the Shir- 
emanstown, Pa.-based chain moved 
into the number one position in drug 
store count, surpassing Revco, which 
was moving in exactly the opposite di- 
rection by trimming store numbers. 

Much of the heavy activity last year 
involved market fortification on the 
one hand and strategic withdrawals on 
the other. Chains sought to increase 
their presence in markets in which 
they already held a healthy share of 
sales, and to ease themselves out of lo- 
calities dominated by others. - 

Longs and Osco, two of the nation’s 
strongest chains, engaged in mutual 
deals that got each of them out of weak- 
er markets and shored up their pres- 
ence in primary ones. 

After struggling for years to in- 
crease its penetration of Phoenix, one 
of the nation’s hottest battiegrounds, 
Longs gave up the battle last year and 
sold 10 drug stores in that capital city 
to Osco Drug, a market leader. At the 
same time, Longs sold five Tucson 
stores to Osco. 

For its part, Osco gave up its pres- 
ence in Longs’ Northern California 
stronghold by selling 11 stores to the 
Walnut Creek, Calif -hased chain. An- 
other Osco store in Colorado was also 
sold to Longs. — 

Some of the biggest potential acqui- 
sitions of the past year were still in the 
fires as this publication went to press. 

These included the sale of 358 
Brooks stores in 10 states to Hook-Su- 
peRx, and the sale of the Begley Co. to 
either Rite Aid or SupeRx Corp., the 
Phoenix-based company headed b 
— Kroger executive Gerry Wol- 

en. 

The Brooks acquisition was unusual 
in that it involved a geographic leap be- 
tween the Midwest stronghold of 
Hook-SupeRx and the Northeast mar- 


megadeals

The two opposing suitors for the 43-

standing shares. SupeRx had given an 
indication that it might raise the ante 
in the bidding war to as much as $30 a 
share. 

For Rite Aid, the acquisition would 


fill out markets in its push to blanket 
i East from New England to Flori- 
a. 

For SupeRx, an aggressive new- 
comer to the expansion wars, the ac- 
quisition would dramatically increase 
its store count. 

SupeRx began its existence by buy- 
ing 48 stores in Phoenix, Georgia, and 
Alabama from the Kroger Co., when 
the giant food and drug store operator 
decided to sell off its freestanding drug 
store business. 

In the past year, SupeRx has added 
a total of 10 drug stores and three home 
health centers to its roster, using the 
deep pockets of its Phoenix-based fi- 
nancial backer, American Continental 
Corp.

After crash-impaired 1987, stocks recover in ’88 


ctober’s stock market dive 
roduced some dramatic 
osses in drug chains’ stock 
prices, but overall, chains didn’t fare 
too badly when compared against 
year-end 1986 prices. 
The total value of drug chains’ stock 
prices at the end of 1987 was down 9 
ercent from 1986, with 1986 values 
or Medicine Shoppe and Genovese 
Drugs adjusted for comparison pur- 
poses to reflect three-for-two stock 


veloped by summer, the decline after 
October looked precipitous. 

The Drug Store News Stock Index 
showed that chains’ stocks lost 32 per- 
cent of their value from Aug. 25 to Oct. 
26, after the Oct. 19 crash. The Dow 
Jones Industrial Average lost 34 per- 
cent of its value during that time. 

Although the DJIA bottomed out 
Oct. 19, drug chain and wholesaler 
stocks didn’t bottom out until a week 
later. 


Chains values grew briskly during the first quar- 
ter of 1988. By March 25, they were 20 percent 


profits. But Perry was on the upswing 
again in 1988, and gained 77 percent in 
value from Dec. 31 to March 25. 

Arbor was down 43 percent, in a 
year when its earnings were affected 
by the costs of renovating the Sentry 
stores it acquired. But its stock also 
was gaining momentum in the new 
year, and by March 25 was up 18 per- 
cent from 1987. 

Pay ’n Save, down 37 percent, and 
Begley, down 26 percent, were others 
whose stock prices dragged as their 
earnings flagged. Pay ’n Save had to 
fight to keep its net assets to minimum 
levels, when its profits started to slide. 

And Begley’s drug store and home 


health -care business continued to be 
unprofitable. 

egley’s stock began a soaring climb 
in January this year after SupeRx and 
Rite Aid became engaged in a bidding 
war for the Kentucky chain. It closed 
at $29 on March 25. 

Although Fay’s Drug’s earnings in 
1987 continued to grow in a long run- 
ning rebound, they were still below the 
chain’s historic levels. Perhaps reflect- 
ing the long term picture, its price was 
down 29 percent from 1986. By March 
25, Fay’s year-end value had jumped 
33 percent, after the chain posted its 
seventh-consecutive quarter of earn- 
ings growth.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 11, 1988 


THE 1988 ANNUAL REPORT OF THE CHAIN DRUG INDUSTRY 


Deep discounters flexing 


their store growth muscle 


count drug retailers marked 
1987. Two of the nation’s biggest 
chains, F & M and Phar-Mor, have 
been barreling into new markets, and 
virtually doubling their store counts. 

Drug Emporium, currently the na- 
tion’s highest-volume deep discount 
drug chain as well as the chain with the 
most stores, has not been as active. 
However, its management did open 23 
stores in 1987, and they entered three 
new markets while continuing to clus- 
ter stores in existing markets. 

Among the more active chains 
emerging on a regional level: Wal- 
Mart has been expanding its Dot 
stores and now has 12 in operation; 
Rite Aid has expanded Drug Palace to 
28 stores; Melville is now up to 14 
Fredcy’s; and Woolworth now has a to- 
tal of eight Rx Places. 

In Ohio, Marbal Corp. has been 
opening more Marc’s and Bernie’s. 

There has also been some consolida- 
tion this year. F' & M has acquired the 
Supermarkets General 10-unit chain of 
Pathmark Super Drug deep discount 
drug stores, and is using it as a conduit 
into the Northeast, particularly the 
major cities of Baltimore and Washing- 
ton, D.C. The acquisition also gave 
F &M entry into upstate New York 
and easy access to Philadelphia. 

The three top-tier chains now operate 
a total of 269 stores, or about 63 percent 
of all the deep discount stores in the 
country. Together, they generate ap- 
proximately $1.6 billion in sales, about 
67 percent of all deep discount volume. 
en deep discounting first began to 


A ggressive expansion by deep dis- 


pendents in relatively depressed eco- 
nomic markets like Youngstown, Ohio; 
Chicago; Detroit; and Cleveland. 

Today, however, the deep discount 
concept has proven itself “viable.” The 
dramatic growth of Drug Emporium, 
Phar-Mor and F & M has shown the 
concept is “portable” and can flourish 
in a wide variety of different markets. 

“What we’re witnessing today is a 
legitimization of the deep discount for- 
mat,” says F & M President Frank 
Newman. 

Five years ago, most sources said 
there were only about 500 to 1,000 lo- 
cations that could support a deep dis- 
count store. Today there are already 
close to 500 deep discount stores in op- 
eration, and there is a feeling that no 
one really knows how many more can 
be opened and run profitably. 

Not all deep discount chains are 
alike, say Newman and Gary Wilber, 
executive vp of Drug Emporium. Each 
of the top three chains—F' & M, Phar- 
Mor and Drug Emporium—target, a 
slightly different niche. In some cases 
their main competitor is a food store; in 
other cases, they tailor their mix so 
they primarily attract business from 
drug and discount stores and from the 
H&BA departments of food chains. 

In the top tier, Phar-Mor, with its 
broad merchandise mix of approxi- 
mately 30,000 SKUs and its io 
40,000- to 50,000-sq.-ft. stores, is the 
least specialized aad the most general- 
ized. Its mix ineludes a broad selection 
of groceries and sundry general mer- 
chandise, as well as H&BA.

Combo operato 


one for the combo store format. 

In market after market, super- 
market chains revitalized their mar- 
keting and sales efforts with new, 
glamorous, food/drug prototypes that 
combined an appealing shopping envi- 
ronment with the convenience of one- 
stop shopping. 

More than ever, supermarket retail- 
ers are committed to the food/drug for- 
mat as the expansion vehicle of choice. 
Said Charles Collings, resident of 
combo pioneer Raley’s in Sacramento: 
“We feel we have to have a pharmacy 
to have a complete store. It’s part of 
our overall concept from the begin- 
ning, anywhere we open.” 

“We try to open with a pharmacy 
wherever we open a new store,” added 
a spokesperson for Vons. 

ecent months have also seen an up- 
surge in supermarket chain consolida- 
tion through mergers and acquisitions, 
so that the retail pie is being sliced not 
only in larger pieces, but in different 
ways. The result: enormous gains in 
market penetration and geographic 
reach by some supermarket retailers 
like Vons Companies, and a wholesale 
cutback in market penetration by for- 
mer giants like Safeway Stores. 

Either way, the forces of consolida- 
tion and expansion mean powerful 
competition for the chain drug store in- 
dustry. Safeway, for instance, aban- 
doned some of its biggest markets over 
the past year, along with more than 
150 stores with pharmacies. But a host 
of other supermarket and combo store 
operators have leaped into the vacuum 
by snapping up former Safeway loca- 
tions, including Cullum Cos., Albert- 
son’s, Vons, Bormans, and Minyard. 

In most cases, the change could spell 
new problems for local drug store com- 

titors in markets like Dallas/Ft. 

orth, Oklahoma City, and Kansas 
City, as the drug chains and indepen- 
dents shift strategies to deal with new, 
perhaps more powerful adversaries 
unburdened by the problems that dog- 
ged Safeway. To many, it must seem 
ke fighting against the mythological 
Hydra: cut off one head, and two new 
a instantly in its place. 

“We knew what we were up against 
with Safeway,” noted one chain drug 
executive. “If an operator comes in 
with a more aggressive pharmacy mar- 
keting program, we might have a 
tougher time against them.”

ciently. Earlier this year, the chain an- 


nounced it would close one of its seven 
facilities: its 228,000-square-foot cen- 
ter in Hammond, La. 

Management said the closing would 
help the chain improve its “efficiency” 
in servicing its stores. The 165 stores 
that the Hammond unit had serviced 
will now be serviced by three DCs in 
Atlanta, Houston, and Dallas. 

One source said the closing was a 
form of “consolidation” for Eckerd. 
“They’ve eliminated the expense of 
running a major facility,” he said, “and 
they’re now using three centers in- 
stead of four to service their stores. 
Assuming the three centers were un- 
der-utilized and have the capacity to 
service the stores efficiently, it should 
be a good move.” 

wo a ty sources, the average 
drug chain hasn’t been able to operate 
its warehouses as consistently as drug 
wholesalers. 

The higher volume drug wholesalers 
can generally maintain a 92 percent to 


98 percent in-store service level for 
their customers, but most chain drug 
warehouses, sources say, operate 
around an 80 percent or lower rate. 

There are exceptions, however. The 
warehouses run by Walgreens, CVS 
and Rite Aid stores are considered 
= above average for the industry, 
and sources say their stores are seldom 
ever out of stock on any warehouse 
item. 

Last year, CVS opened its first 
warehouse facility outside the East 
Coast: a 190,000-square-foot facility in 
Rancho Cucamonga, Calif. CVS’s 
—— says the new facility can 
lig coc support CVS’s expansion in 
its California markets for at least an- 
other five years. 

Delivery time has been shortened at 
these stores from seven days to five, 
but most stores are still getting just 
one delivery a week. 

“We basically traded off hauling ex- 


penses for the expense of warehousing 
in California,” said one source. 

CVS now has 49 stores in California, 
and plans to open another 100 stores 
over the next five years. 

CVS also {pong to open another 
warehouse in New Jersey, either later 
this year or early in 1989. The new fa- 
cility will be about 400,000 square feet, 
and will be able to service about 200 
more stores within a radius of about 
150 miles. 

Management says CVS isn’t plan- 
ning to add any new technology to its 
new warehouse. “Our systems are 
pretty advanced,” said one source, 
‘and we’re at the point where we’re 
getting what we need.” CVS currently 
moves close to 90 percent of its entire 
merchandise mix through its ware- 
houses. 

Walgreens, with a broader mix than 
CVS, moves about 70 percent of its 
products through its six warehouses. 


The average warehousing chain 
moves between 60 percent and 70 per- 
cent of its mix through its own ware- 
houses, and sources estimate the aver- 
age chain warehouse turns its 
inventory about four or fives times a 
year. 

CVS and Walgreens have not re- 
vealed how often they turn their inven- 
tories, but some sources estimate they 
probably turn them about eight or nine 
times a year. CVS could get as many as 
10 or 11 turns a year, one source esti- 
mated. 

Sources say, however, that the deep 
discount chains that warehouse have 
the highest turns. This is because their 
warehouses don’t really stock prod- 
uct—they just break large shipments 
down into smaller shipments that then 
are sent out to all their stores. 

F & M operates this way, and so 
does Rock Bottom and Duane Reade.

Some conventional drug chains also

Chains score breakthroughs in retail automation 


F or even the smallest drug chains, 
automation has become a buzz- 
word in the 1980s. More than 
two-thirds of all drug chains will have 
chainwide pharmacy computers in op- 
eration by the end of the year, accord- 
ing to a recent Drug Store News sur- 
vey, and many will also have converted 
their front-end checkstand registers to 
~—_ automated point-of-sale systems. 

he benefits that pharmacy comput- 
ers have conferred on the profession 
are undisputed. Even chains that held 
off for many years on pharmacy auto- 
mation—Osco is one example—are 
now moving quickly to install the sys-

THE 1988 ANNUAL REPORT OF THE CHAIN DRUG INDUSTRY

EERFIELD, Ill. — When 
Wall Street came crashing to 
earth last October, and the na- 
tion’s economy shook in its aftermath, 
Walgreen Co. barely broke stride. In- 
stead, its top executives battled reces- 
sionary fears head-on by drawing up 
plans to spend a record $160 million 
this year for expansion and moderniza- 
tion efforts, a 30 percent increase in 
expenditures over prior-year levels. 
n January, the chain also revealed 
lans to remain on a fast-growth track 
‘across America”, in the words of its 
chairman, Charles Walgreen III. “Our 
objective is to open 100 stores a year 
for the foreseeable future, and also 
go good acquisitions—ones that 
it our growth strategy and store pro- 
file,” Culenees told shareholders at 
the company’s annual meeting. 

The chain has been in high gear for 
more than three years, adding more 
than 400 new stores, cracking the New 
England market with its purchase of 
Medi Mart, boosting its strength in 
dozens of major markets, and growing 
its store base by a third, to nearly 1,400 
units. It has also remodeled more than 
100 stores a year to stay in retailing’s 
front ranks. 

Walgreens also continues to outpace 
the drug store industry in sales and 
profitability, ending fiscal year 1987 
with $4.2 billion in sales, and net earn- 
ings of $103.5 million. A major part of 
that comes from its prescription busi- 
ness, the largest in the U.S. Rx sales at 
Walgreens grew nearly 30 percent last 
year, to $1.1 billion. 


A half-billion bucks for expansion 


In all, the chain has spent more than 
$500 million over the past five years to 
expand its market reach from coast to 
coast, boost market share around the 
country, modernize marketing and op- 
erations, and improve store decor, lay- 
out and merchandising. 

Those expenditures have borne a lot 
of fruit. With the Medi Mart purchase, 
Walgreens was able to crack an entire 
new region with a strong initial market 
presence in Boston and elsewhere, and 
provide a base for future expansion. 
7 a Fred Canning 
predicted the opening of as many as 
100 new stores in the Northeast in the 
next few years, adding: “The real 
problem now with that market for us is 
that we’re shipping out of our Orlando 
warehouse to su ply the former Medi 
Mart stores, and it’s costing us about 
two percentage _— in gross profits 
in those stores. We need a distribution 
center there.” 

In many other markets, meanwhile, 
the chain has boosted its presence and 
economies of scale with new stores and 
acquisitions. 

“With our store growth and stron 
merchandising efforts, we increase 
penetration in 19 of our top 20 markets 


“Our objective is to open 100 stores a year,” says chairman Charles Walgreen, III. 


last year, and in 80 percent of all Wal- 
green markets around the country,” 
said Walgreen. “Today, Walgreens 
ranks first or second in 38 of our top 56 
markets.” 

The $160 million in capital outlays this 
year will go into new stores, possible ac- 
quisitions and retail technology, includ- 
ing the e ion of its Walgreen Infor- 
mation Network (WIN). The WIN 
program, which will link stores, offices, 
distribution centers, and photofinishing 
labs under a computerized communica- 
tions and processing umbrella, will be in 
place chainwide by the early 1990s, ac- 
cording to the company. en it is, it 
will give store managers and headquar- 
ters merchandising and operations ex- 
ecutives a powerful new tool for boost- 
ing profi tability and speeding decision- 
making. 

POS ‘WINS’ out 


WIN also provides a technology and 
communications base for point-of-sale 
systems, including checkstand scan- 
ning. Walgreens has begun installing 
scanners in its stores in Fort Wayne, 
Indiana, with eventual plans for a 
chainwide rollout within the next four 
years. The goals, according to execu- 
tives, will be faster checkouts, firm 


control of prices from the register, im- 
proved inventory control and labor 
savings. 

“WIN’s most visible application is 
point-of-sale scanning,’ Walgreen 
said. “Scanning was tested in Chicago 
this year and productivity gains were 
— 

algreens is also investing millions 
in its new Strategic murat Man- 
agement System, or SIMS. The sys- 
tem is designed to reduce inventory 
levels at every point in the distribution 
of merchandise within the company 
pratige: » maximum efficiency in buy- 
ing, distribution, display, and alloca- 
tion of product in the stores. 

Walgreens’ bold growth strategy in 
the face of an uncertain economy befits 
its position as the nation’s leading drug 
chain. At the same time, however, the 
chain’s decision to spend record 
amounts on store expansion, expen- 
sive new retail technology, and store 
modernization is an acknowledgement 
that tough times call for tough and ag- 
gressive measures. 


A defensive growth posture 


That is as true for Walgreens— 
which is committed to maintaining a 
leading or dominant position in many 
of the nation’s biggest markets coast to 
coast—as it is for any small, belea- 
guered regional retailer. Walgreens’ 
aggressive growth posture and com- 
mitment to high-tech retailing are a 
defense against a host of new competi- 
tive forces as well as an opportunistic 
move to capitalize on its own market 
Se and image. 

Walgreens’ chairman admitted as 
much, predicting the $4 billion drug 
chain “will have the wind more in our 
face that at our back in the years 
ahead.” He also downplayed the signif- 
icance of a 42 percent jump in net earn- 
ings in the first quarter of fiscal 1988.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 11, 1988 


81 


THE 1988 ANNUAL REPORT OF THE CHAIN DRUG INDUSTRY 


PROFILES 


WINSBURG, Ohio — Just one 

year ago, Revco D.S. was quitea 

different company. Although 
the 2,000-store drug chain had just 
emerged from a leveraged buyout as a 
debt-laden, private corporation, its 
management, organizational struc- 
ture, and general operating principles 
remained essential y those which had 
guided the company for many years. 

Unforeseen by veteran Revco exec- 
utives, however, the buyout set the 
stage for the most wrenching changes 
in Reveo’s history. Those changes, in- 
cluding the departure of co-founder 
and chief executive Sid Dworkin, have 
fundamentally altered every facet of 
the retail giant, from its top and middle 
management team to the way it runs 
its stores. 

The buyout was engineered by 
Dworkin, president Bill Edwards, and 
a group of heavily capitalized outside 
investors to take the company out of 
the reach of hostile raiders and turn it 
back into a profitable cash producer, 
away from the scrutiny of the share- 
holding public. But its cost, $1.45 bil- 
lion, immediately put the firm under 
heavy pressure to service its debt oy 
continuing store operations, and wit 
the quick sale of non-drug-store as- 
sets. 

The LBO had another effect, as well. 
It diluted the decision-making power 
of Revco’s upper management team by 
opening the board of i rectors to rep- 
resentatives of the investment firms 
that had financed the deal, thus shift- 
ing the balance of power. Along with 
the pressing needs of Revco’s $150 mil- 
lion annual debt load, the new board 
members themselves put pressure on 
the company to turn operations around 
quickly, reduce debt, and regain prof- 
itability. 

Last year, Revco’s new board lost no 
time asserting itself. Faced with in- 
tense pressure to reduce its debt ser- 
vice costs, the company launched a 
concerted effort to divest itself of vir- 
tually all assets other than the drug 
stores and the Odd-Lot closeout retail 
division. As part of the original LBO fi- 
nancing agreement, the firm also put 
Odd-Lot on a short leash, giving it a 
tight deadline in which to raise profit 
levels or face divestiture. 

Since that time, the company has 
sold several of its 10 non-retail divi- 
sions and will complete all divestitures 
this year, ahead of the schedule im- 
posed by its buyout agreement, ac- 
cording to chief financial officer Vito 


Cardace. Early this year, Revco also 
threw in the towel on Odd-Lot, and is 
reportedly near an agreement to sell 
the 153 Odd-Lot stores and distribu- 
tion center to an unnamed bidder. 

But the biggest changes at Revco 
have come within the core drug store 
division itself. Those changes began 
one year ago, with the appointment of 
Revco president Bill Edwards to suc- 
ceed Dworkin as chief executive, the 
departure of veteran Revco chief fi- 
nancial officer R. Carroll Hudson, and 
the election of three new, independent 
directors of Reveo and its new parent 
company, Anac Holding Corp. Dwor- 
kin remained as board chairman, relin- 
quishing his role in day-to- day man- 
agement of the giant chain. 

Although characterized at the time 
as a “consensus” move on the part of in- 
side managers and outside directors, 
the shift in top management reflected 
the growing involvement of Revco’s 
new majority stockholder, D.S. Part- 
ners, as well as other outside directors 
on the nine-member board. 

More sweeping changes were to fol- 
low, however. Last summer, Revco 
announced its decision to sell the 45- 
store Carls Drug chain in upstate New 
York, for which it had paid $35 million 
in fiscal 1986. At the same time, the 
chain was cutting back on previous ex- 
pansion plans, targeting some 100 
stores for sale and urging store manag- 
ers to boost profit levels through new 
performance goals and bonus plans. 
“We are challenging people to do a bet- 
ter job,” Edwards said at the time. 

Bolstered by upgraded manage- 
ment information systems and en- 
hanced point-of-sale tracking abilities, 
the chain put the spotlight on under- 
performing stores in the Southeast and 
other areas. 

That intense performance review 
continues in all Revco markets, along 
with an ongoing expense control pro- 
gram. Recently, the chain announced 
that an unspecified number of stores 
will be sold by the end of this summer, 
either because they don’t meet new 
performance standards or because 
they operate in marginal markets 
which the chain has decided to aban- 
don. 

Revco’s cutbacks have had another 
effect, as well. Last fall, Rite Aid 
edged out Revco as the nation’s big- 
gest drug chain in terms of store count, 

llowing that chain’s purchase of Gray 
Drug Fair and Revco’s reduction in 
store totals to its current level of 2,010. 


Revco buyout brings major changes to company 


Revco D.S. is re-emphasizing its core pharmacy franchise and convenience image. 


Along with intensified performance 
reviews and cost-cutting efforts, Rev- 
co’s new board spearheaded a major 
overhaul of top and middle manage- 
ment last year. Longtime executives 
such as vp-MIS Scott Leeseberg and 
vp-marketing Neil Roth left the com- 
pany, and others, including Ellis 
Jones, were reassigned. Jones went 
from divisiona: merchandise manager 
to director of purchase order systems. 

Meanwhile, new posts, including vp- 
sales promotion and vp-inventory 
management, were created .v enhance 
corporate control of marketing and 
merchandising. Last year’s executive 
sweep culminated in September, with 
the induction of former Dayton Hud- 
son president and chief operations offi- 
cer Boake Sells as Revco’s new chair- 
man and chief executive. Capping the 
end of an era, 66-year-old Sid akin 
and his son Mare. who had served as 
executive vp, left the company, and 
Edwards returned to his earlier role as 
president and chief operations officer. 

Sadly, 1987 also marked the passing 
of chain drug industry veteran Henry 
“Hy” Gray, who spent his last 19 years 
at Revco as administrative vp, and lat- 
er as vice chairman of the board. 

Sells’ appointment, meanwhile, sig- 
naled the onset of a more sophisticat- 
ed, broad-based operating structure at 
Revco, and the completion of a sweep- 
ing management overhaul. Backed 
firmly by the board, the 50-year-old 
executive moved quickly to install his 
own hand-picked management team 
and turn the company around.

serving customers.

that, said Sells, will require better in- 
stock positions, faster checkout, more 
continuity in merchandise selection, 
and improved customer service. 

“There are going to be a lot more 
changes at Revco,” Sells told Drug 
Store News recently. “What those 
are a will be is impossible to say. 
But I do know that we can serve the 
customer a whole helluva lot better.”

Eckerd buyout on track; chain sells some assets 


LEARWATER, Fla. — Eck- 

erd Drug’s leveraged buyout 

has sailed into its third year, 
buoyed by cash flow from a smaller 
fleet of drug stores. 

The company reported that retail 
sales were generating the necessary 
cash to cover interest expenses, and 
produce working capital. It was expect- 
ed to report 12-month sales of $2.75 bil- 
lion for the fiscal year ended Jan. 31. 

Eckerd reported to the SEC that 
nine-month sales for the period ended 
Oct. 31 were $1.93 billion. It didn’t pro- 
vide a comparison with the year-earli- 
er period, because last year the compa- 
ny had rescheduled its fiscal year, 
making comparisons difficult. 

Its last annual report was for the nine 
months ended Jan. 31, 1987. Sales for 
those months were $1.91 bilo: {t said 
third quarter sales ended Oct. 31, 1987 
were $626 million, up 13.2 percent from 
the comparable year-earlier period, 
with same-store sales up 11 percent. 

With its LBO two-years-old this 
April 30, Eckerd has essentially fol- 
lowed a program of chs bo. on its retail 
sales to pay the way. Asset sales have 
been limited, and it’s still a player in 
most of the markets it occupied as a 
public company. 

Its net store count declined 2 per- 
cent as it ended the year with 1581 
units, compared to the 1611 stores it 
had Jan. 1987. An Eckerd spokesman 
said new store openings for fiscal 1987 
were in line with the 40 to 50 new

Typical of its promotional programs 
on health care, it began promoting an

launched an arthritis care program.

THE 1988 ANNUAL REPORT OF THE CHAIN DRUG INDUSTRY

ALNUT CREEK, Calif. — 

Longs Drug Stores opened 

this past fiscal year with its 
sights focused sharply on profit im- 
provement. 

The result: the chain ended several 
years of relatively flat earnings with 
its best performance ever. 

Net earnings for the year rose 28 
percent to $49.2 million, as sales in- 
creased 8 percent to $1.77 billion. 

In posting these results, Longs in- 
creased its net profit margin by a full 
four-tenths of a point, to 2.8 percent, 
an extremely potent result by industry 
standards. Sales per store rose to 
$7.74 million, the industry’s best. 

Longs’ performance was robust all 
year, but in the fourth quarter, which 
included the Christmas selling season, 
the results were outstanding. Profits 
jumped 34 percent to $15.1 million 
from $11.3 million, as sales increased 6 
percent to $497 million. 

Longs attributed the fourth quarter 
gains to increases in sales and gross 
margins and a reduction in income tax- 
es. 
That was the simple explanation. 
The fact was that from the beginning of 
the year Longs undertook a total eval- 
uation of every aspect of its business 
with an eye to improving performance 
in all areas. 

Indefensible markets were aban- 
doned and weaker stores were closed 
or sold off. A good training program 
was made even better, as customer 
service and convenience were reaf- 
firmed as top objectives. Cost contain- 
ment became a top drawer priority. 
And even more attention was given to 
adapting the merchandise mix to par- 
ticular markets and stores. 

Additionally, Longs began to inves- 
tigate an increase in the amount of 
merchandise shipped through its dis- 
tribution centers as a step toward pos- 
sible economies through larger-scale 
purchases. 

Fifteen to 20 percent of Longs’ mer- 
chandise is currently handled through 
one of its four small distribution cen- 
ters, two in Southern California, one in 
Hayward, Calif., and one in Hawaii. 
Most of the merchandise handled by 
these centers are promotional goods, 
but Hayward also has some staples. 

Longs appointed a five-member 
committee to consider expanding its 
distribution center activities, and that 
committee was due to report this year. 
Chain officials made it clear, however, 
that even if there were an increase in

Store manager automony has been a

deal with Osco involving the mutual

From Osco, Longs purchased 11 
stores in Northern California and one 
in Colorado. In turn, the Oak Brook, 
Ill.-based drug chain bought 10 stores 
in Phoenix and five stores in Tucson 
from Longs. 

Longs benefited from the greater 
penetration in its Northern California 
stronghold as well as from getting out 
of an extremely competitive market in 
which it had never been able to achieve 
a dominant position. Osco shored up 


its already strong position in Phoenix. 


More recently Longs sold two stores 
in outpost markets that the chain had 
never developed. The two stores, one 
in Bend, Ore., and the other in Yuma, 
Ariz., went to Pay Less NW.

expects to continue its torrid 

growth pace in 1988 with strong 
igo from its parent company Pa- 
ific Enterprises.

lanned for 1988, but Thrifty’s parent 
as made it clear the chain is also look-

could step up this growth. 

These plans continue in the same 
mode as 1987, when Thrifty added 20 
Drug and Discount stores, and 27 
Thrifty Jr. stores, bringing its total 
drug stores to 641. In 1988, Thrifty’s 
new stores will be divided equally be- 
tween the two formats. 

During the past year, Thrifty also 
added to its base of sporting goods 
stores with 42 new stores, raising this 
division to 160. 

The combined new store total in- 
creased Thrifty’s store count 13 per- 
cent, the atest increase in recent 
years.Combined, the stores produced a 
23 percent earnings increase and an 
18.5 percent sales gain, pushing the 
company to $39.5 million in net income 
on sales of $1.84 billion. Thrifty also

LEXANDRIA, Va. — Peoples 

Drug Stores, suffering a seri- 

ous outbreak of red ink in 1986, 
took a stiff dose of healing medicine 
last year. It seems to have worked. 

In the fiscal year that ended in De- 
cember, Peoples said it achieved an op- 
erating profit, compared to a loss the 
previous year. Moreover, there are 
signs that the chain’s recovery has only 
just begun. Shopper count, down as 
much as 4 to 5 percent during Peoples’ 
doldrums, is now on the upswing. The 
average customer transaction is up 8 to 
9 percent. Comparable sales in the four 
new “Boss” prototype stores have ris- 
en 18 percent. 

The change in fortune for the 820- 
store chain is the result of a top-to-bot- 
tom overhaul that took place in 1987 fol- 
lowing Peoples’ plunge. The changes 
were orchestrated by David Bloom, 
chairman of Imasco Retailing Group, 
which includes Peoples as well as Cana- 
da’s Shoppers Drug Mart, and David Ei- 
senberg, Peoples’ senior executive vp 
and chief operations officer. The trans- 
formation has touched every phase of 
business from human resources to mar- 
keting to operations to real estate. 

As part of its total makeover, Peoples 
sold or closed underperforming units in 
weaker markets, including 12 in Balti- 
more, eight in North Carolina and 15 
others in minor markets. Peoples has 
also sold off operations that are no long- 
er central to its new emphasis on core 
drug store retailing, including its B.H. 
Krueger manufacturing subsidiary and 
its five small Smiles card and gift shops. 
The chain expects to sell or close 10 to 15 
additional stores this year. 

To offset the loss of those stores, 
about 30 new units will open this year, 
according to chain officials, but no ma- 
jor acquisitions are planned. The 

owth will occur in markets in which 

eoples already is firmly entrenched. 
hile the influence of Shoppers 
Drug Mart, Peoples’ Canadian sister 
chain under Imasco, has been felt at 
the Alexandria, Va.-based chain, it has 
not been dominant. Bloom, who is also 
chairman and ceo of Shoppers, said the 
idea never was to make Peoples an 
identical twin of the Canadian chain 
but to create synergisms between the 
two operations and build on the indi- 
vidual strengths of each. 

From SDM have come strengths in 

cosmetics, advertising and marketing 
lanning, according to Bloom. From 
eoples has come strengths in seasonal 
and photo department merchandising.

Both chains have strongly established

At the heart of Peoples’ transforma- 
tion is the new Boss prototype (for 
“The customer is boss”). Imasco has 
approved a heavy investment in retro- 
fitting all of the stores, and the job is 
expected to be completed by 1991. 

The newly remodeled stores feature a 
completely revised merchandise mix 
that focuses on the core categories of 
pharmacy, OTC, health & beauty aids 
and cosmetics. Baby care needs and 
photo, always a Peoples strength in its 
markets, have also been given promi- 
nence. 

While beefing up its core drug store 
image, Bicolon hae cut back on general 
merchandise categories such as house- 
wares, hardware, auto, and toys, 
which have been drastically pared to 
the top-moving products. 

In one major example of de-empha- 
sizing general merchandise, Peoples 
dropped running shoes, a $6 million in- 
ventory item, from its stores. 

David Bloom has often said that Peo- 
ples’ intention is to shed its image as a 
general store with a pharmacy and be- 
come a pharmacy with general mer- 
chandise. “We don’t want to be all 
things to all people,” he said. 

The prototype also features a fresh 
department layout that places key cat- 
egories in optimal locations for shop- 
per convenience. Thus, cosmetics and 
toiletries have been moved to the front 
of the store near the entrance. A neat, 
uncluttered look has become standard 
for Peoples stores, and so have clear 
aisle markers for in-and-out shopping 
ease. 

Service has also been reemphasized, 
io at the pharmacy (where con- 
sultation is now being given great 
weight) and in the cosmetics area. 
Many of the newly remodeled stores 
will have cosmetics service bull pens. 

The changes at Peoples have come 
partly as the reaction to a consumer 
study that Peoples conducted at the 
beginning of last year. The research 
found that customers put convenience 
at the top of their list in terms of drug 
store shopping priorities. The re- 
search also discovered that Peoples 
had a high-price image with shoppers. 

To overcome this image and to meet 
increased competition from food and 
drug combo operators like Giant 
Foods, Peoples has cut its overall 
gross margin by 2 full percentage 
points, according to Bloom. The new 
price strategy also includes beefing up

withtwo stores in New York; Mid-At-

stores, we get the benefit of the traffic, 
and in our neighborhood stores, it’s 
convenience and service. 

“We pay attention to the details of 
our business, and that’s what I think 
makes us so successful.”

Perry lightens up on the road to recovery 


ONTIAC, Mich. — Fiscal 1987 

was a year the people at Perry 

Drug Stores would just as soon 
forget. The upper Midwest’s largest 
drug chain reported a net loss of $7.9 
million—the first in its 31-year histo- 
ry—as the high costs of its rapid ex- 
pansion in recent years, combined with 
shrinking gross margins, overtook 
earnings momentum. 

The profit crunch touched off a year of 
wrenching changes at Perry and a com- 
plete re-examination of its strategic di- 
rection. Ina very short time, in fact, the 
chain has reversed its expansion-orient- 
ed strategy, revamped its merchandise 
mix in favor of basic drug store mer- 
chandise, abandoned its 252-store auto 


Perry registers loss 
(Millions of dollars) 


Fiscal year ended Oct. 31. 


Source: Company reports. 7.90 


" 


Softer-than-expected sales in its drug and auto parts stores contributed to Perry’s losses. 


parts division, drastically cut headquar- 
ters staff and almost completely re- 
structured its management team. 

In the process, many of its veteran 
senior executives, including Al Wan- 
der, Don Fox, Mickey Kole and John 
Frazzini, have left the company. Oth- 
ers have been reassigned. 

The sweeping management changes 
began with the retirement early last 
year of longtime Perry veteran Don 
Fox as president and chief operations 
officer, and the appointment, last 
June, of retail veteran David Schwartz 
to take his place. 

Schwartz has realigned drug store 
operations into four groups, and also 
taken direct charge of support func- 
tions like distribution, security, mer- 
chandising, and advertising. His goal: 
a leaner, more responsive structure 
that is more in tune with local markets. 

“Our new organization has given 


each group flexibility to tailor strate- 
gies to the conditions in the respective 
market area,” Schwartz said recently. 

Perry’s problems, which emerged 
despite record sales last year of $726 
million, were due to a confluence of fac- 
tors. Softer-than-expected sales in its 
drug and auto parts stores, including a 
same-store sales gain of only 3 percent 
in drug stores, certainly contributed to 
the loss. High operating costs; reduced 
margins on prescription drugs; and 
other products in a heavily contested 
home market were also among the con- 
tributing factors. 

At the front end, Perry’s decision to 
abandon high-ticket general merchan- 
dise in favor of a more basic drug store 
mix cut into gross profits. Meanwhile, 
the auto parts division had been ham- 
pered. Pressured by a heavy debt load 
and a softening auto aftermarket, the 
company struck a deal to sell its 252 


Auto Works units to Northern Auto- 
motive Corp. early this year for $51 
million in cash. The deal resulted in a 
one-time charge against earnings of 
roughly $11 million in the first quarter, 
but cut the company’s $160 million 
debt by nearly a third, 

Perry’s departure from auto parts 
retailing—including plans to phase 
auto supplies out of its drug stores— 
also leaves the company free “to con- 
centrate its efforts in drug stores and 
health care,” according to company 
spokesman Berl Falbaum. 

With its load lightened, Perry is 
moving quickly to turn itself around as 
a leaner, more concentrated drug store 
retailer. The chain has developed a 
store prototype for the 1990s which 
emphasizes service, shopping excite- 
ment and a high-volume, concentrated 
merchandise mix. The company has 
also shifted away from new store open- 
ings in favor of upgrading and remod- 
eling existing stores in line with the 
new format.

come back.”

F &M’s growth has come rapidly, but 
only after extensive preparation. In 
1986, Newman instituted a series of 
steps designed to beef up the chain’s 
organizational structure in support of 
an accelerated growth strategy. Then 
and now, Newman’s goal was to oper- 
ate at least 100 off-price drug and 
H&BA stores by 1990. 

To gear up for its growth from a re- 


gional operator in Southern Michigan 
into a multi-state retail power, the 
chain boosted internal operating con- 
trols, doubled its warehouse space and 
added to its headquarters and store 
management staff. Newman also 
spearheaded the development of a 
tighter, more focused F&M store pro- 
totype, with greater control by head- 
quarters over merchandising and fix- 
turing, and a far tighter mix. 

In so doing, Newman and other 
planners stripped the stores down to 
their essential ingredients: H&BAs, 
cosmetics, household products, snack 
foods and a few other core categories. 
They eliminated most electronics, 
toys, hardware and other “fringe” cat- 
egories in favor of a more concentrated 
image to draw, with a clear message, 
the upper-middle-income, — fe- 
male shoppers F&M cultivates. Phar- 
macies are present in about half the 
chain’s stores, but only where market 
conditions justify them.

Arbor lays groundwork for Michigan market gains 


ROY, Mich. — Arbor Drugs’ 

central offices are much like Ar- 

bor drug stores: strikingly clean 
and uncluttered, visually appealing 
and colorful. Both reflect the tastes 
and retail philosophy of Arbor’s 
founders, chairman and chief execu- 
tive Eugene Applebaum and president 
Max Ernst. 

At Arbor’s spacious new headquar- 
ters, the almost minimalist decor 
serves to highlight a serious collection 
of modern art, which is Applebaum’s 
passion. In the company’s spotless 
drug stores, the wide, clutter-free 
aisles, bright colors and tight mer- 
chandise focus highlight one of the 
most appealing and effective store for- 
mats in the industry. 

Arbor’s approach—staying close to 
the business and merchandise it knows 
best, with full service, attractive 
stores and competitive pricing—has 
produced a high-volume store format 
and moved the chain into strong sec- 
ond place in Southeastern Michigan 
drug retailing, just behind Perry Drug 
Stores. The chain is well ahead of the 
industry average in per-store sales, at 
$3 million plus; in sales per square foot, 
at $336; and in average inventory 
turns, at 6.5. 

The purchase in 1986 of 19 Sentry 
Drug Stores—17 of which were kept 
open and extensively remodeled—also 
helped boost total sales 42.1 percent in 


INTRODUCING 


1987, to $215.3 million. The Sentry 
purchase and renovations also put a 
drag on earnings last year, however, 
with net down to $5.2 million from $5.4 
million in 1986. 

“Last year we spent the entire year 
absorbing our acquisition of Sentry, 
including the disposal of acquired in- 
ventory, remodeling costs and em- 
ployee training,” Applebaum noted re- 
cently. The result, he said, will be an 
earnings rebound beginning this year 
as the former Sentry stores come on- 
stream and contribute. 


Net income up 


In fact, the Sentry purchase and 
renovation appears to be bearing fruit 
quickly. Converted units (virtually all 
have been renovated) are reportedly 


D 


producing sales gains averaging 20 
percent this year, and profits are ris- 
ing. 

Net income for the first quarter rose 
31.2 percent for the 76-store chain, to 
$1.4 million. Included were the remod- 
eled Sentry units, which Applebaum 
said made a “positive contribution” to 
first-quarter results. 

One key measure of Arbor’s underly- 
ing strength—despite escalating oper- 
ating expenses and Michigan’s fiercely 
competitive marketplace—has been 
continued healthy results in seasoned 
stores. Same-store sales were up a 
strong 9.3 percent last year, fueled by 
Arbor’s increasing name recognition, 
strong photofinishing sales, aggressive 
advertising, convenience-oriented mer- 
chandising , and other factors. 


Ep 


(MOK 


“This is still a convenience business 
of low prices and basic merchandise,” 
Arbor’s chairman is fond of saying. 
“We're still dealing with a customer 
who’s looking for essential items and a 
quick, easy trip into the drug store.” 

Arbor’s leaders say the chain will 
have little trouble growing steadily by 
10 units a year in Michigan, and he en- 
visions a 150-unit operation in that 
state within the next several years.

competition in our home market that 
other chains are just now being hit 
with in other parts of the country,”

discounters and the deep discounters 
and the powerful combo operators, and 
we've established our niche.” 

“We happen to love Michigan as a 
market,” Applebaum said last year. 
The economy is diversifying, the out-

portunity left within our advertising 
umbrella for fill-in expansion.”

for deal A ge and improved inven- 
tory control, say its leaders.

ELVILLE, N. Y. — 
Exhilarated by re- 
cord sales and earn- 


ings achieved in fiscal year ’88, 
Genovese Drug Stores is push- 
ing forward with its recipe for 
success: alert management, 
stringent cost controls, aggres- 
sive merchandising, and store 
renovation. 

“This is just the beginning,” 
said Don Gross, vp-marketing. 

“We’re most proud of our 
12.2 percent comparable-store 
increase in sales and the fact 
that our customer count is up 9 


percent,” Gross continued, cit- 
ing such strategies as aggres- 
sive advertising, seasonal cou- 
pon books and an “excellent 
Christmas catalog” as getting 
the customers into the stores. 

Renovation and enlarge- 
ment of established neighbor- 
hood stores contributed to sales 
increases of from 30 to 35 per- 
cent for those units, he said, 
and that renovation and en- 
largement program will contin- 
ue in 88. 

Genovese alsc expects to 
open eight to 10 newstores this 


year, after opening only four 
units in 1987, partly because of 
construction snags. The new 
stores, in the 11,000-12,000- 
square-foot format, will all be 
located in current market ar- 
eas, especially in Brooklyn and 
Long Island. 

Genovese is breathing a cor- 
porate sigh of relief now that its 
155,000-square-foot distribu- 
tion center, opened in August 
1985, is operating efficiently. 
“The balance of 1985 was 
tough,” Gross acknowledged.

Big B bestowed 4 record year in ’87; lives up to its name 


ESSEMER, Ala. — 

Big B lived up to its 

name in 1987, finishing 
the F gid in a big way, with re- 
cord sales, earnings and store 
openings. 

Year-end earnings shot up 
62.8 percent, to a record $7.3 
million, on sales of $248.6 mil- 
lion, an 18.5 percent increase. 

Alabama’s largest chain 
rolled out a record 33 drug 
stores, for a store count of 188, 
including seven Drugs for 
Less deep discounters and 
five home health care centers. 
Plans are to maintain a rapid 
expansion pace in 1988 by add- 
ing 25 units, to achieve 210 


stores by year end. Expansion 
will be in all five states in Big 
B’s trade area: Alabama, F lor- 
ida, Georgia, Mississippi and 
Tennessee. 

Although Big B’s expansion 
has brought it to within 15 
miles of Atlanta, via a unit 
opened in Conyers, Ga., late 
last year, the chain has no 
plans to enter the Atlanta 
market in 1988, said Arthur 
Jones, executive vp and trea- 
surer. 

In early 1987, Big B bol- 
stered its presence in its home 
state by purchasing 13 drug 
stores from Jack Eckerd 
Corp. for an estimated $6.5

Big B keeps its customers

The typical drug store, which

high-ticket items and raised

stationery and hardware.

two years ago, which supplies

and automated sys-

and handling costs 
and increase the 
chain’s purchasing 
and storage capacity.

to roll out a POS sys-

stores to a central 
computer system. 
The system enables 
buyers to gauge ad- 
vertising effective-

quickly.

Fantle group turning Dart Drug around with cash infusion 


ANDOVER, Md. — 

Dart Drug Stores has 

stepped back from its fis- 
cal precipice, thanks to fresh 
cash infused in November by 
an investor group headed by 
Sheldon “Bud” Fantle. 

The former ceo of Peoples, 
who knows the Greater Wash- 
ington market so well, saw in 
Dart “a great opportunity.” 

His initial $8 million invest- 
ment bought him the chance to 
wrangle once more with the 
likes of Giant, Safeway, Rite 
Aid—and this time Peoples. 
He has been there before. 

He predicted then that the 
initial investment would grow 
to $20 million to $25 million 
over six months. He said more 
cash and the sale of nonper- 
forming assets would raise the 
cumulative investment figure 
to that level. 

The management team, led 
by chairman Fantle and presi- 
dent Jeffrey Fantle, has al- 
ready exceeded its promise to 
invest in Dart’s turnaround. 

Dart announced a $6 million 
stock offer last month, and 
said it will sell its 17 combina- 
tion drug store/home centers. 
Three went to F&M for more 
than $9 million. Dart then im- 
mediately sold eight leasehold 
interests for $21.4 million 
cash; seven of them were com. 
bo drug store/home centers. 

For years, market sources 
felt that these combos con- 
fused shoppers and clouded 
the image of what Dart sought 
to be in the marketplace. 

For all the efforts by the 
team of a ceo Stephen 
Hansbrough , crushing debt 
killed the chain’s cash position 
and put virtually every im- 

rovement plan on hold—as 
art 2 gled to survive. An 
initial public stock offering re- 
| some debt, but didn’t 
e P enough. 
endors clamped down on 
credit, which led to 25 percent 
out-of-stocks in 1987, a Dart 
source told Drug Store News. 
“We were headed for disaster. 
We couldn’t get shipments. 
We had no cash and no credi- 


bility,” the source added. 
Fantle, who eyed Dart on 

and off for six months before 

taking the plunge, “brings 


Dart credibility,” another 


Dart source said. 

Dart management is now 
using its fresh cash to buy in- 
ventory, reduce accounts pay- 


abie and upgrade stores. 
Stores will have a more uni- 
form approach, at about 
15,000-square-feet, and will 
emphasize prescriptions more 
than in the past. Fantle, a 
pharmacist, is expected to 
raise Dart’s script average to 
the industry norm. 


Fantle said he will place 
pharmacy computers in every 
store within two years. 

That will follow the comple- 
tion of point-of-sale installa- 
tions chainwide by mid-1988. 

Dart’s initial performance 
under new management 
showed shrinking losses on 


lower sales. The 83-store 
chain reported losses of $3.1 
million in the second quarter 
ended Jan. 31, compared to a 
$5.2 million loss in the same 
period a year earlier. Sales in 
the quarter were $63.7 million 
compared to $74.0 million for 
the same period a year ago.

create such traffic.

M & H drug business branching into new retail channels — 


EMPHIS — A re- 

vamped franchise 

program spearhead- 
ed a new commitment by Ma- 
lone & Hyde (M&H) to its 
drug business, which is an- 
chored by the 106-store Su- 
perD stores. 

Targeting 100 stores in five 
years, the franchise division 
was to open its 10th unit in 
March. It is also launching 
franchised apothecary-sized 
units under the Consumer’s 
Drug name this year. 

Besides enlisting indepen- 


dents and new store owners as 
franchisees of stores averag- 
ing 6,000 square feet, SuperD 
plans to buy some Revco and 
Eckerd stores for new franchi- 
sees. The stores—scattered 
throughout SuperD’s Mid- 
South market zone—are mar- 
ginal performers, or in mar- 
kets that are not promising for 
Revco and Eckerd, a SuperD 
source said. 

Those units will be resold to 
independent wholesale cus- 
tomers of M&H, who want the 
advantages of operating un- 


der the franchise umbrella. 
Satisfying capital needs 


The franchise push meets 
the needs of M&H’s leveraged 
buyout by allowing the drug 
division to maintain market 
share through new store 
growth that doesn’t require 
significant capital spending. It 
is also suited to market condi- 
tions. Franchises offer a com- 
petitive vehicle for what chain 
officers say is an increasing 
aumber of embattled indepen- 
dents. 


Franchising is only one of 
the new avenues through 
which MEH is pursuing drug 
growth, three years after 
management and Kohlberg, 
Kravis, and Roberts bought 
the $3 billion food and drug 
wholesaler and retailer. 

The pharmacy component 
was added to its Ike’s deep dis- 
count store format, as the first 
Ike’s was launched in Nash- 
ville in May. Ike’s two Mem- 
phis stores—retailing fixtures 
synonymous with everyday 
low prices—were also slated 


for pharmacies. 
Supermarkets seek parity 


Requests by supermarket 
customers of M&H’s whole- 
sale business led the drug divi- 
sion to put three pharmacies 
into Big Star and Piggly Wig- 
gly stores. Officers expect 
that more of the SuperD- 
owned and operated pharma- 
cies will be similarly placed, as 
the supermarkets seek com- 

etitive parity with the com- 
OS. 

M&H’s Megamarket and 
Super One super warehouse 
stores—both corporate- 
owned and franchised—also 
stood in line to receive their 
first pharmacies. 

The drug component was 
set for rollout into units in 
Louisiana, Mississippi, and 
Arkansas, as well as in three 
corporate-owned warehouse 
stores in Nashville. Officers 
predict the stores will fill 500 
to 600 daily scripts, as phar- 
macy accounts for 5 percent of 
the $800,000 to $1 million 
weekly volume. 


Refinement centinues 


SuperD has continued to re- 
fine and experiment with its 
store formats which it feels 
must provide the convenience 
its customers expect. 

The basic format features a 
center aisle running from the 
front door to the rear-of-store 
pharmacy counter. Gondolas 
are slanted toward the aisle, 
and their heights are varied to 
create maximum exposure of 
merchandise.

SupeRx Corp. sends out large ripples on drug chain pond 


HOENIX — While 

some confusion about 

the two SupeRx entities 
will probably always exist, 
there’s no confusion about the 
strides that the Phoenix- 
based version has made in the 
past year. 

Since its creation as a sepa- 
rate chain a little over a year 
ago, SupeRx Corp. has been 
sending out some rather large 
ripples from its Phoenix base. 

tarting with a small acquisi- 
tion of three Walgreens stores 
in Alabama last year, SupeRx 
has gone on to pick up seven 
more drug stores and three 
home health care centers. Now 
it is bidding to acquire Begley 
Company’s 43 drug stores, six 
home health centers and 140 
dry cleaning units. 

At se same time a ag- 
gressively pursues growth op- 
portunties, it is me taking 
steps to remake its marketing 
image with an upgraded mer- 
chandise mix, store layout and 
decor package that emphasizes 
core drug store categories and 
shopping convenience. 

he strategy is being car- 
ried out by a team headed by 
Gerald Wolken, a former 
Kroger Co. veteran who was 
ea yo of the Cincinnati- 
ased SupeRx before Kroger 
decided to sell off its free- 
standing drug store business. 

The purchasers of SupeRx 
included Rite Aid, which ac- 
quired a large chunk of SupeRx 
stores in Florida and the South- 
east; a management-invest- 
ment group that purchased the 
largest block of stores and 
formed a new company called 
Hook-SupeRx Ine. to run 
them; and Wolken’s group, 
which used money from Ameri- 
can Continental Corp., a Phoe- 
nix investment firm, to buy 48 
SupeRx stores in Arizona, 
Georgia and Alabama. 

SupeRx Corp.’s marketing 
thrust is exemplified by a new 
a that opened this past 

anuary in north Phoenix. It’s a 
racetrack store modeled on the 
highly successful unit that Su- 
pe x (Cincinnati) opened in 
ashville several years ago. 


The Phoenix SupeRx team is 
seeking to duplicate the success 
of the Nashville store in the ex- 
tremely competitive surround- 
ings of this capital city. Two 
more racetrack prototypes are 
slated to open this year. 

But SupeRx is not only fo- 
cusing attention on the rack- 


track stores. The company is 
also remodeling and remer- 
chandising a number of older 
stores. It is also rolling out a 
sleek new decor package that 
features a deep green and 
peach color scheme that has a 
distinctively Southwestern 
flavor. All stores not receiving 


major remodeling will get at 
least a freshening up of paint 
this year. 

The chain is also adding cos- 
metics consultants to many of 
its stores in an effort to service 
the all-important woman cus- 
tomer. In addition, in the re- 
modeled stores, the cosmetics 


department has been reposi- 
tioned as a boutique near the 
front entrance. The depart- 
ment has a service bullpen, 
étageres and more space on 
the wall for restige cosmet- 
ics. The aim: high visibility for 
the new upscale department 
store look.

preferred share rights

board of directors of American 
Stores, which owns Osco Drug 
and Skaggs Alpha Beta combo 
stores, recently took steps to 
protect stockholders in the 
event of a hostile takeover at- 
tempt. The company also an- 
nounced increases in sales and 
earnings for the year ended 
Jan. 30. 

The board issued one pre- 
ferred share purchase right 
for each outstanding share of 
the company’s common stock. 

In addition, the board au- 
thorized the redemption of the 
company’s existing rights, a 
move designed to assure that 
all of American Stores’ stock- 
holders receive “fair and equa! 
treatment” in the event of any 
proposed takeover and to 
guard against partial tender 
offers and other tactics to gain 
control of the —— with-

Food Shopping in Nonfood 
Stores is Growing 


Grocery shoppers say they are buying more grocery products in nonfood stores 
today than they were two years ago. Price motivates most sales 


third of all shoppers who buy 
groceries in discount stores 
say their purchases have in- 
creased in the past two years for 
the following categories: candy, 
gum, chips, snacks, non alcoholic 

everages, packaged and canned 
dry groceries, laundry detergents 
and household supplies, pet foods 
and accessories and household pa- 
per products. 

Only consumers who buy beer, 
wine & other alcoholic beverages 
in discount stores say their pur- 
chases on these items is either de- 
creasing or remaining the same. 

Just 8% say their purchases of 
alcoholic beverages in discount 
stores have increased in the past 
two years.

and household paper products.

have increased for these catego-

snacks, and beer, wine and other 
alcoholic beverages. 

One half to two-thirds of all gro- 
cery shoppers in drug and discount 
stores also say that the last time 
they purchased candy, gum, chips 
or snacks in these stores, it was 
done on impulse. 

Of the eight food and grocery

purchase category in discount

in drug stores.

Who Buys Groceries 


in Non Food Stores 


ost drug and discount 

Mi store chains that carry 

rocery products have 

been enjoying double digit growth 

in this product segment, particu- 

larly with snacks, soft drinks, and 
household cleaning products. 

But, according to Food Mer- 
chandising’s first annual study of 
consumer purchasing behavior, 
the nonfood chains have just 
scratched the surface of the gro- 
cery category’s potential for addi- 
tional growth. 

According to our study, which 
was implemented last summer by 
Lebhar-Friedman Research, just 
four out of every ten consumers 
are now buying grocery products, 
includin ie. in discount 
stores, wiile just three out of ev- 
ery ten consumers are buying 
snacks and traditional grocery 
products in drug stores. 

The study’s findings are based 
on interviews with males and fe- 
males who were responsible for at 
least half of all their household gro- 


44% of all consumers buy 
groceries in discount stores and 
31% buy them in drug stores. 


cery purchases. 

Our survey found that there is 
enormous potential for pnt ae. 
grocery purchases in nonfoo 
stores. 


Frequency of Grocery 
Shopping is Low 


Currently more than half of all 
grocery shoppers, 56%, are not 
shopping discount stores for food 
and grocery products, and an even 
higher portion of the grocery buy- 
ing public, 69%, or two-thirds of all 
consumers, are not shopping for 
groceries in drug stores. 

In addition, even though four 
out of every ten shoppers do buy 
groceries in discount stores and 
three out of ten buy them in drug 
stores, these shoppers are not 
making grocery purchases as often 


as they could and should be doing. 

And this is primarily because 
neither drug nor discount stores 
are doing an adequate job of inspir- 
ing food and grocery purchases on 
a frequent basis. 

Among shoppers who buy gro- 
ceries in discount stores, just one 
in ten (25%) say they make grocery 
purchases in their local discount 
stores at least once a week or 
more. 

And drug stores, which are 
more convenient to most shoppers 
than discount stores, do an even 
worse job with their shoppers. 
Just (19%) of all grocery buying 
drug store — say they make 
a grocery purchase in their local 
drug stores at least once a week. 


Lack of Consistency 
A Problem 


From interviews with consum- 
ers and buyers of grocery products 
for nonfood chains, F'm has indica- 
tions that part of the problem is in- 
consistent merchandising of the

ary and Dollar Day specials, and 
packaged commodity items like 
juices and cake mixes or facial tis- 
sues at varying seasonal periods.

Regional shopping patterns 


F'm’s first annual consumer grocery purchasing survey also found that 
there are regional differences in the way consumers shop for groceries. 

Consumers living in the south are the most likely to egies groceries in 
discount stores (56% do) while consumers living in the northeast are the 
least likely to buy eries in discount stores (just 27% do). 

Consumers who live in the west are the most likely to buy groceries in 
drug stores (37% do). But in the midwest, just 26% of all shopped say they 
buy groceries in drug stores. 

oth drug and discount stores also sell more groceries to more affluent 
customers, to the households with incomes of $25,000 and above. Shopping 
at non food stores for grocery items is significantly less likely, the study 
found, among consumers with incomes of less than $25,000.

dising.

McKee retires after 10 yrs. with Harco 


NORTHPORT, Ala. — Russell (Russ) McKee, head 
buyer at Harco Drug, retired April 1 after 10 years with 
the Alabama-based chain. 

McKee handled the buying of electrical appliances, sun- 
dries, candy, housewares, hardware, notions, and ho- 
siery. Frank Gable, vp-sales, said Harco has effected a 
smooth transition in which buying responsibilities have 
been realigned and one buyer has been added. Keith Con- 
nell continues as director of purchasing. 


Mirmelstein buying Revco cosmetics 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Revco has named John Mirmel- 
stein as senior buyer, cosmetics and fragrances.“We’re 
pleased to add John’s strong purchasing and merchandis- 
ing background in cosmeties and H&BA to our revitalized 
marketing and purchasing efforts,” said Jeffrey Doshan, 
Revco’s vp-general maichondliar manager. Mirmelstein, 
42, was most recently a divisional merchandise manager at 
Gray Drug Fair, where he was employed for five years.

Shewmaker named director at Vons 


EL MONTE, Calif. — Vons has named Jack Shew- 
maker, former vice chairman and chief financial officer at 
Wal-Mart, to its board of directors. The 193-store chain 
said Shewmaker’s retail and supermarket experience will 
be an additional asset to Vons board. Although Shew- 
maker remains on the board of Wal-Mart, he announced 
his retirement from the discounter on Feb. 1.

Lucky rejects American’s offer 


DUBLIN, Calif. — Lucky 
Stores Inc. rejectedas “inade- 
quate” American Stores’ $45 

er share tender offer for 

ucky’s common stock and 
said it is considering alterna- 
tives, including a reorganiza- 
tion to focus on its California 
operations, aleveragedrecap- 
italization, or sale of the com- 
pany to a third party. 

The California-based gro- 
cerychainalsorejected Amer- 
ican’s proposal to sweeten the 
offer to $50 a share—condi- 
tionalon Lucky’sagreeingtoa 


friendly, expeditious deal. 

“We are confident that pur- 
suit of one of these alterna- 
tives will provide our best op- 
portunity to achieve greater 
value for our stockholders,” 
said Lucky’s chairman and 
ceo, John M. Lillie. 

The leveraged recapitaliza- 
tion, mentioned as one alterna- 
tive, could involve possible dis- 
tributions to stockholders by a 
dividend or share repurchase. 

Lucky also said its board had 
adopted a a pill” warrant 
dividend plan, under which it 


declared a dividend of one com- 
mon stock purchase right for 
each share of outstanding com- 
mon stock, payable to stock- 
holders of record April 18. 

American declined to com- 
ment on Lucky’s announced 
rejection. Lucky also declined 
to comment further. 

Lucky operates 342 stores 
in California—181 in Southern 
California and 161 in northern 
California. In addition, it has 
94 units in Florida and 49 in its 
Southwestern region of Arizo- 
na and Nevada.

20 years ago 

_INDIANAPOLIS, 1968— Hook Drug in In- 
diana is taking full advantage of its size with a 
program that allows chain units to exchange 
their slow moving Rx merchandise with other 
units. The is called “Profit Recovery No- 
tice” or “PRN.” Each Hook Drug unit, spread 
throughout the state, is asked to select six pre- 
scription items that are expensive and salable 

t unreturnable, Listed drug are compiled at 

eadquarters and sent back out to stores in the 
form of an order sheet. Stores can then order 
needed supplies from the slow moving or over 
ordered stock of other chain units.

Drug stores earn 4.6% share of housewares 


CHICAGO — Drug stores 
currently vie for 4.6 percent of 
the growing housewares prod- 
uct sales, according to a recent 
report by the National House- 
wares Manufacturers Associ- 
ation. 

The 1988 study revealed 
that drug stores came in ninth 
in housewares sales. 

However, the 7.0-percent 
share by supermarkets was 
only slightly higher than —_ 

1 


A shopper examines 


cleaning supplies on Longs’ 
shelves, Horton Plaza, in 
San Diego. 


store sales, and many reta 
segments, such as home fur- 
nishings and appliance stores, 
variety stores, and hardware 
and home centers, dropped 
below the drug store share. 

Retailers seemed to empha- 
size a few key categories. 
Roughly 59 percent of the 
housewares dollar volume is 
generated by small electric 
appliances, cookware and 
bakeware, kitchenware, and 
accessories. 

By itself, small electrics ac- 
counted for 24.2 percent of in- 
dustry volume—a category 
most drug stores include as a 
staple in their housewares se- 
lection. Cookware and 
bakeware similarly account 
for a high 21.7-percent share 
of the sales volume. 

Leading housewares manu- 
facturers seemed to follow 
similar patterns, except that 
overall tabletop, serving- 
ware, and furniture also 
ranked highly. 

A disparity among house- 
wares vendors was also evi- 
dent in the NHMA study. 
About 40 percent of vendor 
sales are attributable to less 
than 4 percent of the house- 
wares manufacturing base. 

In all, manufacturers are 
part of a $31.3 billion house- . 
wares industry. They re- 
vealed that building sales is 
one of their top priorities, fol- 
lowed in importance by new 
product introductions, main- 
taining gross margins, and 
product colors, packaging, 
and pricing.

opened a second one early this month.

because it can expose “virtually every

gories as pharmacy, stationery and 
greeting cards.

Good performances in ’87 


The varied efforts by drug chains in 
markets all over the country resulted 
in a renewed awareness by consumers 
that drug stores are expert providers 
of health care, beauty supplies and oth- 
er core products. 

Chains stepped up their efforts to 
boost their health care image by giving 
pharmacy higher visibility and under- 
scoring the pharmacist’s expertise in 
counseling consumers on UTC items as 
well as prescription drugs.

PERFORMANCE 


Eugene Applebaum 
chairman 


Arbor Drugs 


“In our market area both the 
full service Arbor Drug format 
and the deep discounter have 
continued to expand at a rapid 
pace. We believe that, looking 
ahead, we hold an important 
competitive edge in the number 
of our locations in southeastern 
Michigan, now 77, in addition to 
our growing appeal to the time- 
conscious shoppers of the 80s. 

“At Arbor we never deviated 
from our base business strategy 
with extraneous and often confus- 
ing merchandising classifications. 
A case in point: pharmacy—where 
we place extraordinary empha- 
sis—now represents 30 percent of 
our total sales, up from the 25 per- 
cent level just two years ago. 

“The name of the game, from 
our vantage point, is the consis- 
tency in execution. At Arbor we 
recognize that our customers 
place a great deal of emphasis on 
the value of their own time and on 
what we do best: provide well- 
defined assortments of day-to- 
day needs, present clean and 
well-stocked stores, and offer 
good prices.” 


George H. Bartell Jr. 
president 
Bartell Drug 


“The one thing overriding the 
drug store industry this year is 
that competition is not going to 
diminish, it’s going to increase. 
The country is tending to get 
over-stored. We’re going to see 
more competition from super- 
markets and other purveyors of 
merchandise. 

Because of this, there will be 
changes in the methods of mer- 
chandising. It’s obviously going 
to be hypermarkets, but they’re 
not going to dominate and the 
same applies to warehouse clubs. 

The retail business is a matter 
of the survival of the fittest. 
There is a tendency towards cci- 
solidation, which is going to af- 
fect a lot of the markets. At Bar- 
tell, we don’t have to switch to a 
greater emphasis on core drug 
store merchandising, like some 
drug chains, because we’ve al- 
ways been there. We’re only in 
fourth place in greater Seattle, 
behind Pay ’n Save, Pay Less 
NW, Fred Meyer. All of those 
operate quite large stores, so we 
can’t be in that size store and o 
erate in the marketplace. We 
have to be more of a neighbor- 
hood store, and there is a market 
for that in this area. This year 
we'll continue to emphasize the 
core business because that’s 
where our expertise is: in this 
market. 


Drug chain executives comment on market conditions 


Gene Bass 
vp merchandising 
Bill’s 


“The main area we’re trying to 
work on this year is to better 
merchandise the checkstand 
area. I’ve custom built some spe- 
cial endstands and we'll be rolling 
these out to all our stores this 
year. We have found if the mer- 
chandise is properl displayed 
and priced, it will sell. We're not 
just selling magazines and film at 
the checkstands, but expanding 
into other areas like cosmetics, 
which have higher margins. Bat- 
teries and film still sell best, but 
videotapes are also selling well. 
We are also rolling out some clip- 
strips prograins.’ 


Ira Shain 
president 
Associated 


“The merchandising back- 
ground of a drug chain was the 
obvious—the core drug store 
business, which was the pharma- 
cy and other health needs. 

ough an evolutionary pro- 
cess, § chains went to sundry 
merchandise and for many years 
this was successful. 

“However, as specialists came 
into the field and exploded many 
general merchandise categories 
in a single entity, or a 200,000- 
square-foot store or a ware- 
house, drug chains started to get 
hurt. 

“So now the trend at drug 
chains has been a complete re- 
versal. But I think they are 
wrong—the future of a drug 
chain is not only a core business. 
There is a middle ground where 
they can establish themselves 
with general merchandise. 

“For example, if electronics 
require service and there is 
heavy competition, then drug 
chains should not sell electronics. 
But if housewares can be handled 
then that is where they should be 
and the category should be well 
covered. 

“Space normally devoted to 
two or three categories, that are 
not well ye could be bet- 
ter used if just one category is 
taken on and the chain makes a 
stand with it.”

Middle-aged people are now the fastest-growing group of consumers in the country. Buying power for 35-to-59-year olds is expected to increase 76 percent by the year 2000.

Demographic trends lead to cosmetic profits: U.S. 


ASHINGTON — Cosmetics 
sales will continue to grow 
by more than 2.5 percent 
per year through 1992 if drug store re- 
tailers adapt to the changing makeup 
of U. S. consumers. 

According to a recent U. S. Depart- 
ment of Commerce report, industry 
shipments of all cosmetics, toiletries 
and fra ces will reach an estimated 
$13.6 billion in 1987, a rise of 3.6 per- 
cent. However, to realize the forecast 
growth for 1988 (about 2.5 percent af- 
ter adjusting for inflation) and later 
years, cosmetics sellers must offset 
the decline in the number of prospec- 
tive teen and young adult customers 
by tapping the 45-55 and over-65 age 
groups, “two of the most rapidly grow- 
ing segments of the U. S. population.” 

‘These demographic changes open 


up opportunities for new skin, hair and 
oral hygiene products, including mois- 
turizers, skin lotions, desensitizing 
and antiplaque toothpastes and hair 
conditioners,” said government re- 


“Sales of skin treatment, hair and 
makeup products for the ethnic market 
could double in the next five years, de- 
pending on the availability of products 
suitable to specific hair and complexion 


Cosmetics sellers must offset the decline in 
teen and young adult customers by tapping 
the 45-55 and over-65 age groups. 


searchers. “The current emphasis on 
health and fitness should also spur 
sales.” 

Another key to improving cosmetic 
sales in coming years is the skyrocket- 
ing market for ethnic beauty aids. 


requirements,” economists predicted. 

Researchers estimate the current eth- 

nic market at about 50 million consum- 

ers, including between five and six mil- 

— black women who work outside the 
ome. 


Long-term projections for growth in 
beauty aid sales will be affected by de- 
velopment of new products for “aging 
skin,” as well as sunscreens, tannin 
accelerators and tan-sustaining nts: 
ucts, according to predictions. After 
ailowing for inflation, government 
forecasters said cosmetic shipment 
value should rise 2.6 percent annually 
over the next five years. 

At the same time, drug store cos- 
metic sales, specifically, may suffer 
from growing competition from hair 
stylists, based on salon performance 
last year. 

“Beauty salons, an important outlet 
for cosmetic products, are expected to 
show retail sales of $1.4 billion for 
1987. . . their potential as outlets is 
still far from being realized... ,” 
economists said.
