Competitive pressures make toiletry sales hard won 


majority of chain drug store re- 
tailers say their 1987 sales rose 
mn toiletries, but the gains were 
hard won. A Drug Store News survey 
of toiletry buyers and merchandisers 
puts the average sales increase for this 
department at about 6 percent in 1987. 

Competition from discounters, food 
stores and deep discount drug stores 
made the toiletries category particu- 
larly competitive for chain drug mer- 
chants last year. 

Mass merchandise stores and food 
stores continued to expand their as- 
sortments of toiletries, and buyers say 
these retailers were exceptionally ag- 
gressive with the commodity catego- 
ries like shampoo, styling aids, hair 
sprays, mass skin creams and lotions, 
deodorants, shaving creams, and 
men’s toiletries. 

Buyers for some of the smaller re- 
gional chains complained that they 
weren't able to advertise some popular 
brands like Ivory or Flex shampoos be- 
cause there was “no way” they could 
compete with the bigger food chains or 
with the mass merchandisers, like 
K mart or Wal-Mart. 

However, the pressure of competi- 
tion did give buyers an incentive to be 
more creative with their advertising 
programs. Some buyers found a solu- 
tion in advertising brands, in new or 
emerging drug store categories, as in 
professional hair and professional nail 
care supplies. 

Others looked for fashion items like 
hair clips and hair barrettes or cosmet- 
ics organizers to advertise. Others 
went with exclusive promotions in 
which their stores could give away 
something that competitors couldn’t 
get, such as tickets to a local tennis 
tournament or basketball game. 

A number of chains, for example, in- 
cluding Walgreens and Eckerd tied in 
with the sti ongoing La Sallé 10 Inter- 
national company’s Virginia Slims 
tournament promotion. 

La Sallé, which is one of this year’s 
tournament sponsors, is making tick- 
ets available to retailers who promote 
their line. The retailers, in turn, are of- 
fering their shoppers a free ticket with 
a minimum La Sallé purchase. Perry 
Drug in Michigan tied in to a similar 

romotion with Revlon’s Professional 
air Care Division for a Pistons bas- 
ketball game. 

Buyers also tried very hard last year 
to lock in to category growth trends, 
and to be the first in their markets to 
either stock or promote fashion items 
like a Stiff Stuff styling spritz or a 
sunblock with colored zinc. 

In 1987, buyers also said they were 
under pressure to improve margins as 
well as generate traffic. 

“On the one hand, we have to come 
up with an advertising program that 
will create traffic,” said one buyer fora 
Northeast chain, “on the other, we 
have to protect our gross margins. The 
two goals can be mutually exclusive 
unless you’re very creative.” 

Buyers say that their best chances of 
finding a profitable “hot” item to pro- 
mote comes from segmenting their cat- 
egories. Shampoo, for example, is not 
a profitable category when it’s fea- 
tured on ad, but mass prestige sham- 
poos and salon-originated shampoos 
can be very profitable when adver- 
tised. 

These are still —— new cate- 
gories for drug store retailers, buyers 
say, and so there is less competition 
from chain food and chain mass mer- 


chandise stores. 

Buyers can advertise a Pantene, a 
Vidal Sassoon, a Redmond or a TRE- 
Semmé for 20-percent to 30-percent off 
their everyday retails and still make 
margins of 30 percent or better. 

And because these lines are hot now, 
they also sell well off their shelf at mar- 
gins of 40 percent and 50 percent and 
better. 

Buyers say they are also applying 
this strategy to beauty care accesso- 
ries like hair barrettes and clips, cos- 
metics organizers, hair brushes, per- 
sonal care appliances, and bath 
sponges in personal care. 

In 1987, there weren’t many dra- 
matic growth categories in toiletries, 
but there were a few: Suncare contin- 
ued to be a very strong category with 
growth up more than 10 percent in 
many chains. 

Buyers say their best brands were 
Coppertone, Bain de Soleil, Hawaiian 
Tropics, Pre-Sun, Shade, Sun Down, 
Cancer Garde, and some lesser known 
lines like Banana Boat and Gorilla 
Grease. 

High SPF's continued to outpace the 
lower SPFs in growth, but tanning 
products also continued to do well in 
chain drug stores. 

In 1987, many drug chains decided 
to make sun care a year-round catego- 
ry. Most chains are now merchandis- 
ing the category next to their skin care 
lines in a two to 4-foot year-round plan- 
ogram. 

A few chains, such as Eckerd Drug, 
are also cross merchandising some of 
the higher SPF brands like Cancer 
Guarde, Pre Sun and Sun Down near 
the pharmacy. “Some consumers are 
confused by all the different SPF num- 
bers,” said one buyer, “so if we put a 
display near the pharmacy, we make it 
easier for our shoppers to ask for help 
from the pharmacists. It’s also a good 
way for.us to get our pharmacists in- 
volved with our customers.” 

Skin care also enjoyed moderate 
growth as a category in 1987, but buy- 
ers say certain brands did exceptional- 
ly well this year, including Lubriderm, 

urel, Soft Sense, Jergens, Nivea, and 
Neutrogena. 

Buyers say that consumers seem to 
be buying more of the better or higher 
priced mass skin care brands, and

Bonus and value packs keep ethnic sales afloat 


difficult year in 1987. 

Depending on the market, 
some sources report the category was 
flat, while others report sales increases 
of between 5 percent and 10 percent. 
Based on our own survey of chain drug 
store retailers, Drug Store News esti- 
mates an 8 percent increase for chain 
drug store sales of that category in 1987. 

According to market research esti- 
mates, overall growth across all mass 
classes of trade was modest at about 3 

ercent. Ethnic sales in the drug store 
industry were down 5 percent, accord- 
ing to A.C. Nielsen Market Research 
estimates, but because of aggressive 
promotions, some chains and some re- 
gions did better than that. 

Most chain drug sources say, howev- 
er, that they had to work for growth in 
this category last year, and most say 
that any gains were due primarily to in- 
tense promotions of bonus packs, value 
packs, and a a of manufac- 
turer cents-off coupons in 1987. 

Retailers and ethnic distributors 
say the category is being hurt by a 
change in fashion trends. With some 
exceptions, the curl look is still “out” 
and the relaxed look and very short 
hair is “in.” 

As buyers like to point out, consum- 
ers don’t need as many maintenance or 
after care products when they’re wear- 
ing short hair, and the result is that 
many ethnic consumers are not buying 
the high consumption and high ticket 
after care products as often as they 
once were. 

Instead, they are basically buyin 
shampoos, conditioners, sheens fate 
sprays, and they are ¥ Srp about $8 
every two months on hair care instead 
of about $15 every two or three weeks. 

Manufacturers and ethnic distribu- 
tors are trying to weather this fashion 
lull, therefore, by creating wide vari- 
eties of bonus or value packs for their 
consumers. 

The retailers who have been buying 
the bonus packs say they know they 
are losing some sales to consumers 
who stockpile, but they also feel they 
are getting at least some incremental 
sales from consumers who see the 
packs on display and who buy them im- 
pulsively for their value. 


A trade-off 


“TI know we’re losing a sale when we 
give an 8-ounce conditioner away free 
with an 8-ounce activator,” said one 
buyer, “but I also have to believe we 
make it up = getting more new shop- 
pers to try the product.”

say that some of their best bonus packs 
in 1987 and early ’88 were the follow-

of their total sales. Most distributors,

the nail, eye and blush lines have to 
deal with tough competition from the 
mass brands.

of shades in their lines that they have 
made it much harder for the ethnic 
lines to compete for this business.

although their pricing is not always as

getting more varied and more fashion- 
oriented. 

Distributors say they are becoming 
faster at identifying the right brands 
to carry.

Fixturing, promo strategies support tobacco profits 


rug chains used new fixturing 

and promotional strategies to 

maintain cigarette profits in 
1987, as unit sales declined at many 
chains, following the national trend. 

Dollar sales looked better, largely 
because cigarette manufacturers 
passed along two more price hikes in 
1987, which added $2 to the price of 
1,000 cigarettes, or three to four cents 
more per pack. 

Better margins and profit dollars on 
aiden cigarettes, such as the 

lack-and-white generics and branded 
generics, helped some chains stabilize 
category profits. 

Unit shipments by vendors of brand- 
ed generics remained strong, as items 
such as RJR-Nabisco’s Doral, Philip 
Morris’ Cambridge, Brown & William- 
son’s Falcon Lights, and Liggett & 
Myers’ Quality Lights gained favor. 
Branded generics captured 4.1 per- 
cent of total units shipped, compared 
with a 2.7 percent share in 1986. Black 
and whites, and the value 25’s (25 for 
the price of 20) lost slight share points. 

Buyers say the success of generics is 
tied closely to economic conditions, 
and they work in some neighborhoods 
and not in others. 

Total units shipped dropped 2.1 per- 
cent to 570.38 billion, mirroring the 
slide of recent years. 

Drug chains settled for a smaller 
slice of the market, losing some to con- 
venience stores. Drug chains had an 
eight percent share of 1987 retail sales, 
compared with 10 percent in 1982, 
Brown & Williamson reported. 

Supermarkets lost share, dropping 
to 29 percent compared with 35 per- 
cent five years ago, the vendor said. 

Sales of the slim cigarettes, the so- 
called female styles, continued to be 
strong, drug chains said. Philip Morris’

Our Drug Store News survey re-

drinks, and liquor in chain drug stores

Much of the growth was spawned by 
heavy promotional activity, as drug 
chains continued to feature key gro- 
cery items as traffic generators. 

Candy, beer, soda, chips, cookies, 
jams, jellies, soups, microwave pop- 
corn, cake mixes, and condiments 
were particularly popular as ad items. 

In their ads, most drug chains con- 
tinued to be super-competitive on 
price. Their philosophy continues to be 
to use the popular edibles to lure traffic 
away from such competitors as other 
drug chains, food stores, and discount 
stores. 

The emphasis is on promoting a well- 
known brand at an especially low price 
to create an image of “value.” Osco 
Drug, for example, recently featured 
Nabisco snack crackers for $1.19, 
Planters nuts for $2.99, and Act II mi- 
crowave popcorn at three for$1, all 
proven traffic generators. 

Osco has also run specials on less 
competitive categories like canned ol- 
ives, canned hams, and pineapple 
chunks. Since these are categories the 
food chains don’t promote as frequent- 
ly as soda or tuna or mayonnaise, 
chains like Osco can take a better mar- 
gin on these features and yet still draw 
traffic. 

Longs followed a similar approach in 
one of its recent ads. Longs’ ads usual- 
ly highlight a broad assortment of gro- 
ceries, including Idaho specialty pota- 
toes, Pillsbury Plus cake mix, fudge 
brownie mixes, gelatins, and the like.

Drug chains battle mini-labs for market share 


tography is real, and it continues 

to shower healthy sales in- 
creases on all retailers of photofinish- 
ing services, cameras, film and photo 
supplies, and drug stores. But the 
technological and demographic forces 
which are propelling the market are 
also transforming it. 

For the first time in 1987, chain and 
independent drug stores lost their tra- 
ditional strong place at the top of the 
photofinishing market. As a trade 
class, drug stores saw their unit share 
of U.S. photoprocessing volume slip 
two percentage points last year, to 24 
percent of the total market. 

That —— was due to the incredi- 
ble boom of one-hour photo labs, which 
cater to the new generation of amateur 
35mm shutterbugs with convenient lo- 
cations, speedy service, and at least 
the perception of quality photofinish- 


T he boom in amateur 35mm pho- 


ing. 
Li year, the mini-labs drew 29 
‘sen of the total photofinishing 

usiness in the U.S.—a gain of more 
than five share points in a single 
year—and knocked drug stores from 
their longtime perch at the top of the 
market, according to market data sup- 
plied by the Photo Marketing Associa- 
tion. 

The one-hour centers are a recent 
wialggione saps but their growth has 

een extraordinary. In 1980, there 
were fewer than 1,000 in operation; by 
the end of last year, according to the 
PMA, nearly 15,000 mini-labs had 
blanketed the U.S., providing a pow- 
erful new source of competition for 
drug stores and other outlets. 

“Arguably, no photo processing seg- 
ment has benefited from the growth in 
35mm photo aphy to a greater extent 
than oiuilabe noted a recent PMA 
report. “The [photofinishing] market 
appears to be settling into a two-tier 
structure with price-competitive pho- 
to processing retailers representing 
one tier, and across-the-counter, ser- 
vice-oriented, on-site retail processors 
representing the second tier.” 

The report goes on to say, however, 
that “these two markets can _ 
co-exist given the fact that the overall 
processing marketplace is made up ofa 
variety of photographic consumers.” 

On the other hand, a few drug and 
supermarket retailers have leaped 
into the fray with their own in-store 
one-hour labs. Leading the march 
among drug chains is Eckerd Drug, 
which already has more than 60 in- 
store labs open throughout Florida, 
and Canada’s London Drug, which op- 


by store entrance.

erates a dozen of the centers and reaps

Despite the development of highly 
automated, easy-to-install “washless”

not jumping on it yet, because there’s 
still a lot to be decided in terms of how

ig scale,” said one chain drug photo

Indeed, many drug chains are still 
adapting to the rapid consolidation of 
the wholesale photofinishing business, 
which still accounts for a major share 
of the processing work done by most 
chains. The biggest example of consoli- 
dation has been the recent merger of 
Eastman Kodak’s photofinishing oper- 
ation with Fuqua Industries’ Color- 
craft into a new company called Qua- 
lex. The merger was completed at the 
end of March, creating the country’s 
largest wholesale photofinishing oper-

Whatever method drug chains use to 


process film, however, is not as impor- 
tant as the benefits they are reaping 
from an unprecedented boom in ama- 
teur photography. The growth has 
been sparked by the development and 
accelerating popularity of low-cost, 
easy-to-use point-and-shoot 35mm 
cameras in the 1980s. 

This overall boom has helped pro- 
duce a 10.1 percent sales increase in 
photo-video departments at chain 
drug stores in 1987. 

The new-generation compact 35mm 
models led the camera market last 
year, with sales to dealers up substan- 
tially to about 7 million units compared 
with 5 million in 1986. Although much 
of that growth came at the expense of 
the waning disc format and the almost 
extinct 126 pocket model format, the 
110 pocket camera remains a strong 
seller, with sales last year of nearly 6 
million units. Polaroid’s line of instant 
cameras also continues to sell extreme- 
ly well, and the company is developing 
some highly touted new product inno- 
vations—including a filmless electron- 
ic imaging system—to maintain sales 
momentum. 

The auto-focus 35s, however, have 
boosted sales in all photo categories 
and elevated amateur picture-taking 
to amore serious, quality-oriented lev- 
el. For instance, 35mm film now ac- 
counts for nearly three-fourths of all 
film processing, compared with just 30 


percent a decade ago. In addition, 
30mm now accounts for well over half 
of all types of film sold, and its share 
should rise to as much as 75 percent by 
the end of the decade, according to in- 
dustry estimates. 

“It’s more and more competitive, 
but it’s a dea thing what the manu- 
facturers have done with 35mm pho- 
tography,” noted Osco spokesman 
John Kromer recently. “They’ve got- 
ten more and more away from pocket 
cameras and into higher-quality pho- 
tography, and it’s driving our process- 
ing business.” 

eanwhile, manufacturers are now 
developing new, more advanced point- 
and-shoot 35s at a frenzied pace. This 
year, a spate of new auto-focus models 
with dual lens capabilities has been 
launched in the U.S., including zoom 
lens point-and-shoot cameras. As com- 
petition among the various manufac- 
turers intensifies and prices come 
down, the dual-lens models will be- 
come more of a standard item for drug 
retailers. 

Disposable cameras represent an- 
other area of opportunity. First devel- 
oped by Fuji in 1986, the throwaways 
now represent a viable alternative, es- 
peeially as a seasonal item in vacation 
areas. The first disposable with a built- 
in flash unit was unveiled at the Photo 
Marketing Association Convention in 
late February.

Video boom s 


na few short years, the home video 

revolution has spawned a mature, 

reaitik tition aclies industry. The 
growth of that industry has tapered off 
into single-digit figures, but with VCRs 
now found in about 50 percent of all U.S. 
households and the level of household 
penetration still increasing, the outlook 
calls for a stable, growing market for 
blank videotape for years to come. 

“We are now deca with a market 
which can be considered mature and this 
translates to more conservative growth 
rates,” noted R. Stanton Bauer, general 
manager of Fuji Photo Film’s Magnetic 
Products Division, in a report on the 
magnetic tape industry. “We will no 
longer see the dramatic double-digit an- 
nual growth experienced during the pe- 
riod 1983 through 1986.” 

Nevertheless, Bauer adds, “Single- 
digit growth on an immense base is still 
ae ey, owth.” 

he VCR boom has drawn thou- 
sands of competitors into the fray, 
however, and made the videotape 
rental business a competitive head- 
ache, at the very least. On the blank 
tape side, prices have come down 
steadily as more major manufacturers 
and virtually all retail classes have be- 
come embroiled in the war for sales. 
Top brand blank videotape can now be 
found for as little as $3 a tape on multi- 
pack promotion, and the price competi- 
tion shows no signs of abatement. 

“We bought a big shipment of major- 
brand videotape on deal, and put out 
stacks of it in three-packs at $3 a tape,” 
noted George Jeffers, president of 
Price Less in Sacramento. “It has 
blown out of here every time we do.” 

Despite the intensive price promo- 
tions, the video market represents a ma- 
jor opportunity for incremental sales 
and profits. Video and audio tape com- 
bined now constitute a market over $2 
billion, according to industry estimates, 
and the market is big enough to give ev- 
eryone a slice of the pie. 

In addition, as drug retailers have 
moved into the category with more 
complete selections of major brands, 
their sales have mushroomed. And by 
offering the convenience of multi- 
packs and multiple store locations in 
tandem with periodic price specials, 


te 


pawns new sales,

Deep discounter Rx Place displays public domain tapes on spinner racks, promotes 
selected name movies at less than $20, and sells blank cassettes and accessories in a 
high impact department. 


drug chains have been able to maintain 
decent margins in the category. 

“Blank video has been a very strong 
category for us, with sales up 300 per- 
cent in the past year,” noted PeM is- 
tributors president Frank Newman 
recently, echoing the comments of sev- 
eral chain executives. 

“We do very well by stocking a few 
of the major brands, but we avoid the 
low-end, cheaper-quality tapes,” add- 
ed a chain drug buyer. ‘We don't want 
to risk dissatisfied customers.” 

Over the past year, most dru 
chains have capitalized on the growt 
in demand for high-quality Siatk topes 
by stocking more top-name brands and 
boosting space for the category. 
Among recent examples: Pay ’n Save, 


Eckerd Drug and Phar-Mor. Many are 
also homing tapes in multiple loca- 
tions, including a floor stand facing the 
electronics/photo counter and at end- 
caps or dump bins facing the check- 
stands for impulse buying. 

Drug chains are also capitalizing on 
the growing importance of female buy- 
ers In a category once considered the 
a of males. As blank videotape 

as become a commodity item, with 
low price points, high use rates and fa- 
miliar brand names like Kodak, Polar- 
oid, TDK and Scotch, women have 
emerged as a major part of the market. 
And because they comprise the bulk of 
drug store and supermarket buyers, 
women have helped swing the balance 
of the videotape market in favor of 


competition 


those trade classes. 

The video rental market, on the oth- 
er hand, seems fraught with peril for 
chains without adequate financing to 
handle the large inventory carrying 
costs and other expenses involved. 
More and more, the rental business is 
going to a few major players in each 
market, as underfunded mom-and-pop 
operations fall by the wayside. 

The handful of drug chains which 
made an early commitment to movie 
rental departments in their stores, with 
adequate staffing, inventory and sys- 
tems to make the concept work, seem to 
have overcome the accelerating market 
shakeout and have made video rentals a 
viable part of their overall sales picture. 
Among the most successful are Rite Aid 
(the nation’s leader in rental volume, 
with hundreds of locations offering 
thousands of titles), Wellby Super Drug 
and Phar-Mor. 

Phar-Mor, in fact, has begun open- 
ing off-price stores with greatly en- 
larged video rental alcoves after scor- 
ing a big hit with the movie business. 
Its success with the concept is due to 
its widely advertised price of 69 cents a 
night—the lowest in town—as well as 
its ability to keep service costs low and 
customer traffic high. The chain has 
also succeeded in using its video de- 
partment as a customer draw to boost 
sales throughout the store. 

Other major chains which are test- 
ing the video rental business include 
Walgreens, Pay ’n Save and Genovese. 
Reveo and Hook Drugs, meanwhile, 
have installed video dispensing ma- 
chines in some of their stores to test 
the feasibility of service-free movie 
rentals. The machines offer several 
hundred VHS titles and fully automat- 
ed customer transactions, using either 
a credit card or a membership card. 

Nevertheless, the jury is still out 
about the long-term feasibility of mov- 
ie rentals for drug chains. Said one 
chain drug resident in the Midwest 
recently: “You can’t build a profitable 


business renting a $70 item at a dollar a 
night, which is what a lot of these peo- 
ple are doing. I think it’s going to go 
the way of optical centers; in a few 
years, most drug chains will be out of 
it. It’s just too competitive.”

Sunglass sales top $1 billion 


Over-the-counter sunglass sales na- 
tionwide topped the billion-dollar mark 
for the fourth consecutive year, rising to 
$1.3 billion nationwide in 1987, from $1.2 
billion in ’86. Of the 189 million pairs 
sold, drug stores accounted for 21 mil- 
lion, or 11 percent, of total units, accord- 
ing to the Sunglass Association of Amer- 
ica (SAA). The average price paid for a 

air was $7, compared with an average 

.85 in 1986. 

Drug store chains, which generally 
beef up their sunglass selection during 
the prime spring/summer selling sea- 
son, report healthy turns and margins 
year-round. But growing competition at 
both ends of the spectrum—street ven- 
dors and other conduits of cheaper im- 
ports at the low end and upscale special- 
ty sunglass shops and department 
stores at the other—have eaten into 

rofit margins. In addition, many chains 
eel compelled to discount sunglasses 
everyday or through promotions. 

Sunglasses are often displayed near 
checkouts, reaping high impulse sales, 
but some chains also position them near 
cosmetics or in other high-traffic areas. 

Minneapolis-based Thrifty ¢ White 
Drug Stores, for example, maintains a 
half-price spinner rack as well as its 
vemuiat name-brand sunglass spinner 
near checkouts in its larger stores. 

“We go with the fashions—that’s 
where the sales are,” said Ronald 
Ransdell, director of merchandising. 


Jewelry, with an accent on earrings, is displayed with cosmetics along 
the front wall of this Norwood, N.J., Cost Cutters, the deep-discount 
arm of Community Distributors (Drug Fair of New Jersey).

Pantyhose sales flat 


Pantyhose sales nationwide were 
basically flat in 1987 at $1.8 billion, 
possibly dampened by a significant 
shift to longer-wearing Spandex sheer 
styles, according to a spokesman for 
MCRA, based in Stamford, Conn. 

Overall, pantyhose average $1.90 a 
pair, while drug stores’ average price 
is $1.55. Discount stores and catalog 
mail-order operations grab the largest 
share in units, with 20 percent apiece. 
Drug stores have a 9 percent share of 
units; food stores, 14 percent; depart- 
ment stores, 10 percent; the remainder 
is accounted for among such operations 
as Sears and JC Penney and small ho- 
siery outlets, according to MRCA sur- 
veys.

near cosmetics, for multiple sale op- 
portunities.

Non-pros fuel do-it-yourself sales growth 


ome chains favor do-it-yourself 

departments as a way to capture 

the weekday convenience trip, 
though the category has carried less 
importance at drug chains with the rise 
of mammoth home center chains. 

Still, DIY posted a nominal 1.2 per- 
cent sales gain at drug chains in 1987 to 
$405 million. 

There is plenty of consumer demand 
for home improvement and auto sup- 
plies. 

The growth of spending for home re- 
pairs among nonprofessionals in fact 
fueled most of the overall growth of 
home repair spending in 1987. Home- 
owners spent $67.95 Fillion, eight per- 
cent more than the year before, as the 
total home improvement market hit 
$99.46 billion, the Do-It-Yourself Re- 
search Institute reported. 

The automotive aftermarket is ex- 
pected to rise as much as 15 percent in 
1988, the Automotive Parts & Acces- 
sories Association predicted recently. 
This will be fueled by a large number of 
cars bought two to three years ago 
coming out of warranty. 

Such jobs as tuneups and fluid and 
chemical changes, often ordered while 
cars are being repaired in the garage, 
will be resumed by the car owners, 
sparking retail demand, an APAA 
spokesman said. 

But 1987 was a year that saw some 
notable drug industry cutbacks in 
automotive supplies. 

Perry Drug took the a leap 
from auto parts retailing when it sold 


off its auto parts division. Concurrent- 
ly, auto parts departments in its drug 
stores have been pared back, as part of

DRUG STORE NEWS/INSIDE PHARMACY, April 25, 1988 


__1988 ANNUAL REPORT OF RETAIL PHARMACY — 


Pharmacy gets back to the basics 


Chains and independents alike found that profit opportunities resided 
in core categories, and in providing a personal touch 


Editor’s note: Annual sales figures 
for 1987 may not portray 1987 as the 
best year the pharmacy business has 
had, but for the profession overall it 
was a good year. 

Chain and independent pharmacy 
owners returned to promoting their 
core business, the most notable part be- 
ing the prescription department. Com- 
puter technology and encouragement 
from management brought more phar- 
macists from behind their counters to 
counsel patients on prescription and 
OTC medications. 

With this renewed flurry of profes- 
sional activity in the marketplace, it is 
only fitting that Inside Pharmacy 
launch its Annual Report of Retail 
Pharmacy. 

Although pharmacists enjoyed an 
enhanced professional image in 1987, 
the year was not without problems. Ex- 
clusive third-party contracts took a 
toll on the bottom line, especially for 
the more vulnerable independents. 

Pharmacists also saw the spread of a 
new breed of competition from mail or- 
der pharmacies and dispensing physi- 
cians. At the same time, nontradition- 
al pharmacy competitors like 
supermarkets, combos, and discount 
stores cut a larger slice of the prescrip- 
tion and OTC pie. 

We hope that our Annual Report of 
Retail Pharmacy not only offers a re- 
view of these events, but also gives 
some insights on to what to expect for 
pharmacy in the future. 


Chain and independent drug store 
retailers took a giant step back to ba- 
sics last year with a strong emphasis 
on pharmacist-patient consultation 
and aggressive marketing of their pre- 
scription departments. Although 1987 
was somewhat disappointing for retail 
pharmacies financially, with only mod- 
est gains in prescription sales, profes- 
sionally it was a rewarding year. 

A heavy concentration of third-par- 
ty prescription business, with its em- 
phasis on substitution of lower-priced 
generics, kept dollar sales of prescrip- 
tions at chains and independents lower 
than expected. The retailers scored a 
somewhat disappointing, but still re-

Does the future lie in the 
hands of consumers? 


NEW YORK — What can retail pharmacy expect in the 
future? While all indications 
year. competitive spirit that has gripped the profession over the 
past several years, many industry observers believe that 
the future will be in the hands of the consumer. 

As third-party contracts with major corporations con- 
tinue to drive the number and dollars of prescriptions be- 
ing filled, ultimately it will be the consumer who must put 
up with busy pharmacies who are contracted to fill their 
prescriptions, or have prescriptions filled only by mail. 

As the costs of innovative new drugs continue to rise be- 
cause of heavy R&D, cost containment will become an 
even greater priority for prescription benefit planners. 
While the generic-versus-brand 
be fought in the retail pharmacy marketplace, branded 
pharmaceutical companies may be facing their most criti- 
cal issue yet—therapeutic substitution, or as some prefer 
to call it, therapeutic interchange. 
ty. Substituting from a formulary based on therapeutic cat- 
egory, similar to what is being done in hospitals around the 
country, could have disastrous effects on research-inten- 
sive pharmaceutical manufacturers. Efforts to pass legis- 
lation that will stop or curtail therapeutic substitution is 
already underway in several states. 

The increased competition will also breed new players in 
the retail pharmacy marketplace. Plans are already afoot 
by at least two cable TV companies, Home Shopping Net- 
work and Cable Value Network, to provide a 
shopping of prescription drugs and other health-related 


And finally, this year will probably see the passag 
new Medicare catastrophic drug benefit that will enable 
Medicare-eligible individuals to get prescriptions filled for 
a nominal co-payment once a deductible has been met.

WASHINGTON — Despite 
continuing efforts by the Food 
and Drug Administration to 
shave the average time re- 

uired for approval of new 
ay the process from lab- 
oratory to pharmacy shelf can 
still take well over a decade. 

According to a recent FDA 
study on new drug develop- 
ment in the United States, “im- 
portant medical advances” in 
1985 took nearly two years less 
from completion of laboratory 
testing to final FDA approval 
than drugs processed in the 
early 1980s. Nevertheless, in 
an analysis of the time required 
for research, development and 
approval, the FDA study 


PYTARMACY 
FDA’s approval process still a long row to hoe 


showed that the process from 
initial synthesis to approval of 
new drug application can be a 
long one. For example, com- 
bined industry research and de- 
velopment and FDA testing 
and approval required an aver- 
age of about 100 months. 
Specifically, the report found 
that time required for preclini- 
cal research and development 
(initial synthesis and animal 
testing) ranged from one to 
three years, with an average of 
18 months. Clinical testing re- 
quired from two to 10 years, 
with an average of five years. 
Finally, FDA review by the 
agency required from two 
months to seven years with an 


average of two years. 

According to FDA Commis- 
sioner Frank E. Young, the 
agency is committed to getting 
safe and effective drugs to the 
marketplace in the shortest 
possible time. However, the 
road to “safe and effective” new 
drugs is a long one. 

“The drug development pro- 
cess can be viewed as a series of 
progressive steps, each de- 
signed to highlight drugs of real 
promise and to weed out those 
that could be harmful or simply 
won’t work,” Young said. 

Initially, pharmaceutical 
firms conduct thousands of lab- 
oratory and animal tests, and 
with FDA approval proceed to 


human (“clinical”) testing. Ac- 
cording to Texas A&M econo- 
mist Steven Wiggins, manufac- 
turers spend an average of $65 
million to develop a new drug. 
Before an investigational 
drug can proceed to clinical tri- 
als, the FDA must review re- 
sults of the lab and animal test- 
ing, information on testing of 
the product in other countries 
and plans for the human test- 
ing. Only after the IND re- 
ceives this initial FDA go- 
ahead can clinical tests begin. 
“Normally, clinical trials are 
carried out in three phases in- 
volving progressively larger 
numbers of people,” explained 
Office of Health Affairs steffer

Annual Report of Retail Pharmacy 


Ken Flieger. 

Phase One trials focus on 
“learning more about the safety 
of the drug.” The tests usually 
involve less than 100 healthy 
volunteers. 

Phase Two uses a few hun- 
dred patients “and is designed 
to show whether the drug 1s ef- 
fective in treating the disease 
or condition for which it’s in- 
tended.” 

Phase Three clinical trials of- 
ten involve several thousand 
patients “who have the condi- 
tion against which the drug is 
effective.” This research seeks 
information on “less common 
and even rare side effects and 
adverse reactions.”

on the rise in recent years as a result of 
a sharp upsurge in the number of phy- 
sicians selling prescription drugs di-

profit charge patients far more than 
they would pay at retail pharmacies.

America and the National Consumers

NARD, and the National Pharmaceu- 
tical Association to form a new anti- 
physician dispensing group called the 
Coalition for Consumer Prescription 
Protections.

tive of physician dispensing is to enrich 
doctors, not save consumers money. 

Noting that drug repackagers “ad- 
vertise to physicians that they can in- 
crease their annual incomes by $30,000 
to $60,000 a year,” the group is warning 
consumers about “the potential for over- 
charging” by dispensing physicians.

drugs sold. . . reveals that repackag- 
ers’ sug ested retail prices for the 
drug sold in doctors’ offices are an av- 
erage of 13.2 eee higher than the 
average retail prices for the same 
drugs sold in pharmacies,” the coali- 
tion maintained.

A marked increase in consumer 
health interest is playing a greater role 
in the OTC market. As consumers hun- 
grily seek out more information about 
health issues and become more sophis- 
ticated consumers, journal studies im- 
pacting on health are quickly finding 
their way to consumer publications. 

This trend, a combination of sky- 
rocketing health care costs, and a de- 
creasing willingness by third party in- 
surers to pick up equal share of their 
members’ health care tabs, is creating 
a market in which consumers self-med- 
icate more often. 

Market experts see no signs that 
these trends are abating. If anything, 
they’re expected to accelerate. For re- 
tailers, the trends translate into more 


OTC sales. 
Journal studies played a part 


Journal studies reported in consum- 
er publications, and fueled by manu- 
facturer advertisements, impacted the 

mw sale of products in at least two OTC 

categories in 1987. 

Fish oil supplements gained popu- 

| larity as a result of a study indicating 
the supplements could reduce choles- 
terol levels. That popularity subsided 
when subsequent studies questioned 
its benefits, and raised the possibility 
of risks associated with taking too 
s much of the supplement. 

Then came studies indicating that a 
daily regimen of aspirin could reduce 
the risk of second heart attack, and lat- 
er, that aspirin was effective in pre- 
venting first heart attacks. These re- 
ports fueled the demand for aspirin.

Self-medication trend 
accelerates OTC sales 


100 OTC categories, according to a 
1987 Drug Store News study of those 
markets. That cough/ cold products 
sell well year-round is not surprising. 
The average consumer gets one to 
three colds per year. At any given time 
one out of every seven consumers will 
be congested. 

Those statistics support Drug Store 
News’ finding that more than a quarter 
of the items on the top 100 OTC list 
were cough/cold preparations. J. Rich- 
ard Wuest, professor of clinical phar- 
macy at the University of Cincinnati 
estimates that 60 percent of the OTC 
dollar spent in retail pharmacies is 
spent on cough/ cold products. 

Strong year-round sales are due to 
more than summer colds. Cough/cold 
and allergy products have high cross- 
over use. Consumers are using prod- 
ucts designed to treat allergies to re- 
lieve the stuffiness and runny nose 
symptoms common to colds and flus. 
Cough/cold products are also being 
used to treat allergies. 

Rx to OTC switches, generally suc- 
cessful in any OTC category, account 
for a large portion of successful cough 
/eold products. FDA Commissioner 
Frank Young holds that almost all suc- 
cessful OTC products in the last 10 
years were Rx to OTC switches. 

Consumers view OTC products that 
once had prescription-oniy status as 
more potent than other products. The 
products command fierce brand loyal- 
ty. And as more patients opt to self- 
medicate rather than incur expensive 
visits to physicians for cold, flu and al- 
lergy symptoms, the sale of these for- 
merly prescription-only drugs can only 
grow.

Pregnancy and ovulation tests have

to the formulated strips for blood

Aspirin study 


While the popularity of analgesics in 
general remained stable in 1987, it was 
aspirin’s turn to drive the category this 
year. 

Journal studies which showed that 
aspirin use prevented a second heart 
attack, or unstable angina, created 
new excitement in the category early 
in the year. A later study indicating 
that an aspirin every other day could 
significantly reduce the risk of heart 
attack in people with no previous heart 
disease, added fuel to the fire. 


Advertising claims 


Manufacturers were quick to jump 
on the new claims—too quick as far as 
the FDA was concerned. Although he 
has allowed aspirin labeling that re- 
lates to the reduced risk of second 
heart attack and unstable angina 
claim, Commissioner Frank Young 
wrote to manufacturers, recently to 
request that they drop advertising 
claims pertaining to the results of the 
more recent studies. 

Rep. Henry Waxman, chairman of 
the Health Subcommittee, fired 
charges at manufacturers promoting 
the claims, calling such ads a “disser- 
vice to consumers and a public health 
hazard,” since they “fail to fully and 
fairly inform the public who should not 
take aspirin.” 

The furor has not affected the sale of 
aspirin. At least or \ product is being 
marketed in a calendar pack to make 
daily aspirin taking easier. Two other 
manufacturers have introduced low- 
dose aspirin for patients whose physi- 


Condoms did so well 
that only problem was 


keeping them in stock 


No longér relegated to the back of 
the counter, condoms are being dis- 
played prominently in the pharmacy, 
often in a secondary location in the 
feminine hygiene sections as well as 
near the pharmacy counter. In fact, 
the only problem retailers seem to be 
having with condoms is keeping them 
in stock. 


Safeguard against AIDS 


Endorsed as the one safeguard 
against contracting the deadly AIDS 
virus and other sexually-transmitted 
diseases, condoms were the fastest 
moving category in the family planning 
section. Sales for the first eight 
months of 1987 were up 32 percent in 
dollars and 27 percent in units over 
previous year levels, Pipeline Re- 
search reported. 

The category did so well this year 
that many retailers had problems 
— them in stock. Demand for the 
product was so great that manufactur- 
ing and distribution capacity could not 
keep up in some instances. The prob- 
lem worsened when products were re- 
called by the FDA for failure rates. 
Problems have since been corrected, 
but manufacturers and retailers were 
= by the struggle to meet de- 
mand.

the heterosexual population will con- 
tinue to drive the category in 1988.

keting condoms to women, who ac-

analgesics 


OTC analgesics sales received a boost on reports that aspirin could reduce the risk ofa 
second heart attack and may be effective in preventing a first heart attack as well. 


cians recommend less of the medica- 
tion. 

The fuss being made about aspirin 
did not drown out the sale of non-aspi- 
rin products. Fueled by introduction of 
products in caplet form, ibuprofens 
continued to perform well. The sale of 
ibuprofen-based products grew 54 per- 


cent in 1987, according to a study by 
Pipeline Research, a marketing re- 
search company. 

Acetaminophens held their place in 
the category. Sales of grape and fruit- 
flavored chewable products for chil- 
dren were popular products in the cat- 


egory. 


Overall, the analgesic category re- 
mained strong and stable, accounting 
for 23 percent of the places on Drug 
Store News's top 100 OTC products in 
1987. 


Lens products hot 


Greater consumer awareness and 
concern played a part in increasing 
sales of lens products this year. React- 
ing to publicity about corneal ulcers 
and infections due to improper lens use 
and maintenance, consumers in- 
creased their compliance to recom- 
mended eye care regimens. 

For consumers, better compliance 
meant removing lenses more often and 
cleaning lenses more frequently. For 
retailers, better compliance meant 
higher sales. 


Innovation in lens care 


Innovation in lens care also contrib- 
uted to the growth of the category. 
Systems that use hydrogen peroxide 
gained greater market share. 

A Barnes-Hind 12-month study 
showed that the number of doctors rec- 
ommending the systems increased by 
70 percent last year. Doctors are also 
recommending procedures that either 
combine or speed up the lens cleansing 
process. 

Price reductions also figured in 
building sales of lens care products. 
Manufacturers slashed prices on saline 
solutions, and buyers felt that the 
price cuts reflected consumers’ unwill# 
ingness to pay high prices for lens caré 
products.

By Joseph Swartz 

Attracting customers to 
shop at a particular drug store 
for OTC medications is an art 
form that utilizes such strate- 
gies as picking the right loca- 
tion, scouting out competi- 
tion, and creative advertising 
campaigns. 

Determining the likelihood 
that a customer will buy a spe- 
cific OTC product once inside 
the store requires a closer look 
at some key demographics, 
like age and income. 


Age before affluence 


Most OTC categories have 
strong correlations between 
age and the likelihood of use, 
but the correlation between 
income and use is not always 
as clear. 

As the average consumer 
ages, the need for medication 
will increase. In many cases, 
the less affluent will concen- 
trate their earnings on drugs 
and food as they get older. With 
the direction to self-medica- 
tion, much of the drug pur- 
chases will be in OTC products. 

On the other hand, afflu- 
ence can play a predictable 
role in some OTC expendi- 
tures. Two good examples are 


in the purchase of soft contact 
lens products and stomach 
antacid remedies. Only the 
more affluent customers are 
more likely to wear contact 
lenses, while marketing stud- 
ies have shown that successful 
business people are the prime 
purchasers of antacid and an- 
tiuleer OTC products. 
Perhaps the best correla- 
tion of OTC product use to the 
age of the purchaser is in the 
category of at-home pregnan- 
cy testing kits. While only 4 
percent of the adult female 
population use these prod- 
ucts, 70 percent are purchased 
by women under age 35. 
Within that age group, 
women aged 18 to 24, the 
group most likely to become 
hs ay 5 are 52 percent more 
ikely to use these products. 
If you chart the likelihood of 
purchasing at-home pregnan- 
cy tests by income, the picture 
is not as clear. Customers with 
annual household incomes un- 
der $25,000 are more likely to 
buy at-home pregnancy test 
kits, while those with incomes 
ranging from $25,000 to 
$39,999 are less likely. Con- 
sumers with incomes ranging 
from $40,000 to $49,999 are 
again more likely to be heavy 
users, but those earning 
$50,000 are less likely. 
Although no one demo- 


Joseph Swartz is an associate 
editor at American Demo- 
graphics. 


graphic segment emerges as 
the most likely customer for 
all OTC drug products, each 
category has its own demo- 
graphic picture. That’s why 
retailer product selection for 
individual stores should be de- 
termined based on a product’s 
most likely customer profile 
and the demographics of the 
trading area. 


Age an important factor 


Categories of products car- 
ried by the retailer should also 
relate to the ages of customers 
in a particular trading area. 
But sometimes pure market- 
ing figures don’t tell the whole 
story. 

A good example is with OTC 
indigestion remedies. Latest 
statistics show that these 
products are used by 50 per- 
cent of the adult population at 
least once in six months. Yet a 
recent study conducted b 
Mediamark Research (MRI) 
finds that the likelihood of be- 
ing a heavy user of indigestion 
and upset stomach aids de- 
creases with income level, but 
increases with age. 

MRI defines a heavy user of 
indigestion aids as someone 
who uses a product eight or 
more times in a-30-day period. 
Heavy users of indigestion 
aids and stomach remedies 
make up 26 percent of all cus- 


tomers in this OTC category, 
but they consume 78 percent 
of stomach and indigestion aid 
products. 

Use of OTC indigestion 
remedies also varies with in- 
come. Consumers with annual 
household incomes below 
$35,000 are more likely to be 
heavy users of OTC indiges- 
tion products and stomach 
remedies. More specifically, 

eople whose incomes are 

5,000 to $34,999 are five 

ercent more likely to be 
ein users; those in the 
$15,000 to $24,999 range are 
10 percent more likely to be 
average users; and those earn- 
ing under $15,000 are 25 per- 
cent more likely to be heavy 
users. Conversely, those indi- 
viduals with household in- 
comes of $35,000 and above 
are less likely to be heavy us- 
ers. 

If you look at OTC stomach 
and indigestion products by 
age, all age groups under 45 
are less likely than average to 
be heavy users. Age groups 45 
and over are at least 20 per- 
cent more likely to be heavy 
users, and people who are 65 
and over are 65 percent more 
than average to heavily use 
products that treat their indi- 
gestion and stomach aches.

American adults continues to

WASHINGTON — As part 
of an agreement with Federal 
regulators, the nation’s over- 
the-counter drug manufactur- 
ers have temporarily shelved 
ads claiming that aspirin may 
reduce the risk of heart at- 
tacks.

Drug Administration and the 
Federal Trade Commission,

continue newspaper and tele- 
vision advertising which pro- 
motes aspirin use to prevent 
primary heart attacks. Mean- 
while, FDA Commissioner 
Frank Young said the agency 
is analyzing “full data and in- 
formation” from the recent 
study which triggered the ad-

priate professional labeling 
can be established. . . .”

A more effective job of sell- 
ing OTC products can be 
achieved by knowing who the 
customer is. This can be ac- 
complished with in-store sur- 
veys, or overall demographic 
data for the store done by pri- 
vate data companies. Once 
that data is compiled, market- 
ing companies can determine 
which preducts have the best 
likelihood of selling to particu- 
lar retail audiences. 

In today’s drug store, it’s 
not enough to know the com- 
petition’s strategy in selling 
OTC products; it’s imperative 
to determine the demograph- 
ics of a particular marketin 
audience and create individua 
strategies to meet the de- 
mands of that marketplace.

which can be complicated as a 
result of aspirin use. He noted 
that for the purposes of the 
study, researchers used only 
healthy doctors with no aspi- 
rin intolerance, peptic ulcers 
or cardiovascular problems. 
Under the agreement 
reached between aspirin in- 
dustry, FDA and the FTC, 
manufacturers have stopped 
claiming that aspirin can pre- 
vent first heart attacks, but 
will continue to premote the 
drug as useful in the preven- 
tion of second heart attacks.

ues to discourage claims to

doctor’s care and advice. (The 
agency has, however, ap- 
proved the promotion of aspi- 
rin to physicians as a potential 
aid in curbing second heart at- 
tacks.) 

According to Young, when 
the final FDA report on the 
latest study is available, doc- 
tors will have clear guidelines 
to use in determining which of 
their patients will benefit 
from an aspirin every other

agency is “expediting” analy-

rovide prompt “physician’s

DRUG STORE NEWS/INSIDE PHARMACY, April 25, 1988 


Chain and independent 
pharmacies looking to carve a 
niche for themselves in an 
overcrowded drug store mar- 
ketplace are rethinking their 
front-end business and becom- 
ing providers of home health 
care supplies, equipment, and 
services. 

Some industry observers 
believe home health care could 
put a little zing back into 
slumping register sales, as 
traditional front-end drug 
store business continues to 
erode because of competition 
from such non-traditional 
drug outlets as supermarkets, 
combos, and deep discount- 
ers. 

It is estimated that home 
health care, fueled by an aging 

opulation, could become a 
© $12 billion to $14 billion busi- 
ness by the end of the decade. 

By the year 2000, the num- 
ber of Americans aged 85 or 
older will grow 83 percent, 
putting that age group at 
about 4.9 million people. And 
because a large percentage of 
those octogenarians-plus can 
take care of themselves, sales 
of home health care supplies 
cannot help but grow. 

A survey conducted by Na-

aging money. 

As would be expected, a re-

health spending in this coun-

the study, those households 
headed by an adult aged 65 to 
74 spent an average of $211 on 
medicines and medical sup- 
plies. Medical spending rose 
to $292 for households headed 
by an adult aged 75 or older.

Giant sales, earnings 
up in 4th quarter, year 


LANDOVER, Md. — Giant 
Food Inc., which operates su- 
rmarkets and food/drug com- 
ination stores, posted sub- 
stantial increases in sales and 
earnings for the fourth quarter 
and year ended Feb. 27. 

For the fourth quarter, net 
income rose to $27.15 million, 
or 90 cents per share, on sales of 
$883.1 million. For the compa- 


rable quarter last year, net in- 
come was $14.98 million, or 50 
cents per share, on sales of 
$861.2 million. 

For the year, net income 
was $75.6 million, or $2.51 per 
share, on sales of $2.7 billion, 
compared with last year’s net 
income of $46.5 million, or 
$1.55 per share, on sales of 
$2.5 billion.

Revco sells Crown Store Equipment Co. 


HOLLAND, Ohio — Revco said it has sold the Crown 
Store Equipment Co. to David Barker and Ron Madden of 
Meridian Holdings, Inc., the U.S. affiliate of Meridian 
Holdings, Ltd., Great Britain, and Fred Brown, a U.K. 
drug store retailer. The sale of the company, which de- 
signs and makes store fixtures, was completed March 28 
for an undisclosed amount. Barker said Meridian plans to 
expand Crown rapidly as a major fixture vendor and add 
European fixture designs. 

Besides a plant here, Crown has woodworking plants in 
New Castle, Va. and Pineville, La. 


Stevens succeeds Robertson at Meyer 


PORTLAND, Ore. — Fred Meyer has named Freder- 
ick Stevens to succeed Oran Robertson as chairman and 
chief executive. Stevens, 51, last served as executive vp in 
charge of specialt retailing at K mart, where he oversaw 
the operation of Pay Less NW and other specialty divi- 
sions. Robertson, 70, remains a director. 

Fred Meyer is a leading Northwest retailer of food, 
drug, general merchandise and home improvement prod- 
ucts, with sales of $1.36 billion and net income of $18.3 mil- 
lion in the first nine months of this fiscal year.

the import program, Reagan will have responsibility for 
convenience line purchasing activities. 


Leonard and Conway out at Zenith Labs 


RAMSEY, N.J. — Smarting from heavy losses in the 
past two years, Zenith Laboratories has dismissed presi- 
dent and chief executive James Leonard and chief opera- 
tions officer Kevin Conway. Replacing them are board 
chairman John Farber and new president Larry Weber, a 
management consultant. 

Zenith is also proposing a number of cost-cutting mea- 
sures and is negotiating with creditors to ease debt bur- 
dens, which have risen sharply in the past year after man- 
ufacturing irregularities were uncovered by the FDA. In 
1987, Zenith’s sales dropped 14 percent and the company 
had a loss of $11.8 million. 

Zenith has worked with the FDA to correct its plant 
psi and Farber said drug sales are again on the rise. 

n addition, the company has developed several new prod- 
ucts for marketing following FDA approval.

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 9, 1988 


Ethnic overview 


Black women are great cosmetics/fragrance shoppers, buyers 
and cosmeticians tell Drug Store News. In addition to buying 
black cosmetic lines like Posner and Ultra Sheen, black women 
also tend to buy the darker Cover Girl, Revion & Maybelline 
shades. Also popular with black shoppers are designer fra- 
grances like Passion, White Linen and Obsession. Store clerks 
say black shoppers willingly pay full price for the convenience 
of buying designer fragrances in their local drug stores. 


oe . z aid a 
7 : “ 


Ethnic consumers tell Drug Store News that price matters to 
them when they buy commodity hair care products. A value 
pack or a discounted price is apt to influence a purchase deci- 
sion for many consumers. But shoppers also say they want 

_ certain guarantees of quality in the products they buy, and 
products without alcohol or lye in their formulas are especial- 
ly popular today. 


Buyers say that shower caps & hair care accessories sell like “gangbusters” to ethnic consumers. 
Buyers say women are buying all sorts of hair accessories from barrettes to pony tail holders, but 
shower caps fill a special niche. Many black women use them to cover their hair after it’s been 
conditioned. Caps help the conditioners really penetrate the hair and allow women the freedom 
to go wherever they like, while conditioning takes effect.

SCHENECTADY, N. Y. — Price Chopper Supermar- 
kets, which operates 75 supermarket and convenience 
stores in the Northeast, opened its fifth supermarket with 
pharmacy April 27 in Newburgh, N. Y. Price Chopper is 
owned by Golub Corp. 


Marketplace show coming in June 


ORLANDO, Fla. — NACDS will hold its second annual 
Marketplace Conference June 19-22 at Marriott’s Orlando 
Worid Center here. 

The conference, which was cape ote by merging the 
association’s cosmetic-fragrance marketing and merchan- 
dising conferences, is designed to bring together chain 
buyers and supplier executives in order to improve work- 
ing relationships. 


Kendall named F&M operations vp, cfo 


WARREN, Mich. — F&M Distribu- 
tors has appointed Laura C. Kendall as 
vp-central operations and cfo. 

Kendall was formerly with Perry Drug 
Stores as vp-finance since 1986. Prior to 
that, she was a senior manager at Arthur 
Andersen & Co. for 11 years. 

A graduate of Western Michigan Uni- 
versity, Kendall will be responsible for fi- 
nance and accounting, data processing, 
warehousing and distribution.

American Stores makes a move to Calif. 


IRVINE, Calif. — American Stores Co. announced it 

will move four of its 464 employees from its main head- 

uarters in Salt Lake City to a building here July 1 and call 
this its new headquarters facility. 

The firm rationalizes the move by saying it wants to be 
closer to one of its major markets. 

The four will be in the same building that houses the 
company’s Skaggs Alpha Beta division headquarters, 
which has been located here since last year, according to 
Michael Holt, vice president of investor and government 
relations. 

Holt said the remaining 460 employees in Salt Lake will 
—_ as the branch office support staff for American 

tores. 

In addition to operating —— Alpha Beta stores in 
Southern California, American Stores’ Osco drug store di- 
vision also has a strong presence in the area. 


Neuman headquarters goes state-of-art 


PATERSON, N. J. — Neuman Wholesale Drug Co. 
plans to move to a new administrative and warehouse fa- 
cility in Ridgefield, N. J., by mid-summer. 

Designed by Jack Frost Associates of California, the 
105,000-square-foot building will double Neuman’s space 
and incorporate a state-of-the-art computer system for or- 
der processing, among other efficiency features. 

“The new home warehouse will allow us to more than 


double our current output comfortably,” said president 
Sam Toscano.

When you hold a trade show for an industry as 
diverse as the $31.3 billion Housewares Industry, 
manufacturers know there's no single time of year 
that will be absolutely perfect for everyone. So why 
all the excitement about NHMAs midyear show? 

Because manufacturers and buyers alike, all 
know what is perfect—and that’s the way NHMA 
has continually brought the Industry together for 
nearly 50 years. This July will be no exception. 
That's why so many companies have registered 
early—with more and more streaming in every day. 

Here is an all-new midyear event filled with new 
products and new ideas. NHMA members/ 
exhibitors will be displaying more than one mil- 
lion products within 400,000 square feet under 
one roof. Many of these exhibitors have scheduled 
product introductions and special promotional 
activities expressly around this show, so that 
Housewares buyers and merchandisers can pre- 
view new products and fine-tune their merchan- 
dising plans for the months ahead. 

It truly is a “Customers Show.” And being there 
means being abreast of the latest Industry ideas, 


So be sure to be on hand. Because this show is 
the best way to stay at the forefront of the House- 
wares Industry—hands down.

the market’s going, and the 
middle seems to getting 
squeezed out of the picture, 
said one chain drug merchan- 
diser in the South. “There 
doesn’t seem to be much de- 
mand in the middle anymore.” 

The low end of the market, 
however, appears to holding 
up, he said. “The guy who 
comes in with a dollar and 
wants a simple, on-the-spot

lashlights and disposables

eral market, where the custom-

the thing. Maybe it’s too both- 
ersome for today’s consumer to 
do that.”

Lucky accepts American Stores’ offer 


DUBLIN, Calif. — Lucky Stores ended its efforts to re- 
main independent by agreeing May 20 to a $65-per-share, or 
$2.5 billion, sweetened offer from American Stores. 

American Stores’ Alpha Beta stores are expected to be 
converted to the Lucky lo 
American Stores has said it intends to put Lucky’s manage- 
ment in charge of the combined operations, which will have 
headquarters here. “Lucky, with the combination of Alpha 
Beta, will become the largest supermarket chain in Califor- 
nia, with eng $8 billion in sales and more than 550 stores,” 

airman and ceo, John M. Lillie. 

Under the agreement, American Stores, which plans to 
move its headquarters from Salt Lake City to Irvine, Calif., 
in July, continued its tender offer for all Lucky shares. 
Lucky’s board terminated its April 28 merger agreement 
with Gibbons, Green, van Amerongen for $61-per-share. 


Revco D.S. amends revoiving credit line 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Revco D.S. has amended the 
terms of its revolving credit facility with its banks to give the 
company more flexibility in man 


and low-price strategy, and 


aging cash flow, 


Revco’s direct borrowings under the $112 million revolv- 
ing credit facility had been limited to $60 million. With the 
amended facility, the company’s direct borrowings are limit- 
ed only by the outstanding amount of letters of credit. 

“These new terms provide us greater access to the funds 
available under our credit facility and demonstrate our bank- 
ers’ support for Revco’s financial objectives,” said William P. 
Holmes, Revco cfo. “This will assist us until we implement 
the capital restructuring plan that we are developing with 
Drexel Burnham Lambert.”

Longs adds new flexibility 
to store format approach 


By Pamela Krein 

WALNUT CREEK, Calif. 
— Longs Drug Stores will con- 
tinue to emphasize market 
flexibility in store openings 
throughout the rest of 1988, 
said president Bob Long. 

Speaking at the chain’s an- 
nual shareholders meeting 
here last month, Long said the 
limited availability of 25,000- 
square-foot sites—which is 
Longs’ average size—and the 
increased presence of combos 
has forced Longs to seek alter- 
native ways to grow. 

“Today’s varied market- 
place calls for a diversity of re- 
tail applications,” Long said. 

The 231-store chain has 
shown the course it will take 
earlier this spring. In March, 
Longs opened its first Longs 
Pharmacy in a downtown mall 
in San Diego. The store is 
12,000 square feet, with 9,704 
square feet of selling space— 
less than half the chain’s usual 
size. While the chain said the 
store was not a prototype, 
Longs executives did admit 
the concept could provide the 
chain with a platform from 
which to launch a small-store 
format. 

Later this year, Longs will 
open a 17,000-square-foot 
store in Davis, Calif., which 


DRUG STORE NEWS, June 6, 1988 


will play to the market by in- 
cluding this area’s agricultural 
background in the store’s de- 
cor. 

Long said in all the drug 
chain will open 12 to 15 stores 
this year, with five of these 
sites already operating. Ex- 
cept for one in Hawaii, the 
chain’s growth will be in Cali- 
fornia, the chain’s largest 
market. 

Long said market adapt- 
ability, along with better cus- 
tomer service, strong phar- 
macy sales, expense and 
inventory controls, and a re- 
alignment of stores were im- 
portant factors in Longs’ fiscal 
1988 performance. During the 
year, Long said the chain pro- 
duced average sales per store 
of $7.8 million, and sales per 
square foot of selling space of 
. ae 

Continuing its strong per- 
formance, Long released the 
chain’s first quarter results at 
the meeting, which showed 
Longs achieved a 20 percent 
increase in net income and a 7 
percent increase in sales. The 
gains brought Longs’ net in- 
come to $13.3 million on sales 
of $450 million for the quarter 
ended April 28. 

For the fiscal year overall, 
$41 million in capital expendi- 


tures will go toward new 
stores and remodels, Lon 
said. This compares wit 
$50,000 per store the chain 
spent last year on remodeling, 
excluding the money spent to 
renovate 12 acquired Osco 
stores. 

As updating continues, 
Longs is also looking to im- 
prove select areas of opera- 
tions, such as inventory man- 
agement. Long said an 
inventory me me sys- 
tem introduced last year in 
some stores “accelerates in- 
ventory turns and reduces in- 
ventory levels, while eliminat- 
ing out of stock situations.” 

ong said once all stores 
adapt this inventory system 
the chain could add $20 million 
dollars in working capital. 

At the same time, Long said 
the company is studying the 
“possibility of more pore Shay

sult P<! set blame cost of 
goods.” While the study is due

would supply an alternative

ings in purchasing costs. 


Maxidrug’s 4th deep-discount unit bows 


EAST SPRINGFIELD, 
Mass. — Maxidrug opened its 
fourth deep-discount store here 
May 18, in “the most active re- 
tail area of Springfield,” said 
Michel Coutu, president of the 
U.S. offshoot of the Jean Coutu 
Group based in Quebec. 

The 15,000-square-foot (sell- 
ing) store, situated amid “lots 
of malls, retailers, restaurants 
and food stores,” was at one 
time a theater, and its high ceil- 
ings allow for 7-foot-tall gondo- 
las throughout. 

The store’s size and mix are 
similar to Maxidrug’s third 
unit, opened last fall in Pitts- 


field, with a heavy emphasis on 
sundries. Pharmacy gains im- 
pact here in its location by the 
entrance. 

Maxidrug touted the openin 
with billboards, radio spots an 
a news r insert featuring 
such specials as 2-liter Coca- 
Cola at 77 cents, Lay’s potato 
chips at 66 cents and three rolls 
of Marcal paper towels for 88 
cents. Makeup artists were on 
hand for the launch, which also 
featured prizes including trips, 
VCRs and bicycles. 

The chain, representing the 
parent company’s $10 million 
expansion into Massachusetts, 


has developed a family of car- 
toonlike pen ingen to — rec- 
ognition with shoppers and un- 
derline its “fun store” image: 
Big Max, the original charac- 
ter, has been joined by Mama 
Max and three little shoppers, 
who appear on fliers and signs. 

The Jean Coutu Group is 
also mo new stores: one 
opened in Laval West (Que- 
bec) May 5, and three others 
are scheduled to open this 
month and the next, in La- 
chute and Gaspe, Quebec, and 
in Hawkesbury, Ontario. The 
Canadian chain’s total store 
count will be 141 by mid-July.

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 6, 1988 


Prerecorded videotapes 


Ample variety, competitive prices and a display area that allows for comfortable 
browsing help build tape rental business at Raley’s, Woodland, Calif. 


Chains’ experimentation spurs 
profits for prerecorded videos 


P 


rerecorded videotapes have 
continued to inspire experimen- 
tation among drug chains, 
which are testing the relative values 
of renting vs. buying inventory, pric 
ing philosophies, and what level of as- 
sortments are needed. 

With their multiple locations and 
quick shopping slant, drug chains, as 
well as supermarkets, convenience 
stores and mass merchandisers, have 
gained successes in prerecorded 
tapes, as a highly- ented retail 
market undergoes a shakeout and 
consolidation. 

“Mom and Pop” specialty stores 
and smaller specialty chains—their 
ap ens battered as tape prices 

ead down—are being absorbed by 
the larger ones. 

Specialty stores accounted for 50 
percent of prerecorded videotape unit 
shipments in 1987. Drug stores ac- 
counted for 2 percent, according to 
EBM Market h estimates. 

Rite Aid’s home video business has 
continued to grow. More than half the 
chain, or 1,013 stores now have video 
departments, with about 1,000 titles 
a store, and new departments will 

roiled out “at a measured pace,” a 
spokesman said. 

Chains including Genovese and 
Richardson’s Pharmacy, in Ann Ar- 
bor, Mich., have recently followed 
Rite Aid’s lead in owning videotape 
inventory. 

Genovese purchased inventory for 
50 stores, and rolled out a program of 
selling prerecorded tapes last month. 
Each store carries 47 titles, said buy- 
er Lenny Genovese. 


“With the prices of videos coming 
down, people are starting their own 
libraries,” said Genovese. 

by aE “ey from $4.95 to 
$29.95—will be in 4-foot racks with 
self-service Plexiglass doors at a front 
end location to allow oversight by 
checkout clerks. 

Genovese will discount top titles to 
compete with outlets that are dis- 
counting, such as convenience stores 
and mass merchandisers, and recover 

ins on non-promotional stock. 

_ A five-store chain, Richardson’s re- 
cently bought tape inventory for one 
store, feeling it could maintain a more 
current selection than by renting. 

“We felt if we have enough good ti- 
tles, it will be cost efficient,” said 
buyer Jim Decker, who plans to build 
an initial 175 title stock to 300. 

Richardson’s had been renting in- 
ventory from a video store chain, but 
felt the titles weren’t fresh. 

Decker expects the new program to 
boost profits as well as be a good 
traffic draw. (Tapes are along 16 feet 
of wall, with the title covers in 4-foot 
trays, and the tapes behind the 
counter. ) 

Decker felt the better selection 
would allow his chain to raise prices. 
Once at $1.99, with 99 cents for the 
second (matching convenience stores’ 
prices), videos were raised to $2.49 
and $1.99 for the second, just under 
what local specialty stores charge, 
Decker said. 

Despite Richardson’s approach, the 
trend with drug stores has been to- 
ward lower pricing, and heavily pro- 
motional activity, particularly at 


. Christmas time. 


Deep discounters such as Phar-Mor 
often lead the _ charge in their 
markets. Phar-Mor is known for its 
69 cents a night rental price. 

Drugs Plus, the first deep discount 
store opened by Cullum Companies, 
owner of Page gs, recently un- 
veiled an exteisive video rental de- 
partment in Dallas. ; 

It is set in a se shop, with its 
own checkout, and quickly accessible 
through one of two of the stores’ 
front doors. Carrying 6,000 titles, it 
should rent 4,000 to 5,000 a week at 
its 98 cents-a-night price, a store offi-

Cumberland purchases Kane chain 


MONTREAL — Cumberland Drugs Ltd. has boosted 
its store count to 46 with the purchase of Kane’s Super 
Drugmart, a six-unit chain in Montreal. Cumberland will 
reset the stores under its own banner over the next sever- 
al months, according to a spokesman. 


Imasco sells 6 Pharmaprix Carnavals 


MONTREAL — Imasco’s Koffler Group subsidiary has 
sold six Pharmaprix Carnaval deep-discount drug stores 
to McMahon Essaim, a division of grocery wholesaler Met- 
ro-Richilieu Inc. The stores will boost the company’s Ciou- 
tier drug store chain to a total of 20 units. 

The Pharmaprix Carnaval stores were once operated by 
Imasco’s Shoppers Drug Mart division. 


Big V adds four units in Ontario 


LONDON, Ontario — Big V has upped its store total in 
Ontario to 98 units with the purchase of four Canada 
Apothecary stores in its home market. 

The chain—one of Canada’s three largest drug chains— 
will reportedly peg sales of approximately $250 million 
(C ian) this year, comune with sales of $150 million 
last year. 


NACDS sets pharmaceutical conference 


ALEXANDRIA, Va. — Managed health care, elec- 
tronic claims processing and future technologies are 
among the issues NACDS members will examine during 
the association’s 3lst annual Pharmaceutical Conference 
scheduled for Aug. 28-31 in San Diego. 

To be held at the San Diego Marriott Hotel & Marina, 
the conference, on the theme, “Accepting the Challenge,” 
will also focus on bar coding and point-of-sale scanning in 
pharmacies. 

Mini-seminars will include such topics as catastrophic 
illness health insurance and prescription drug coverage, 
the future of pharmacy technicians, and the impact of an 
aging population on drug utilization.

By Elizabeth Parks 
he mascara/eye color 
category is starting to 
overtake the nail care 
segment as the hottest growth 
area in color cosmetics. 

According to reports from 
cosmetic/fragrance buyers 
around the country, the hot- 
test new product right now is 
Max Factor’s No Color Mas- 
cara. Buyers say the item is so 
hot and so unique that many 
chains sold out “practically 
overnight,” and then they had 
trouble restocking because 
Max Factor couldn't keep up 
with the demand. 

A few chains are still wait- 
ing for their first shipments, 
and the typical comment from 
these buyers is “if we had it, it 
would be the hottest thing in 
our stores.” 


Growth segments 


Buyers also say that al- 
though No Color is making the 
biggest splash in their stores 
right now, all their mascara 
lines are selling very well. In 
fact, most buyers say the mas- 
cara segment is currently 
their fastest growing area in 
cosmetics. 

In Kansas City, Gwen Bat- 
chelor, the cosmetic supervi- 
sor for Dot, reports that all 
her mascara lines are grow- 
ing. “Cover Girl’s Lash Prim- 
er is doing very well,” she 
says, “and so is their Sensitive 
Eyes Mascara. L‘Oréal’s Lash 
Out is doing well, and Maybel- 


line’s Ultra Thick Lash is 
strong. They’re really all do- 
ing well.” 

n Detroit, David Van 
Howe at Arbor also reports 
that all his mascara lines are 
selling well; in Alabama, the 
cosmeticians for Harco Drug 
report they also are seeing 
such a trend, and in the West, 
Longs Drug sources also say 
mascara is selling well. 

A few buyers report that 
some shades right now are 
selling better than others. 
Several said their best sellers 
are the basic black and brown 
mascaras and the cobalt blue. 
One source said the purple 
shades were not selling well at 
all in her stores because “it 
doesn’t bring out the eye.” 


Nail treatment sales 


Last year the total nail care 
category was the fastest 
growing segment in most drug 
stores, but this year nail sales 
have slowed down. The treat- 
ment section of nail care is still 
very strong, but buyers 
across the country report that 
sales of artificial nails are 
down “considerably,” and col- 
or is erratic. About half the 
chains we talked to reported 
their color sales were flat, 
while the rest said they were 
up, sometimes as much as 30 
percent. 

In nail treatments, most 
buyers sa their sales are still 
going up between 20 percent 


to 25 percent this year. The 


DeLore line is frequently 
mentioned as a strong seller, 
and several buyers also sin- 
gled out Sally Hansen’s new 
Nail Therapy which is en- 
riched with vitamins, aloe and 
collagen. 

Most buyers also say that 
Revion’s new Calcium Gel is 
starting off very strong, and 
that L’Oréal’s Rocio Grow, 
the La Sallé No Chip, and 
Del’s Sally Hansen Maximum 
Growth are also doing very 
well. 

Both the full Sally Hansen 
and the La Sallé treatment 
lines get good reviews, with 
most buyers saying their 
strongest sales are for the nail 
hardeners. 

Many buyers also reported 
sales were ity | on the 
Revlon Liquid Nail Wrap line. 

Artificial nails down 


Almost every buyer we in- 
terviewed said artificial nail 
sales were down, even for cat- 
egory leader Lee Nails. “Peo- 
ple are afraid of buying the ar- 
tificial nails because of the 
bacteria you can get. Also, the 
tabs are a nuisance. Many 
women report they just don't 
keep the nail on,” said a source 
for Brooks Drug. 

However, a few buyers said 
that even though their artifi- 
cial nail sales were down, the 
professional lines in their 
stores were outperforming 
the category, as were the nails 
made by West Cabot Indus-

Fragrance buyers are reporting that many women customers prefer to buy several 
brands of fragrances rather than one so they can have a “wardrobe of fragrances” to 
match their different moods. Focal point displays are a key way to capture more of 
these impulse sales. 


Chains brace themselves for 
a flood of new fragrance intros 


Thef: ce category in mass drug 
stores is about to get a strong injection 
of new product excitement. 

A number of manufacturers have 
new launches planned for later this 
year, and several others are relaunch- 
ng or revamping older and more es- 
tablished lines. 

In men’s fi ces, which is a 

wth area for drug chains, Shulton is 
unching a new scent called Santa Fe 
targeted to the younger, contempo- 


~~ male.

last year. They are also continuing to

maintain share for their traditional 
best selling brand, Old Spice. 

Shulton is also Pes Pierre 
Cardin which has been relatively soft 
in Fang for the past year.

New in women’s fragrance 


In the women’s segment, which is 
flat in drug stores, Revion is launching 
Trouble, which is its first internally de- 
veloped scent since Jontue in 1975. 

Revlon is also reacting to the success 
of its Xia Xiang fragrance by introduc- 


ing a new Charlie Oriental fragrance 


this spring. 

Xia Xiang, which was launched by 
Charles of The Ritz before Revlon ac- 
quired Ritz, was the surprise success 


of 1987 and cosmetic buyers said the 


scent is still selling well in their stores. 

Revlon is also bringing back the for- 
mula for the original Intimate. The 
new Original Intimate will be sold in 
line with Revion’s Modern Intimate. 

Almay has a new “hypo-allergenic” 
fragrance that, if successful, would be 
a unique new addition to the category. 
Almay also plans to spend at least 
million to support the launch. 

Calvin Klein has a new prestige fra- 
grance debuting which, with its $17 
million ad budget, could create a new 
a for ADF sales. It’s called 

ternity, and the distribution for the 
first year will be limited to 700 doors. 

Prince Matchabelli has its first spray 
cologne launching as an extension of its 
Impulse Body Spray line. It’s called 
Tres L.A. and it will be supported by a 
$7 million ad campaign. 

Coty is also working on a new wom- 
en’s scent which will probably launch 
later this year. 


Buyer’s assessments 


Many buyers said they are a little 
“overwhelmed” by all this new excite- 
ment in the category. Some said it 
could be just the shot in the arm the 
category needs in their stores, but oth- 
ers are afraid that so many new prod- 
ucts, all coming out during the third 
and fourth quarters, could confuse the 
consumer and make it hard for any in- 
dividual new product to stand out “as 
something special.” 

“I don’t ever remember seeing so 
many things come out at once like this 
before,” said Marlene Isaccson of Aus- 
tin Drug. “It’s a little confusing, even 
for me as a buyer.” 

“T think it will be good for my fra- 
grance sales,” said David Van Howe, 
the senior cosmetics buyer for Arbor 
Drug. “Whenever _ have new prod- 
uct ches, it helps the overall cate- 

ory. Right now without the new 

unches, my f ce sales are up 
about 4 percent. Hopefully with the 
new launches, I may be able to end the 
year with sales up between 8 percent 
and 10 percent, said Van Howe.” 

At By time, most buyers hadn’t 
seen all the new brands yet, and some 
had seen them but not smelled them all.

optimisim for Trouble, Sante Fe, Mex-
