@ Just 17 percent of all American women who use hair 
styling products buy them most often in drug stores. Most 
women who use hair styling aids (22 percent) buy them 
most often in beauty salons, and 17 percent said they buy 
styling products most often in food stores. 


@ Most women said that they pick a store to shop for styl- 
ing aids on the basis of its convenience to their home or 
work and on prices. Very few women said they picked a 
store because of its selection, service or other amenities. 


e@ Skin moisturizers are very important to most women. 
Seventy percent of the respondents said they used a skin 
moisturizer in the past month. 


®@ Forty-eight percent of the respondents said they use 
skin moisturizers more today than in the past. 


@ Most American women chose Oil of Olay as their favor- 
ite moisturizer brand. 


® Just 21 percent of all women said they buy their mois- 
turizers most often in a drug store. 


@ Forty-six percent of all respondents said service was ei- 
ther somewhat or very important to them when buying a 
moisturizer. 

@ Sixty-four a of all women used a hair spray in the 
past month; 28 percent used a styling gel; 35 percent a 
mousse; and 13 percent a spritz.

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 20, 1988 


Teenagers are important skin care shoppers, and drug store buyers 
say the best way to catch their attention is with eye-appealing, col- 
orful POS displays. 


Gallup: women feel

the marketing of cosmetics to- 
day are: anti-aging and skin 
a 6g 

hether women are shop- 
ping department stores for 
cosmetics or their corner drug

In the cosmetic user survey 
that Gallup did for Drug Store 
News this year, seven out of 
every ten women interviewed 
reported that they had used a 
moisturizer within the past 
month. 

The heaviest users, as you 
might expect, were women 
between the ages of 25 and 49. 


effective skin care Is 
heart of true beauty

women in the 18 to 24 age and 
women in the 50-plus age 


group. |

much publicity about skin care 
needs today that women are 
starting to try moisturizers at 
a —— age, and they seem 
to be using moisturizers 
much more consistently and 
seriously. 

When we compared this 
year’s Gallup survey to last 
year’s—when we looked at us- 
age for color cosmetics and 
fragrances—we found that 
women today use moisturizers 
more often than eye liners or 
eye shadows. In addition, 
women today use moisturizers 
as often as they use their mas- 
caras.

think they can become beauti- 
ful by just putting on make- 
up,” said one cosmetic buyer.

ty starts with the skin and that 
you have to eat right, sleep 
right and make sure you mois- 
turize your skin.”

moisturizers about as much as 
they did several years ago. 


Facial products with SPF 
A surprisingly high per- 


centage of women also use 
moisturizers or facial cosmet- 


ics with sun protection ingre- 
dients, and one in five uses the 
trendy and usually expensive 
lotions that are specifically 
marketed as anti-aging or re- 
juvenation creams. 

Women between the ages of 
35 and 49—-the age group in 
which skin damage becomes a 
major concern—are the most 
frequent users of cosmetics 
with sun protection factors. 
However, the woman who is 
50 or older is the best candi- 
date for purchasing anti-aging 
creams right now. 

In terms of brand prefer- 


ences, Oil of Olay, despite the 
emergence of so many glam- 
ourous department store 
brands, is still the favorite 
choice of American women. 
Fully 13 percent of all the 
women in our survey picked 
Oil of Olay as their favorite 
brand.

vorite choice of women aged 
35 to 49, with Olay a close sec-

In 1988, women seem to 
have two major cosmetic con- 
cerns: the suppleness of their 
skin, and the shine and tex- 
ture of their hair. 

While the overall hair care 
category is flat these days, the 
styling segment, which is 
made up of products that add 
sheen, volume and hold to the 
hair, is growing dramatically. 
Some segments like gels and 
spritzes are up 20 percent to 
40 percent, according to mar- 
ket research estimates. 

Women are telling drug 
store cosmetic clerks that 


the frequency of use.

spritzes, and now they are ev- 
erywhere on the market. For 
a while, women were shying 
away from sprays, but now 
just about everyone uses 
them.” 

In this year’s Gallup cos- 
metic survey, Drug Store 
News found evidence that 
bears out this perception. 
More than a third of the wom- 
en in our survey reported they 
were using hair sprays more

than just about anything available on the mass

One treatment begets another in nail care 


It was so simple in 
the days when 
Madge, the Palmolive 
lady, told us to soak 
our hands in dish- 
washing liquid. Now- 
adays, marketers of 
nail care products 
have other, far more 
complicated ideas. 

In the “an apple a 
day keeps the doctor 
at bay” tradition, and with the 
help of chemists and market 
researchers, marketers are 
making the time-file-and-buff 
history, while ushering in the 
era of cuticle massage creams, 
night nail defenses, and pro- 
tective coats and glazes that 
battle brittleness and break- 
age. Now, following the high- 
end skin treatment trail, there 
are dozens of new nail treat- 
ment products, dramatic in- 
creases in shelf and advertising 
space to sell them, and millions 
more tailored hands shelling 
out millions more dollars to the 
new Midases (but unable to 
undo shoe lace knots or pull on 
pantyhose fearlessly. ) 

Last year, “ope de- 
signed to lengthen, strength- 
en and beautify the horny 
plates that protect fingertips 


Bernice Kanner is a senior 
editor with New York maga- 
zine. 


Eye on the | 


raked in $750 million, more 
than 50 percent more than 
their sales five years ago. By 
the end of this year, nail care 

roduct sales should reach 

75 million, and by 1992 they 
should climb to $1.3 billion, 
said David Weiss, president of 
Packaged Facts. 

Credit the new product ava- 
lanche, its domino effect and 
the new receptivity of self- 
confident women, said Weiss. 
More than 100 new nail care 
products were introduced last 
year—and even more are ex- 
pected this year—com 
to 31 in 1984. Many attracted 
new customers to the market. 

Once in the market, many 
women added to their trove, 
voluntarily or otherwise. 
“Once women put on lacquer, 
they have to take it off, they 
focus on their hands, and that 
instigates a snowball effect 
where one treatment begets 
another,” said Nick Mottola, 
director of marketing devel- 


opment at Elizabeth Arden. 
At the same time, so many of 
the products damage nails, 
(lacquers can stain and artifi- 
cial nails can damage the nail 
beds) so women must turn to 
remedy products. “It’s like af- 
ter you’ve had your hair col- 
ored, you're forced to use re- 

pair products,” said Mottola. 
The fact that manicure mad- 
ness has flourished in salons 
within the last few years sug- 

ests the home market wi 
m even more. This year 


some 160,000 technicians na- 


tionwide will manicure almost 
81 million a of hands (at an 
average of $8.20), or roughly 
9.2 percent more than the 74 
million they manicured in 
1987, says Jody Byrne, editor 
of American Salon Magazine. 
(They will also administer 
about 19 million icures at 
an average cost of $16.95.) 


The ripple effect 


Still, only two percent of 
women get a professional 
manicure weekly, 17 percent 
occasionally, and 81 percent 
never. “The ripple effect 
means that this year treat- 
ment sales should grow 20 per- 
cent and become, by itself, a 
$600 million segment,” said 
Paul Spindel, vice president at 
Revion. He added that the ac- 
tion is mainly in the mass mar- 
ket, bypassing the prestige 


lines which usually set the 
pace. 

And what a pace it is. Max 
Factor’s Second Nail, a nail 
saver launched last year, “is a 
runaway hit,” declares prod- 
uct manager Sharon Levan. 
Nails Again, a $10-a-bottle, 
one-step restorative, has seen 
sales climb 180 percent since 
its introduction last year, 
prompting developer eo 
mond Cohen to promise a $27 
cuticle mousse in September. 

Cutex now has cuticle mois- 
turizer and vitamin-packed 
nail developers. Cover Girl 
has hardeners and healers, in- 
cluding a ridge filler primer 
and glaze for tiny flaws and 
white spots. Revlon has an 11- 
product Neat Touch line 
which includes disco-pads 
(two-faced pink files) and 
black beauties (emery boards 
especially designed for fake 
nails), as well as an enamel 
correcting pen that erases er- 
rors and a calcium gel nail 
builder. 

Avon’s Ultra Touch line 
comes with mending tapes and 
a nighttime defense that “re- 
stores moisture to dry, dis- 
tressed nails while you sleep. ' 
Chanel has instant thickeners, 
Christian Dior has lubricating 
oils, and Sally Hansen has Re- 
new a Nail, night-time revita- 
lizer, and Nail Therapy, a con- 
ditioning and repair gel. 


Although treatments are 
the hot growth area, polish is 
the far larger segment and the 
reason people buy. Today’s 
color customers insist on con- 
ditioners in the enamel, great- 
er durability, and easy appli- 
cation, said Barbara asinski, 
group director of Cutex. In 
the meantime, however, 
they’re glitzing up the enamel 
packages they have with cus- 
tom glass, bread-faced bottles 
(instead of the typical round 
cylinder), and splashy graph- 
ics. 


Ads tout more than colors 


The manufacturers are ad- 
vertising more than just the 
colors. Revlon touts its lon 
lasting quality, color an 
shine, but also its pen delivery 
system. Maybelline shows a 
cue ball finish, and Max Fac- 
tor—after excellent test mar- 
ket results—contends that its 
enamels are diamond hard. 
Avon argues that no lacquers 
wear better. 

Perhaps more important 
now than segmenting sales is 
uniting women in the pursuit 
of treatments, suggested 
Spindel. “We want to get the 
message across that a treat- 
ment line is to the decorative 
end what a brush is to a comb, 
a horse to a carriage, even wa- 
ter to soap, that is, obvious 
coupling.”

Teenagers become important people for chain 


Teenagers are important 
customers for chain drug 
stores. 

According to our Gallup cos- 
metic user survey implement- 
ed this year, 27 percent of all 
young women ages 13 to 24 buy 
moisturizing products in regu- 
lar drug stores and 16 percent 
buy their styling aids in drug 
stores. One in every 10 cosmet- 
ic users ages 13 to 24 also sho 
discount drug stores for beau

air styling products. 

The study found that six out 
of every 10, 13- to 24-year olds 
use moisturizers and most 
women this age say they are us- 
ing items like moisturizers 
more often now than they were 
several years ago. 

In another study done by 
TEEN m ine in Los Ange- 
les, researchers found other ev- 
idence of teenage use of cos- 
metic products growing in 
intensity. 

According to the TEEN sur- 
vey, teenagers are using make- 
up at earlier and earlier ages, 
and they are using an increas- 
me hry variety of products.

@ 86 percent of all teenagers 
were wearing makeup by age 
13; and

with the season.

teenagers learn about cosmet-

source of information while 
television is a far distant third 
for information on cosmetics 
and ranks sixth as a purchase 
influence.

of all their respondents were 12 
or younger when they first 
started wearing makeup, and 
that face powders, blush, eye 
shadow, eye liners, mascaras 
and lipsticks or gloss were the 
most ently used products.

Shoppers Drug 
Mart is revamping its 
prototype for new 
stores, and in the pro-

highlight cosmetics 
while bringing the 
stores “into the 1590s.”

nue Road in Toronto that Shop- 
pers execs say will probably be 
the prototype for most future 
Shoppers, as well as the proto- 
type for most remodels of all 
“A” stores in the Shoppers 
chain. 

The Avenue Road store, a 
high-volume “A” store in an up- 
per income market, has a new 
signing package: new corporate 
interior and exterior colors of 
red and white, and a new layout 
and design for cosmetics. 

Arthur Konviser, vp-public 
affairs for Shoppers Drug 
Mart, says the new colors are 
“very gh epee They make 
us look like an exciting retail 
entity.”

ith average sales increases 
of 10 percent for their photo- 
video departments in 1987, 
and camera and film manufacturers 
keeping the heat on in their quest for 
new product breakthroughs, the na- 
tion’s drug chains continue to reap the 
rewards of the amateur photography 
boom of the 1980s. 

Laemerageay: § film and camera 
sales remain on the rise at chain drug 
store photo counters, in spite of the 
growth of one-hour minilabs and the 
increasing incursions of supermarkets 
and discount stores into the photofin- 
ishing market. 

Nevertheless, say drug retailers, 
the days of automatic sales increases at 
the photo counter are over. More and 
more drug chains are turning to photo 
marketing specialists to drive their 
photo services more aggressively, cre- 
ating or expanding positions for photo 
department marketing managers and 
boosting advertising support for the 
category. 

“Those who promote aggressively, 
offer convenient locations and market 
quality in their photofinishing, as well 
as price, will do well,” said one photo 
marketing manager for a major drug 
chain. 

“The business is more and more 
competitive,” added another chain ex- 
ecutive. 

Supermarkets, in particular, are 
makin ater inroads in photofinish- 
ing and film, and many are beginning 
to market cameras as they broaden 
their reach with combo stores and su- 
perstores. 

Another aggressive photo retailer is 
King Soopers, the leader in food and 
drug retailing in Denver, with 67 com- 
bo stores operating along Colorado’s 
Front Range. The chain opened its 
own photo processing plant 15 years 
ago, and remains the only supermar- 
ket retailer with its own large-scale de- 
veloping facility. 

Soopers makes a point of ad- 
vertising that fact, according to photo 
marketing manager Pat Greaser. Last 
month, it even featured a photo of its 
plant crew in its re circular. 

“We definitely believe in what we’ve 
done,” Greaser said. “With our own 
cree plant, the profitability is 
there, and we can offer better service 
to our customers. We have total con- 
trol over the quality of our prints, and 
more control over photo marketing 
events we want to create. Having our 
own plant gives us more promotional 
flexibility; we’re not restricted like we 
would be with an outside wholesaler.” 

It also allows King Soopers to under- 
cut many of its competitors in develop- 
ing prices. For the chain’s regular, 
one- to three-day service, processing 
for a roll of 24-exposure 35mm or 110

rug chains which have ven-

through the sale and rental of

they are up against large-scale, sophis- 
ticated video specialty stores which 
have already forced many smaller vid- 
eo vendors out of business and carved 
out the lion’s share of the rental mar- 
ket in many cities. 

“The video rental market continues 
to be in a state of flux,” reports the 
Photo Marketing Association in a clas- 
sic case of understatement. “While 
rental revenues on prerecorded video- 
cassettes climbed 20 percent in 1987, 
to $4.4 billion (retail), retailer attrition 
marches on.” 

It’s no secret that the market for 
blank and prerecorded videotapes is 
rife with competition and littered with 
business failures. It is also no secret 
that profits on sales and rentals— 
which were once easy to come by—are 
under increasing pressure, aS more 
and more competitors battle for share. 

But the biggest development affect- 
ing the video rental market over the 
past two years has been the consolida- 
tion of the industry, as a handful of 
chain video giants like Blockbuster 
Entertainment ge up former com- 
petitors and push aside smaller, inde-

dustry,” observes the PMA in its most

Blockbuster and other large-scale 
video specialists have quickly gobbled 
a large share of the rental market 
through aggressive expansion and a 
huge commitment of capital for inven- 
tory. In giant, conveniently located 
settings, they offer 10,000 or more 
movie titles, including dozens of copies 
of the hottest new movies, compared 
with the average offering of 1,000 to 
2,000 offered by most other operators, 
including drug chains. 


Service merits a higher fee 


For this, Blockbuster now pays 
$89.95 or more for the hottest new titles, 
recouping its investment with higher- 
than-average rental prices of $3 aimed 
at high customer traffic. Customers, it 
has been proven, are willing to pay more 
than the current average rental price of 
$2.02, if they have a good chance of find- 
ing a tape they want and keeping it long- 
er than one day—two conveniences 
Blockbuster specializes in. 

Coupled with growing competition 
from heavyweights like Blockbuster, 
drug chains must now battle a —— 
ing array of non-specialty video cen- 
ters to gain market share. Some pow- 
erful examples include Southland 
Corp.’s 7-Eleven—which now offers 
99-cent overnight rentals in at least 
6,500 of its convenience stores—and 
Phar-Mor, the expanding off-price 
chain which has introduced nt 
overnight rentals on a few hundred 
fast-turning titles in some of its newest 
outlets. Both operators key in on the 
convenience aspects of the business, 
sacrificing margins for a boost in store 
traffic. 

_ Another sticking point has been the 
rising cost of “A” movie titles—the 
most popular new releases. Prices on 


“A” titles have risen to $89.95 on aver- 
age, squeezing margins further for 
vendors who depended on low rental 
prices to compete. The high movie 
prices also pressure drug chains, 
which can’t commit the capital for 
more than a few copies of each hot title 
for each store, but can’t get along with- 
out the “A” offerings, either. 

The reason is obvious. Of the 300 
new feature films released by the 14 
major home video suppliers in 1987, 
the 78 best-sellers accounted for fully 
65 percent of all revenues, according to 
Rand Bleimeister, Nelson Entertain- 
ment executive vp. According to one 
study, video retailers already lose 2 
million rentals a week because con- 
sumers can’t find the movie they want. 

Despite the increasing competition, 
industry consolidation and high inven- 
tory costs, a number of drug chains 
have followed industry pioneer Rite 
Aid into the movie rental business, and 
blank tapes have become an indispens- 
able part of the drug store mix. For 
drug retailers, the rental business 
must serve as a traffic draw and cus- 
tomer convenience as well as a profit 

roducer. Chains like Walgreen’s, 

andall’s Food Markets and Wellb 
have successfully welded a limited vid- 
eo selection in some stores onto their 
agnosis. | departments by hold- 
ing down overhead and, in some cases, 
by leasing tapes instead of buying 
them outright. 

Bob Gowens, executive finance 
and administration for Randall’s, ar- 
gues that video rental centers can be 
pg cm and a good traffic build- 
er if retailers prepare the proper 
groundwork. Many questiens about in- 
ventory levels, variety and turnover 
can be answered by studying the small 
equipment or home appliance rental 
business, Gowens said. In addition, he 
added, retailers should develop finan- 
cial models and make pe pong de- 
cisions avout the kind of movies they 
want to carry. 


The ‘R’ world 


“You must decide how far you will go 
into the ‘R’ world,” Gowens said. “The 
movies you rent make a public state- 
ment of who you are. . . we want our 
video center to be family-oriented.” 

One recent entrant into the movie 
rental business is Discount Drug Mart, 
the 26-store chain based in Medina, 
Ohio. “We’re getting into videota 
rentals, with about seven or eight 
stores to begin with, as another cus- 
tomer convenience,” said Dennis Wie- 
land, vp-finance. “We plan to offer cur- 
rent movies at $1.99 and 99 cents, 
along with 69-cent specials.”

Discounting and fashion keep sunglasses moving 


rug chains have kept sunglass- 

es as one of the fastest grow- 

ing general merchandise cate- 
— through everyday and seasonal 

iscounting. 

‘ Many chain executives feel that by 
regularly promoting the under-$20 
lines they most often carry, they can 
reach price points that conform to their 
stores as image, and compete 
against deep discounting competitors. 

A countervailing position holds, 
though, that it isn’t necessary to dis- 
count sunglasses, since sales are pri- 
marily fashion-driven. Chains with 
broad assortments meeting a range of 
fashion needs can achieve strong sales 
at full price. Higher-end glasses, 
above $30 and as high as $200, are also 
an alternative for drug stores if the 
products conform to the leading styles, 
7 drug chain merchandisers. 

ines by Bonneau, Opti-Ray, Visual 
Scene, Cool Ray, Opti-Shield and Fos- 
ter Grant have proven most successful 
for drug stores. 

Regular discounting seems to be the 
prevailing drug store industry trend. 
Although unit and dollar sales of sun- 
see increased from 1986 to 1987 in 

rug stores, the average price paid in 
iy stores declined, from $10.29 to 
$8.57, according to the Sunglass Asso- 
ciation of Amer'za (SAA). 

Among ail retail channels, the aver- 
age price rose from $6.85 to $7 in 1987, 
as sunglass retail sales hit the $1.3 bil- 
lion mark, the SAA said. 

Big B, Rix sage and Douglas 
Drugs all carry sunglasses pre-ticket- 
ed with everyday discounts off the 
manufacturers’ list price. 

Big B combines its everyday 20 per- 
cent discount with monthly 50-per- 


cent-off ads, which allow the stores to 
compete with chains such as Eckerd 
and K mart who are also discounting, 
said Bob Little, vp-store operations. 

Foster Grant and Opti-Ray assort- 
ments at Big B provide “good margins, 
even on sale,” although loss from 
shrink has to be factored out. Big B po- 
sitions racks to force the consumer to 
shop the front, allowing better surveil- 
lance, Little said. 

Rix Dunnington similarly offers ev- 
eryday 20 percent discounts on its 
Bonneau assortment, supplemented 
by spring and summer 50 percent-off 
promotions, said buyer Jay Weiner. 

“Everybody discounts glasses; 
CVS, Brooks, and all the mass mer- 
chandisers. We feel we should also,” 
said Weiner. 

A Bonneau program of tailoring the 
$10-to-$18 mix to individual stores’ 
needs has helped, and sales reps visit 
Rix’s Cape Cod, Mass. units twice a 
week in the summer months as op- 
posed to the normal monthly visit. 

Rix uses locked cases and two-sided 
racks to combat shrinkage. 

This year it is testing an Opti-Ray 
a Ss in five stores, Weiner said. 

ith an eye on low-pricing tactics b 
local discount department stores suc 
as Ann and Hope and deep discount- 
ers, including Woolworth’s Rx Place, 
Douglas Drug shows a 25 percent ev- 
eryday discount on its Foster Grant 
and Bonneau lines, said senior buyer 
Anna Iacono. The range at discount is 
$4.50 to $13.50. 

An April buy-one-get-one-free cou- 
pon offer for sunglasses was “tremen- 
dously successful” and sunglasses 
have been a growth category for Doug- 
las, Iacono said.

DRUG STORE NEWS/INSIDE PHARMACY, June 20, 1988 


| PTIARVACY 
Generic dispensing’s promise lies ahead 


IP17 


Third-party pressures and enhanced margins drive substitution, 


according to an exclusive Drug Store News/Inside Pharmacy study 


By Harold Cohen R.Ph. 

— impressive inroads generic 
drugs have made in the retail prescrip- 
tion marketplace over the past several 
the dispensing of generic drugs 

“ still not reached its fullest poten- 
tial. 

According to a survey of approxi- 
mately 700 pharmacists conducted by 
Drug Store News, it is estimated that 
over half (56 percent) of all prescrip- 
tions at chain and independent drug 
stores are currently being filled ge- 
nerically. But the potential for generi- 
cally filled prescriptions stands at 75 
percent of all prescriptions written. 

A more in-depth analysis shows that 
20 percent of all prescriptions filled by 
the pharmacists were written for the 
generic to begin with, and another 55 
percent were written for the brand but 
with “generic substitution permissi- 
ble,” yer | a 75 percent potential for 
generically filled prescriptions. Con- 
Many 25 percent of the prescrip- 
tions filled were written for the brand 
only with no substitution permitted 
(creating an 80 percent potential for 
prescriptions filled with the branded 
product). 

Pressure from cost conscious third- 
party qT and a heavy depen- 
dence by retail pharmacists to keep 
gross profit percentages in their pre- 
scription departments high, have cre- 
ated a situation where the bulk of gen- 
erics currently being dispensed at 
retail pharmacies are substituted for 
brand name drugs. 

On close examination of the study’s 
data, nearly two-thirds (64 percent) of 
all generic prescriptions dispensed 
were the result of a substitution for a 
branded drug product. 

While much of the heavy substitu- 
tion practices at chain and independent 
pharmacies can be attributed to more 
discretionary power among staff phar- 
macists and sletiat understanding of 
generics on the part of the consumer, 
there is also a trend toward more phy- 
sicians writing “substitution permissi- 
ble” on prescriptions for branded drug 
products. 

According to the study, there was a 
two percent increase over last year in 
prescriptions written that allow ge- 
neric substitution (53 percent in 1987 
compared to 55 percent in 1988). At the 
same time, there has been a two per- 
cent decrease in the number of pre- 
scriptions written for brand only, with 
no generic substitution permissible (27 
percent in 1987 compared to 25 percent 
in 1988). The number of prescriptions 
written generically remained un- 
changed at 20 percent. 

A rosy picture was painted by phar- 
macists’ perceptions of the substitu- 
tion thant. To no one’s real surprise, 
the study showed that 90 percent of

key to generic substitution 


NEW YORK — One of the 
major complaints pharmacists 
have voiced over the dispens-

in finding the right generic 
product to substitute. 

Through a survey answered 
by approximately 700 phar- 
macists nationwide, Drug 
Store News has been able to 
extrapolate major factors in 
pharmacists’ decisions to sub- 
stitute one particular product 
over another. 

Although recent price wars 
in the generic industry would 
lead one to believe that cost 
savings to the customer was of

Liability increase feared 


What’s holding pharma- 
cists back from prescribing? 
For the most part, fear of 
increasing their liability. Of 
all chain and independent 
pharmacists surveyed, 57 
percent cited personal liabil- 
ity as the No. 1 deterrent to 
prescribing. 

“You bet they’re con- 
cerned about liability,” said 
Rod Presnell, executive di- 
rector of the Florida State 
Board of Pharmacy, “but I 
don’t think it’s a valid con- 
cern. If I were a pharmacist 
in practice today, I would 
not choose the issue of liabil- 
ity. After all, there is an as- 
sumed liability that goes 
along with just practicing 
the profession of pharmacy.” 

Powers also dismisses the 
concerns about liability, call- 
ing it “a smokescreen.” “The 
same people who raised the 
issue of liability in drug 
product selection are raisin 
the issue again,” he said. “If 
that’s the case, you’d be 
afraid to drive to work in 


the morning because you 
have liability. We all have 
professional liability. Do you 
think Eckerd would allow 
their pharmacists to pre- 
scribe if it was so danger- 
ous?” 

Eckerd indeed allows its 
poe to prescribe, 

ut like Rite Aid, which op- 
erates 195 drug stores in 
Florida, does not mandate 
it. Mike Zagorac, vp of pub- 
lic relations for Eckerd, said 
that the chain was not “an 
advocate of the Florida law” 
but that, when it became ap- 
parent that the law would be 
passed, the chain worked 
with the Florida Pharmacy 
Association to assure that 
the law would be appropri- 
ate for pharmacists and con- 
sumers. 

“We were et, con- 
cerned about liability,” he 
said. “We wanted to make 
sure we were adequately 
covered. Since the law was 
adopted, I’ve seen no prob- 
lems with it.” 

“When the law was 
passed, we had an obligation 
to prepare our pharmacists,” 
said Stewart Turley, chair- 
man and president of Eck- 
erd, at a press conference 
held at the NACDS Annual 
Meeting. “It wouldn’t bother 
me in the least if the Florida 
law went away. I hope it 
doesn’t spread to other 
states.”

TITUSVILLE, Fla. — Red Camp, owner of 
Camp Pharmacy here, has been prescribing since 
the —— began two years ago. 

. ro ee in the program the same way I par- 
ticipate in drug selection or anything to my advan- 
tage,” he said. “I can’t survive in the marketplace if 
I’m just another pharmacist.” 

Camp’s pharmacy is one of 16 in an area with 
30,000 residents—and competition is tough. Al- 
though he concedes that prescribing the drugs the 
law owe him to without a doctor’s prescription rep- 
resents only a small part of his business, he feels that 
offering the service gives him an edge on the compe- 
tition. 

“In terms of dollars, it’s not a tremendous financial 
boon. The dollars would be negligible. In the best 
month, prescribin only represents a few hundred 
dollars,” he said. “But it’s hard to measure the value 
in terms of dollars. As far as I’m concerned, prescrib- 
ing is only one more tool that allows me to be more 
aggressive, more innovative.” 

amp primarily prescribes pediculocides, topical 
cortisones, and anti-histamines from a list of drugs 
provided by the limited formulary under the law.

DRUG STORE NEWS/INSIDE PHARMACY, June 20, 1988 


‘| can’t survive in the 
marketplace if I'm just 
another pharmacist.’ 


—Red Camp 
owner 
Camp Pharmacy 


“There are certain patients who feel that if the 

roduct they are using requires a prescription, it’s 

better ” he said. And the people who want that kind 
of treatment represent a market to Camp. 

“Head lice are a problem in any warm climate. This 
law allows pharmacists to treat patients effectively 
and under the Medicaid law as well. A mother who 
brings her kid in with head lice doesn’t have to spend 
money to take the kid or kids to the doctor but can be 
reimbursed.” 

And, contrary to some pharmacists’ opinions, con- 
sumers, claims Camp, are happy about the law. 


“Patients don’t have much of a problem with our 
competence in treating them,” he said. “They get a 
little upset when we can’t treat their strep throat.” 
He’s making sure that more consumers are aware of 
the services he and other prescribing pharmacists of- 
fer by speaking to consumer groups and displaying 
brochures explaining the service in his pharmacy. 

Camp doesn’t buy other pharmacists’ fears about 
provoking physician ire and increasing his liability. 

“The perception that we’re going into the doctor 
business depends on how well we communicate the 
reality of the law to physicians,” he said. “I know of 
an instance where a pharmacist cleared all of the bro- 
chures detailing the service out of his store because a 
doctor in the complex was so upset about it. The next 
day the doctor was referring patients back to him 
telling them ‘You don’t need to see me for that. Go 
see Joe, he’ll write you a prescription.’ Once physi- 
cians understand the law, there’s no problem.” 

Liability is less of a problem for Camp. “That’s 
how we got into the mess that we are in now. We’re 
not only slow to accept change, we’re slow to accept 
responsibility,” he said. “The folks who are most suc- 
cessful are those who want to make decisions.”

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Perry caps management realignment 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drugs has named Peoples 
Drug veteran Richard Barker as executive vp and chief 
financial officer, filling a spot vacant since the resignation 
of Alvin Wander. 

Perry has also named Michael Klein, formerly of Baxter 
Travenol, as president of its Health Care Division. In ad- 
dition, the company has promoted vp, general counsel and 
secretary Bob Berlow to senior vp. 

Also, Gary Allen, executive group vp for drug store op- 
erations, has been named to the additional post of corpo- 
rate senior vp-store operations. 

Perry recently consolidated all drug store operations 
under Allen, who reports to company president David 
Schwartz. 

“These appointments take care of our senior realign- 
ment,” said vp-corporate communications Berl Falbaum.

Growth for condoms 
seen to continue 


hen Drug Store 
News surveyed re- 
tailers last year on 


what categories were the hot- 
test, it was no surprise that 
condoms showed strongly. 

Sales for the first eight 
months of 1987 were up 32 per- 
cent in dollars and 27 percent 
in units. And retailers predict- 
ed that this hot pattern would 
continue, and possibly build, 
in 1988. Merchants surveyed 
predicted 36.1-percent sales 
growth in the year. 

Chain merchandisers across 
the country reported strong 
demand, fueled by two major 
trends. As AIDS e pub- 
licized, le began to take 
better health precautions. 
Also, some alternate forms of 
birth control, such as the Pill 
and intra-uterine devices, are 
perceived as less desirable by 
consumers who seek non-inva- 
sive methods. Condoms have 
became a more attractive 
form of pregnancy preven- 
tion.

DRUG STORE NEWS, July 4, 1988 


Triple-A Product Study: Analgesics 


help keep the analgesic category in motion 


he success of ibuprofen 
products, combined 
with the comeback of 
Tylenol, have kept the analge- 
sic category in motion. 
Although some drug chains 
have reported a slowdown of 
ibuprofen growth, the sales 
growth of oe products is 
still among the fastest of any 
drug store category. Ibuprofen 
sales grew 54 percent in 1987, 


as extra-strength aspirin and 
acetaminophen products’ 
growth slowed somewhat. 
Pipeline Research, a ser- 
vice of the consumer products 
division of IMS America, re- 
ported that the aspirin and ac- 
etaminophen products each 
declined 2 — last year. 
Drug chains supported 
strong growth of tehall’s 
Advil and Bristol-Myer’s Nu- 


A STRIKING 
DIFFERENCE. 


prin with promotisnal expo- 
sure. And Nuprin’s new cap- 
lets gained followers. 

But Tylenol continues to 
capture prime retail shelf 
space, and has been the num- 
ber-one acetaminophen. 
McNeil Labs launched Chil- 
dren’s Grape-Flavored Ty- 
lenoi to join the chewable Chil- 
drens’ Fruit-Flavored 
Tylenol, which has been a hit 


at some chains. 


Buyers feel there is little } 


doubt that the heavy publicity 
pertaining to the use of aspirin 
as a possible defense against 
heart attacks has continued to 
propel sales. Bayer, for in- 
stance, has been a notable 
beneficiary of this trend. 

But the debate on the ef- 
fects of aspirin isn’t over. Offi- 
cials reintroduced research 
results on aspirin’s effect in 
blocking the formation of 
blood clot-aiding hormones to 
show that the medication can 
be abused.

Brokers Want To Give Regional 
Marketing Support To Retailers 
& Manufacturers 


Grocery gon buyers for nonfood chains often 
rely on brokers to obtain product and information 
from grocery product manufact 


urers. 

_ Now a new survey su ts that brokers, who tra- 
ditionally have performed primarily as manufacturer 
sales representatives, will have a broader role to play 
in helping manufacturers better service their retail 
and consumer customers. 

According to the survey, which was recently spon- 
sored by the National Brokers Association, 
many brokers today are ap aren. | into regional mar- 
perp. S oo. saa that are designed to improve the re- 
= sell throughs of the brands and products they bro- 

er. 

The survey revealed that 81% of all manufacturers 
and 92% of all brokers believe that brokers should be 
involved in the regional marketing of their client’s 
products. 

The survey also showed that currently 81% of all 
brokers say they are involved in regional marketing of 
dry groceries while 22% are involved in the regional 
marketing of non-food groceries like pet foods and pa-

65% Of All Teens Drink One Soft 
Drink A Day Most Tell Their Parents 


The Brand To Buy 


Teenagers are big spenders in todays affluent youth 
market. Not too surprisingly, one of their favorite 
purchases is soft drinks. However, have you ever 
wondered how many teenagers consume soft drinks 
and how often. 

TEEN Magazine was recently curious about that so 
they did what their editors call a “soda quota” special 
market research survey. 

Here are their findings from a survey that was done 
last Fall. 

@ 65% of all teenagers enjoy a soft drink “at least” 
once a day. 

@ 41% quench their thirst with a soft drink more 
than once a day. 
~ @ 36% prefer regular soft drinks; 26%, diet, and 


36% have no preference. i 

@ Of those that prefer regular soft drinks, 59% are 
weight watching.

Warehouse club stores appeal to businessmen, professionals and off the street consumers. 


Membership Warehouse 


Club Sales Soaring 


Sales for membership clubs jumped 31% to $10.7 billion in 1987. 
Top 12 chains now account for 95% of total industry sales. 


industry continued to show 
dramatic growth in 1987. 

According to the Fm’s sister 
publication, Discount Store News, 
sales for the industry rose an esti- 
mated 31% in 1987 to $10.7 billion. 

About 95% of the industry’s vol- 
ume is generated by the nation’s 
dozen largest warehouse club 
chains, led by San Diego-based 
Price Club which has a 32% share 
of all major wholesale club chain 
sales. 

The Top 12 chains, Discount 
Store News also estimates, now op- 
erate a total of 273 units (some 
wholesale club operators object to 
the word stores because their 
units perform a cash and carry 
wholesale service). Altogether, 


T he wholesale/warehouse club 


their unit count is up 54% over 
1986. 

For 1988, Discount Store News 
is estimating that the Top 12 chains 
will open another 60 units, for a 
store universe growth rate of 22%. 

If the industry achieves its 
growth plans, and it is likely that it 
will, then DSN and F'm are esti- 
mating that dollar sales for all 
chain Membership Clubs will top 
$13 billion in 1988, and sales for the 
industry may exceed $14 billion.

Margins average about 10% 


Mark-ups in a typical Ware- 
house Club are typically low to 
generate turns. Most Clubs say 
they charge wholesale prices plus 
a small mark-up of approximately 
5%. Profit margins generally aver- 
age about 10% overall. 

Most Clubs also charge mem- 
bers a fee to join as well as an annu- 
al fee to remain a member. Most 
Clubs usually insist on cash pay- 
ments rather than checks or credit 
cards. 

The typical club also has a mix of 
about 3,500 to 4,000 sku’s and gen- 
erally turns its inventory between 
12 and 20 times a year. 


Who’s Who In Membership 
Clubs

California back in 1976.

— from second place and it 
looks like his Sam’s Wholesale 
Clubs, based in Bentonville, Ark., 
may overtake the Price Clubs for 
the number one spot either later 
this year or sometime in 1989.

approximately $3.2 billion in sales, 
up 25% over last year. Their unit 
count rose from 27 to 37 and they 
are planning to end 1988 with 41 
units. 

Sam’s Wholesale Clubs now 
numbers over 84 units, an increase 
of 71% over last year. Walton says 


his chain will probably end the 
year with about 102 units.

enerated $2.67 billion in sales and 
ad a market share of 26% among 

the Top 12 chains. Their sales were 
up 59% over last year.

units. They plan to end 1988 with 
55 units.

K mart enters the fray 


In February of 1988, K mart 
came into the wholesale club pic- 
ture by — a controlling in- 
terest in Makro. Makro currently 
has over a dozen units on the draw- 
ing board for next year, and K 
mart has said that it wants to have 
about 20 units by 1990, and that in- 
cludes opening several new mar- 
kets in the northeast and the up- 
per midwest. 

In an unrelated diversification, 
K mart is also in the process of de- 
veloping a hypermarket. Wal- 


K mart says it wants to have 20 
Makro units by 1990, but Wal- 
Mart already has 84 Sam’s and it 
plans to have over 100 units before 
the end of this year. 

Wal-Mart has already become 
the first wholesale chain to break 
the 100 unit (store) mark. 


Marketing changes 


In terms of positioning them- 
selves to customers, the wholesale 
clubs still seem to be following two 
major thrusts: some chains are 
trying to beef up their wholesale 
businesses so they can back away 
from their retail customers who 


spend less per visit than wholesale 
customers. Meanwhile others, like 
Makro, are adding more service 
departments to enhance their ap- 
peal to retail consumers. 

Makro, for example, is adding 
service bakeries al deli sections 
to its current clubs, and will in- 
clude these departments in all new 


stores. 
The Wholesale Club, on the oth- 


er hand, is looking for ge to pro- 
vide more service to the small 
business customer or to the profes- 
sional doctor, dentist or veterinar- 
ian who needs to buy office su 

so and other stables in relatively 

Re quantities. 

heir management tells F'm 
that they believe volume is the key 
to a successful wholesale club op- 
eration and they say they do not 
want to tie up their registers with 
a $20 or $40 purchase when a small 
business customer will spend $400 
to $700 in one visit. 

Price Club, too, is trying to en- 
hance its image as a business-ori- 
ented club. Price now considers in- 
dividual professionals and 
contractors as small businesses, 
and as such, they are entitled to 
their own membership cards rath- 
er than group memberships. 

Price 1s also, however, moving to 
i its mix into categories that 

ill appeal to off-the-street con-

a gas station and pharmacy are un- 
derway. 

Sam’s is also trying to up the vol- 
ume in its stores including the 18 
Super Savers it purchased in mid 
1987. The typical Sam’s averages 
about $50 million a year in sales, 
far less than the $100 million that 
the typical Price Club can gener- 
ate. 

Costco is also going after more 
off-street traffic by rolling out an 
expanded offering of fresh meats 
and produce. Last year, Costco 
also expanded pharmacies and be-

Many nonfood chains also have a 
policy of only featuring the nation-

The rest of the time they’ll keep 
some of the nationals, like Tide, 
Clorox, Dawn, Wisk, etc., in their 
regular cleaning department but 
they won’t give them off-shelf ex- 
posure. 

A typical strategy is to put one 
or two facings of a Dawn or Dove 
next to one or two facings of their 
ke label item. The private la- 

lis usually 20% to 30% less than 
the national brand so the chains 
can offer their customers a signifi- 
cant savings while still making 
margins of between 20% and 40%. 

However when chains do buy 
cleaners on promotion, which most 
chains say they do between 90% 
and 95% of the time, they give 
them ample off-shelf exposure.

said one buyer. “When we buy on 
deal, we can be competitive with 
food stores and still take 18% to 
20% margins. Everyday, we sel- 
dom make less than a 30% mar- 
gin.”

Hot Trends in Cleaning Products 


In the household products category, the hot buzz words in 1987 
were “lemon fresh,” “outdoor fresh,” and convenience. 

According to the Kline & Company in Fairfield, N.J., the hottest 
new products were those with the word “lemon” in their brand 
names and those with fragrances reminiscent of the outdoors. 

Convenience was also very important to consumers in ’87, and 
Kline says many of the most successful launches featured either 
some form of convenience in either the product or the meesnee. 

Many manufacturers brought out lemon scented household 

roducts last year, but the strongest sales came from the major 
rands such as Lemon Brillo, Lemon SOS, Lemon Fantastic, Lem- 
on Cascade, Lemon Fresh Dash, and Lemon Comet. 

In outdoor scents, Tide Clothsline Fresh Scent stood out and so 
did Sun Rinse Fresh Liquid Downey. Surf’s Fresh Scent, intro- 
duced back in 1985, continued to do well. Mountain Spring Dawn is 
— well and so is Downey’s April Scented Dryer Sheets in test 
markets. 

Colgate did very well with the introduction of the Fab One Shot 


Pouch which contains everything a woman needs to both wash & ma- 
chine dry her clothes. Ki Clark is now testing a similar single 
dose product called Co and P& G is testing Bold Washer/ 


Dryer packs. Cheer also has Power Punches in test and P& G is 
testing Tide Multi Action Sheets and Tide Redi Paks. 

Carey Ahsler, a marketing consultant for Kline, says that lemon 
seems to be hot because so many people associate the scent with 
efficient cleaning. She says the outdoor scents are doing well be- 
cause they make people think of the fresh outdoors. 

Convenience is important because so many women work. “When 
a woman is home,” Ahsler says, “she doesn’t want to spend all her 
time cleaning, so she buys products that will let her take care of 
several tasks at once or products that are easier to use like a spray.”

Pepsi creates value with E.T. 
rebate promotion 


Pepsi is also offering new pro- 
motions built around sweepstakes 
and special values. Later this fall 
and in early winter, Pepsi will 
launch a promotion built around a 
tie-in with the distributors of the 
soon to be released video of E.T. 

Mass merchandise stores are 
now a major source of video pur- 
chases, and many drug chains have 
video centers as well. The Pepsi 
promotion will let a chain adver- 
tise Pepsi by stressing, not price, 
but the availability of a special $5 
rebate that Pepsi is offering on the 
E.T. video purchase. 

The event will break just in time 
for the holidays, and it will give 
consumers a chance to buy a $24.95 
copy of E.T. for $19.95. Retailers 
who feature the promotion should 
be able to get a video sales, plus a 
soft drink sale. 


Wal-Mart will test new 
locations for soft drinks 


“Soft drinks are not just a food 
store item anymore,” said a Wal- 
Mart manager. “We’ve sold them 
for years, but we don’t think we’re 
fully utilizing the category. There 
are other things we can do to make 
this category more profitable and 
we're going to do it.” 

Several sources also say that 
Wal-Mart is about to test new 
ways of merchandising soft drinks. 
Right now the chain primaril 
stocks soft drinks in its “wall of val- 
ues” right beyond its cash regis- 
ters. 

Later this year, sources say that 
Wal-Mart will begin testing soft 
drinks in the snack category which 
is right across from its registers. 

K mart is also testing various 
ey ga and locations for 
soft drinks. 

The attitude among buyers is 
that the category is great for 
growth, but that profits could be 
even higher with some merchan- 
dising and promotional refine- 
ments.

Fay’s sells N. Y. & Mass stores 


LIVERPOOL, N. Y. — Fay’s Drug has pulled out of 
Connecticut and Massachusetts, se nine stores to 
CVS and shutte the remaining five in those states. 

“We weren't getting an adequate return on our invest- 
ment,” said Warren Wolfson, vp-general counsel and sec- 
retary. 
Included in the nine were the eight stores Fay’s pur- 
chased in 1985 from Genovese Drug in the Hartford, 
Conn., and Springfield, Mass. markets. 

Six of the stores CVS is buying are in the Hartford area, 
with the rest in western Massachusetts. 


Arbor siots Enokian, Tempalski 


TROY, Mich. — Ar- 
bor has named 
John Enokian director of 
health services and 
Leonard Tempalski di- 
rector of pharmacy and 
store operations. The 
announcements were 
made by Markus Ernst, 
executive and chief 
operations officer. 

As director of health services, Enokian will be responsi- 
ble for negotiating and managing third-party health insur- 
ance contractual agreements. He will also serve as a liai- 
son between the chain and various health care institutions. 
Previously he was Arbor’s director of pharmacy opera- 
tions. 

Tempalski, an Arbor district manager before his pro- 
motion, will oversee 4 Spies pharmacy and store op- 
erations for Arbor’s 78 drug stores in southeastern 
Michigan. 


American Stores units targeted for sale 


DUBLIN, Calif. — Acting quickly to satisfy Federal 
Trade Commission requirements arising from the merger 
of Lucky Stores with Alpha Beta Co., American Stores 
has reached an agreement to sell 15 Lucky and Alpha Beta 
stores in California to Certified Grocers of Los Angeles. 
No purchase price was disclosed. 

e FTC sti that a total of 37 Lucky and Alpha 
Beta units must be sold to satisfy antitrust regulations in 
California, including 24 in the northern half of the state. 
Those sold to Certified include three stores in San Jose and 
individual units in Hayward, Union City, Novato and oth- 
er markets in northern and southern California. The re- 
maining units to be sold include five more stores in San 
a and others in scattered markets throughout the 
state. 

“Many of these stores are smaller units, in the 20,000- to 
25,000-square-foot range,” said Lucky spokesperson Judy 
Decker. of their small size, she said, most do not 
contain pharmacies.

National Wholesale buys Chaffee 


TAYLOR, Mich. — National Wholesale Drug Co. has ac- 
quired Chaffee & Co., a local sundries wholesaler which sup- 
plies drug stores in Michigan and Ohio. Founded in 1919, 
Chaffee did approximately $5 million in sales last year. 

National, a $130 million wholesaler which services close 
to 1,000 retail clients in the Midwest, will operate Chaffee 
as a separate division. “With the combined resources of 
National and Chaffee we can expand our customer base, 
our merchandise offerings, and our distribution areas,” 
said president Mickey Kole. 


Perry enters joint home care venture 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores has launched a 
joint marketing venture with The Detroit Medical Center 
(DMC), one of Michigan’s largest health care providers, to 
sell and rent home medical equipment and supplies. The 
venture, called DMC Home Medical Equipment, will be 
managed by Perry ComfortCare, the home health care 
segment of Perry’s $21 million Health Care Division. 

e DMC consists of six acute-care hospitals and one re- 
habilitation hospital, as well as a network of ambulator 
care clinics and “extensive” links to private medical staff 
practices in greater Detroit. 

“This agreement brings together two of the area’s most 
important health care providers,” said Michael Klein, Per- 
ry Health Care Division president, “and the venture will 
give consumers the best in home medical supply service.”

Polaroid enters film print market 


CAMBRIDGE, Mass. — The color print film business, a 
core category at drug stores, is about to be host to a new 
competitor. 

Polaroid, king of the instant film business, announced it 
will soon market a brand against the likes of Kodak, Fuji, 
Konica, 3M and Agfa-Gevaert. : 

tailers can appreciate the irony of Polaroid’s entry into 
this arena where odak reins. Just two years ago, Polaroid 
won its patent infringement suit against Kodak, and forced 
Kodak’s exit from the instant photography business. _ 

Retailers may stand to gain the most, as film suppliers 
develop promotions and incentives to win market share. 


Chicago hosts hardware show 


CHICAGO — The 1988 National Hardware Show, held 
in conjunction with the Hardware Industry Week, will 
give housewares exhibitors a chance to expand their base 
of qualified buyers in the hardware and allied lines, chain 


store and home center categories. 
The show opens August 14 and runs through 
Wednesday, August 17 at McCormick Place here.

Candy-loving Americans respond to ads 


According to the National Confectioners Association 
and eo Research Corp., 90 percent of all American 
households buy confectionery, and 9 percent of adult con- 
sumers eat confectionery every day. 

Men outnumber women among these adults consumers, 
but age and formal education are not factors. Those earn- 
ing less than $25,000 a year outnumber those earning 
more, but they tend to be both blue- and white-collar em- 


ee te 
g chains price aggressively to capture everday can- 
dy eaters, of which there are millions. Eckerd recently ad- 
vertised a Whoppers 13-ounce milk carton at 99 cents, and 
SupeRx sold Hershey’s standard bars, such as Milk Choc- 
olate and Milk Chocolate with Almonds, Kit Kat and 
Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups, at four for $1.00. Walgreens 
recently offered the bonus size of Tootsie Rolls at four for 
$1.00 with a Walgreens coupon.

Survey, 90 percent of 60 headquarters and store level mer- oe 
chandise managers chose candy/gum as a checkstand fa- ae . £ . 3 )

Nielsen: Nail color sales gain strength 


Nail color sales in mass market outlets were weak last year, 
but the category has been getting stronger in the past six 
months, according to Nielsen Marketing Research estimates 


Nielsen reports that after several years of relatively strong 


growth, nail color sales in food, drug and mass merchandise 
stores declined 6 percent for calendar year 1987. 
Mass stores were the hardest hit last year. Nail 


color sales in these stores were down almost 9 percent for 1987. 
stores suffered a 5.8 percent drop in nail color sales in 1987, 

but food stores escaped with just a 3.5 percent decrease. 
The picture for drug stores, however, has b ew a little 
brighter in the last six months. Nielsen reports the catego- 
ry went up 3.5 percent in the November/December two-month 
reporting period, and it was up 4.7 percent in January and Feb- 


ruary. 
However, in March/April ’88, the growth rate slowed some- 
what, and Nielsen only registered a 1.7 percent increase for

Many drug chains are converting to a family presentation of nail coloring products. 
Buyers and merchandisers reason that most women are brand loyal and if they tend 
to buy, say, Revlon face and lip products, they will also want to buy Revion nail enam- 
els. Putting the nail color in the family set then just makes it more “convenient” for 
brand loyal shoppers. It also makes it more likely that drug chains will generate in- 
cremental impulse sales.

three sections in the store to

shop one section. It’s more

DRUG STORE NEWS, August 1, 1988 


FACES panel say 


How can retailers 
get more growth from 
their cosmetics/- 
fragrances depart- 
ments? 

According to a pan- 
el of retailers and 
manufacturers who 
gathered at the Fra- 
grance, Accessor 
and Cosmetic Exposi- 
tion and Showcase 
(FACES) in New York re- 
cently, the answer is “be dif- 
ferent.” 

The cosmetics buyers for 
several major department 
store chains who were on the 
FACES panel and several 
chain drug store retailers in 
the audience agreed that the 
way to maximize cosmetics 
sales in today’s market is to 
“be different” and to stand out 
with as many new and exclu- 
sive brands as possible. 

Toni Hopkins, vp/divisional 
merchandise manager of cos- 
metics for Neiman-Marcus, 
said that many cosmetic shop- 
pers today are simply “tired” 
of the way most chains treat 
the category. 

They’re “tired of the fact 
that most stores look alike,” 
she said, and they’re tired of 
“me-too products.” 


Calls for better direct mail 


Hopkins’ solution is to do 
“more forceful direct-mail 
pieces” and to create her own 
mailing pieces with an eye to 
“giving consumers a reason to 
use our stores.” 

Two drug store retailers 
who eae ed ee FACES 
program, Austin Drug presi- 
dent Gary Spielfogel and 
Brooks cosmetics buyer Susan 
Godfrey, agreed that the cus- 
tomer today wants “some- 
thing she can’t find anywhere 
else.” 

Spiegfogel said it was im- 
perative for both mass and de- 

artment store retailers to 
erret out new or exclusive 
brands that they can be the 
first to promote. 

Dorothy Foster, who until 
recently was the senior buyer 
of cosmetics and fragrances 
for JCPenney, and who now 
has her own business, DCF 
International, said the “key to 
being a successful merchant 
today is giving consumers 
something they didn’t know 
they to begin with.” 


Leslie F. Grunberg, 
founder and president of Ben- 
etton Cosmetics, said that re- 
tailers, above everything, 
“need to know their reason for 
being. 

“It has to be ce be making 
money or beyond killing the 
competition and gaining mar- 
ket share,” he said. “A presi- 
dent of a retail company has to 
know what the cornerstone of 
his businessis . . . what niche 
it is he or she fills and satis- 
fies.” 

Retailers on the panel also 
talked about the constant 
need to upgrade one’s image in 
the market, a necessity just as 
much for drug chains as for de- 
partment stores. 

Michael L. Vincent, presi- 
dent and ceo of Guerlain, said 
that all stores today can get 
“discounted or diverted mer- 
chandise,” so no chain can rely 
on its identity as a provider of 
exclusive products. 

“That means chains have to 
upgrade,” he said, “because 
eventually the only distin- 
guishing feature will be a 
store’s ability to offer a pleas- 
ant environment to shop in as 
well as sales clerks who are 
knowledgable and efficient.” 

Foster added that most re- 
tailers shouldn’t try to rely on 
—— “all things to all peo- 

“Saw 
r She said they have “to make 
choices. They have to limit the 
brands they carry so they can 
make a marketing statement 
about the brands they carry.” 

In another panel, retailers 
also tried to identify opportu- 
nities for growth in the men’s 

ces market. 

ul Cohen, who publishes 
Beauty Age magazine and 
who created the FACES 
trade show, said the real 
h in men’s fragrances is 
in cologne sprays, up 18 per- 
cent versus last year. Ihe seg- 
ment, as a whole, is up 5.6 per- 

cent in year- sales.

In my July 18th column, we saw that 
purchase rates of H&BA products 
through drug stores can vary dramati- 
cally from one SAMI market to anoth- 
er. We suggested that more effective 
marketing programs could be tailored 
to both high consumption and low con- 
sumption markets. 

Also important to watch: the signif- 
icant differences in category trends 
among the 54 major markets in which 
SAMI/Burke is tracking food and 
drug store movement. In order to fo- 
cus on this point we have selected 10 
product categories with important 
dollar volume gains nationally in re- 
tail drug store movement for the 12- 
week period ended May 20, 1988, 
which corresponds closely with the 
second quarter of the year. For each 
of these expanding categories, we 
have shown the trends in ten geo- 
graphically dispersed markets for the 
same time interval. 

In some instances, category growth 
has been aided by volume contributed 
by new brands which were not on the 
market during the corresponding 
year-ago period. Among appetite sup- 
pressants, Stay-Trim is both new and 
national. There are three new major 
entries in the hair spray category: Sa- 
lon Selectives, Boid Hold and St. Ives. 
The mouthwash category boasts two

Prescription diuretics still considered as ‘water pills’ 
Soe 


NEW YORK — Still con- 
sidered a first-line medication 
to combat mild to moderate 
hypertension, the long-time 
dominance of first- a, sec- 
ond-generation diuretics in 
the antihypertensive market 
may be threatened as a result 
of ee eee studies 
promoting the efficacy of some 
newer third-generation di- 
uretic products. 

ile many of today’s diur- 
etics are presented in the liter- 
ature as antihypertensive 
‘agents specifically indicated in 
the lowering of blood pres- 
sure, many physicians still 
turn to older first- and second- 
generation diuretics (“water 
pills”) when a medical condi- 
tion is diagnosed as edema or 


an abnormal retention of wa- 
ter or electrolyte metabolism. 

Since the 1950s, diuretics 
have been used to decrease the 
amount of water in the body by 
increasing the flow of urine. In 
the course of doing so, they of- 
ten cause the body to excrete 
dissolved metabolites such as 
potassium, sodium, calcium, 
magnesium or bicarbonates. In 
general, they should be pre- 
scribed with caution to persons 
with diabetes, gout, kidney dis- 
ease, and liver disease, and 
those currently taking lithium. 
Anyone who is on a special diet, 
pregnant (or hoping to become 
so) or nursing should also use 
diuretics with a de of cau- 
tion. Because they tend to 
cause sodium retention and

may therefore interfere with 
the action of diuretics, ibupro- 
fen and other non-steroidal 
anti-inflammatory drugs 
should not be taken concurrent- 
ly with diuretics.

Trio named Longs senior vps 


WALNUT CREEK, Calif. — Longs Drug Stores an- 
nounced that Bill Brandon, George Duey and Dan Wilson 
have been named senior vice presidents. Brandon and 
Duey are currently vp’s and district managers and have 
been with Longs since 1959. Brandon became a vp in 1978, 
and Duey in 1974. Wilson has held a number of posts in-

Arbor eyes new headquarters 


TROY, Mich. — Reflecting its rapid growth in recent 

ears, Arbor Drugs is readying a move to a new corporate 

sed suareati site this December that will more than double 
its central office space. 

Arbor’s new corporate center is a three-story building on 
West Big Beaver Road in Troy with 52,000 square feet of of- 
fice space. It replaces both the existing 20,000-square-foot 
headquarters site and a nearby satellite office. 

“Arbor today has 80 stores and 2,600 employees company- 
wide, up from 30 stores and 900 employees just five years 
ago,” noted Eugene Applebaum, chairman and president. 
“Our new headquarters allows us to bring together our ad- 
ministrative ani support staff under one roof, with the flexi- 
bility for expansion.” 


FTC okays Vons’ Safeway purchase 


EL MONTE, Calif. — The Federal Trade Commission 
has given final approval for Vons Cos. $408 million-acquisi- 
tion of 172 Southern California Safeway stores. Prior to the 
consent, Vons was required to divest 12 stores—nine 
Safeways and three Vons—which it sold for undisclosed 
prices to Certified Grocers, Ralphs and Hughes. To poe 
its new ownership of the Safeway sites, Vons ran a full page 
ad in the Los Angeles Times, promising customers price roll- 
backs at the acquired stores. Vons said it plans to remer- 
chandise the Safeway stores, and in some instances, make 
major remodeling changes. 


Fays taps Novara for P.L. marketing 


LIVERPOOL, N. Y. — Paul Novara has been named by 
Fay’s Drug to the newly created post of private label mar- 
keting manager for the drug division, Jim Wuest, vp-mer- 
chandise, announced. 

Novara will be responsible for all aspects of purchasing 
and marketing of Fay’s private label products. He previously 
worked for International U.S.A., Peter J. Schmitt, Pueblo 
International and Chatham Supermarkets, Wuest said.

By James Frederick 

he recent Democratic 

National Convention 

shone a spotlight on At- 
lanta, revealing to the world a 
bustling, broiling metropolis 
in love with the notion of pro- 
gress and growth. Atlanta 
prides itself on its leadership 
role as the hub of business, 
transportation and culture in 
the New South. 

But Atlanta is a hub for an- 
other important reason: It is 
Fb ag the best example of 

lack economic and political 
progress in the nation. Atlan- 
ta’s political establishment 
has long drawn much of its 
leadership and support from 
some of the nation’s highest- 
profile black politicians, in- 
cluding Mayor Andrew Young 
and state Senator Julian 
Bond. The last two mayors 
have been black, as is the city 
council president and many 
other prominent leaders. 


In Atlanta sub 


With some justification, the 
city is also called the birth- 
place of the modern civil rights 
movement. Here, just blocks 
from downtown, Dr. Martin 
Luther King, Jr. presided 
over the Ebenezer Baptist 
Church and began a crusade 
which transformed American 
society. King’s burial site on 
Sweet Auburn Avenue—in 
the midst of the Center for So- 
cial Change which bears his 
name—remains a touchstone 
for the pride and aspirations of 
black Americans. 

Atlanta also prides itself on 
its race relations, and on its 
ability 20 years ago to avoid 
much of the violence and up- 
heaval that accompanied the 
struggles for civil rights in 
other U.S. cities. 

Typically for this town, the 
decision by Atlanta’s image- 
conscious white power struc- 
ture to practice accommoda- 
tion rather than confrontation 
in the 1960s and 1970s sprang 
as much from economic con- 
cerns as from social con- 
science. It was perceived, cor- 
rectly, that what was good for 
Atlanta’s black community 
was ultimately good for the 
economic growth and stability 
of the whole region. 

In the end, Atlanta’s busi- 
ness and political establish- 
ment had no choice but to open

the doors to the city’s growing 
black population. Within the 
city limits, nearly 70 percent 
of Atlanta’s population of 
425,000 is A according to 
the 1980 U.S. Census. Of the 
metropolitan region’s nearly 
three million people, at least 
25 percent are black. 

ose numbers translated 
for black Atlantans into voting 
power in the 1970s, and led to 
a larger share in the prosperi- 
ty that has fueled the city’s 
growth. Black political lead- 
ers applied pressure on local 
businesses, bank lenders and 
others for jobs, minority con- 
tracts and an end to various 
forms of economic or racial dis- 
crimination. 

Atlanta’s politicians, busi- 
ness leaders and citizens con- 
tinue to wrestle with eee 
racial tensions, unequal jo 
and housing opportunities and 
a seemingly permanent un- 
derclass of unemployed 
blacks. Nevertheless, what 


has emerged here is one of the 
nation’s largest concentra- 
tions of the black middle- and 
upper-middle classes. 

ithin the city and in well- 
groomed suburbs to the south 
and east, tidy homes and new 
office and retail developments 
testify to the growing earnin 
and spending power of black 
consumers in Atlanta. 


Key center for ethnic 


The size and relative pros- 
pany of much of Atlanta’s 

lack population have made 
the city a key center for the 
marketing of products aimed 
at black consumers—most no- 
tably ethnic-oriented hair care 
products, cosmetics and other 
toiletries. 

Drug and discount chains 
like K mart, Drug Emporium,

and east, catering to urban

earned lessons about ethnic 
marketing and consumer de- 
mand that can apply to hun- 
dreds of metropolitan areas 
around the country. In gener-

meeting the demand for black- 
oriented products in largely 
black neighborhoods is a key 
image aan traffic builder.

tomers almost exclusively,”

a strong, nice middle-class 
area with a great clientele, 
and were going to give our 
customers what they want.”

Beauty and barber shops (B&Bs) are in- 
creasing ethnic sales from 10 percent to 20 
percent a year, according to distributors. 

In contrast, with some exceptions, many 
drug store ethnic product buyers estimate 
that sales of ethnic products in their stores 
have slowed to increases of between 5 per- 
cent and 10 percent a year, and some buyers 
say overall sales in their chains are flat. 

In the B&B industry, the competition is 
coming not just from the major chains like 
Alberto Culver’s Sally Beauty Supply 
Shops, but also from small independent op- 
erators, many of them Koreans who run 
their stores as family-owned businesses. 

Many distributors are now estimating 
that perhaps as much as 30 percent of all eth- 
nic product sales are now generated in B&B 
stores. The B&B operators are almost al- 
ways the first to get the new maintenance 
pig coming out in the professional sa- 
on market, and they also are able to buy 
large quantities of the more established re- 
tail brands direct from the vender. 

Several sources estimate that B&B own- 
ers often sell their merchandise at gross 
margins as low as 5 percent. Drug stores, in 
contrast, usually ike 25 percent to 40 per- 
cent on everyday ethnic items and 15 per- 
cent to 20 percent on featured ethnic items. 

Exact statistics are hard to come by on the 


B&B market, but it appears the industry 
has two branches: the major chains like Sal- 
ly, Mylo and Save Way, which generally 
stock general market hair care lines as well 
as ethnic lines; and the small family-owned 
B&B stores that mostly stock ethnic lines 
and basically operate in neighborhoods 
where the population is more than 60 per- 
cent black or His anic. 

Most of the B&B stores are usually small, 
averaging about 2,000 square feet, sources 
say, and stocking 1,500 to 2,000 SKUs at a 
time. 

Some drug chains that go head to head 
with the family-run B&Bs are reacting by 
lowering their prices in high-volume ethnic 
stores. Many are also promoting ethnic 
more often to make it more visible in their 
stores, and they’re beefing up their selection 
so they can make a stronger presentation 
statement. 

However, in addition to aggressive pric- 
ing, many buyers also say the B&B stores 
have a strong service program working in 
their favor. “They can answer questions 
about the products,” says one buyer. “When 
someone asks what’s the best relaxer for me 
to use, a B&B store clerk can generally give 
an answer or an opinion. Our clerks general- 
ly don’t know that much about the category, 
and we can’t give the service.” 


Chains like SupeRx of Arizo- 
na, Drug Emporium in Colum- 
bus, Eckerd in Florida and 
Dart and Peoples in the Wash- 
a tnd irginia market are all 
taking this approach. 

At the same time, many 
chains including Perry Drug, 
Osco, Thrift, Dart, Peoples, 
F&M and Eckerd are now pro- 
moting ethnic more, giving it 
increased exposure on ends, 
and using POP to highlight 
special value buys. 

As Perry’s assistant vp of 
H&BA merchandising, Steve 
Lund, puts it, the goal for 1988 
and 1989 is to let shoppers 
know “we are seriously com- 
mitted” to the category and 
are prepared to provide shop- 
pers with a broad assortment 
of quality products at reason- 
able prices. 


Make it ‘stand out’ 


A source at F&M says this 
Detroit-based deep discount 
chain tries to make the catego- 
ry “stand out. 

“We put in eight- to 12-foot 
sections wherever they’re 
warranted,” he says, “and 
we're constantly changing the 
mix. We’re dropping old items 
and putting in the hot new 
products as they come out. We 
use a distributor, and they 
stay on top of the category. 
We won't let our stores just 
stock anything. We’re also 
price competitive in all our 
stores. You have to be.” 

In fact, competition this 
year has become an issue for 
most buyers. K mart, Wal- 
Mart and Zayre, three of the 
nation’s strongest discount 
store chains, have aggressive- 
¥ stepped up their merchan- 

ising, advertising and pro- 


motional efforts in the ethnic 
area. 

Zayre now has ethnic prod- 
ucts in all stores. The chain 
has also steadily promoted the 
category to build visibility and 
image. K mart, the first dis- 
count chain to go aggressively 
after this category, continues 
to give ethnic products gener- 
ous promotional space and full 
presentations in all higher- 
volume ethnic neighborhood 
stores. Wal-Mart has a strong 
everyday low-price image in 
this category. 

In markets where there are 
60 percent or more black cus- 
tomers, chains are also facing 
increased competition from 
family-run beauty and barber 
(B&B) supply stores. Most 
buyers complain that these 
small family businesses, often 
run by Koreans, are very cost- 
effective. 

“They buy competitively, 
pay very low rent for their 
stores, often live in the same 
building as their stores, and 
use only family members to 
run the business,” says one 
buyer. “They discount every- 
thing, and I can’t even come 
close to matching their 
prices.” 

Other sources, however, 
say that many of the family- 
run B&B shops can’t compete 
with drug stores on either va- 
riety or presentation of prod- 
uct. These sources feel that 
chains with a strong merchan- 
dising — in place can 
lower their prices selectively 
and compete with the family- 
run B&Bs as well as with the 
discount department stores, 
which are not always conve- 
niently located.

At Perry Drug in Pontiac, 
Mich., management is trying 
to fend off competition by up- 
grains ethnic sections and 
owering prices. 

Perry upgraded its ethnic 
merchandising and expanded 
its presentations in high-vol- 
ume stores earlier this year. 
In March, the chain gave the 
category an extra shot in the 
arm by taking price reduc- 
tions on its 50 best-selling hair 
care SKUs. 

Steve Lund, director of 
merchandising responsible for 
ethnic H&BA, says the chain 
lowered prices as much as 25 

ercent on the most visible 
rands, and the results have 
been very strong. 
“We face very strong com- 
etition from the barber and 
eauty supply shops in our 
ethnic markets,” he said, “and 
their strongest feature is 
price. Before we took our 
ea roll-back, my sales were 

lat, even down a bit for the 
first quarter of 1988. 

“But my six-month sales 
show that I’m up 3 percent in 
dollars and 10 percent in units, 
and I think we’re going to be 
able to build on that growth 
for the rest of the year.” 


Reasonable profits 


Lund says he’s now as com- 
etitive as the majority of 
&B shops on price. Even 

with the price roll-back, how- 
ever, he says he’s still able to 
generate reasonable profits 
out of the department. 

“We’ve been working ciose- 
ly with both the manufactur- 
ers and our distributors on ac- 
quisition costs,” he says, “and 
as a result, I’m averaging 
about 15 percent to 20 percent 
on the items we feature in the 
department today.” 

coveal distributors and a 
number of buyers also told 
Drug Store News that there is 
a general trend to lower mar- 
pe in the ethnic department. 

everal sources said the chain 
drug industry is trending 
away from everyday margins 
in the 40 percent-plus vicinity 
in favor of more competitive 
margins averaging between 
28 percent and 33 percent. 

“T still have stores that are 
all over the lot with their pric- 
ing,” says Kent Humphreys, 
vice president of Jack’s Ser- 
vice Distributors in Oklaho- 
ma, “but the major chains are 
definitely becoming more 
competitive and more promo- 
tionally-minded. I’d say mar- 
gins in the vicinity of 30 per- 
cent are definitely becoming 
the norm.” 

But buyers and distributors 
like Humphreys are still quick 
to point out that although eth- 
nic customers are sensitive to 
price, they are also strongly 
influenced by other consider- 
ations, such as the conve- 
nience of shopping, the look of 
the store and the visibility of 
the department. Also impor- 
tant, he says, are the strength 
of the store’s ethnic presenta- 
tion and whether or not the 
mix includes the latest new 
products and shades.

the category’s relative stagna-

Eckerd Drug 


At Eckerd Drug in Florida, 
George Gebhart, director of 
merchandising, says that in 
spite of increased competition 
for ethnic sales, the category 
is growing in the Eckerd chain 
at an average rate of about 7 
percent a year. 

Gebhart says the growth is 
primarily the result of better 
merchandise implementation. 
“We are following the rule 
that about 20 percent of our 
stores do about 80 percent of 
all ethnic sales,” says Geb- 
hart. “So although we now 
have a three-foot minimum set 
for ethnic in almost all our 
stores, we are expanding the 
department in all high-volume 
stores. Before where we 
might have given eight feet to 
ethnic in a good neighborhood, 
now we give it 12 or 16 feet. 
Some of our stores even have 
30-foot sets.” 

Eckerd has also ong photos 
of black models in the cosmet- 
ics departments of all its ap- 
proximately 200 high-volume 
ethnic stores to create a better 
ambiance for its customers, 
and in the higher-volume 
stores, they are also putting a 
select number of Dark & 
Lovely hair coloring SKUs in 
the mass market hair color 
section. “That’s where women 
expect to find hair color,” Geb- 
hart explained. 


Drug Emporium 


Drug Emporium, head- 
quartered in Columbus, Ohio, 
is also increasing space for the 
category in all stores where 
the volume warrants expan- 
sions. In high-volume ethnic 
stores, sources say, the aver- 
age set is expanding from four 
to eight feet, and in some 
stores it is going as high as 12 
feet. 

“We are making a state- 
ment to the local community 
that we are in the ethnic busi- 
ness,” a source said. 

Both Rx and Peoples 
Drug in Alexandria, Va., are 
cutting back on select general 
market SKUs in order to make 
room for products tailored to 
black needs. Black hosiery 
lines like Afrotique and 
Brown Sugar have been added 
to many stores, and in some 
cases, they have been given as 
much as eight feet. 

Ethnic hair color lines like 
Dark & Lovely and Creme of 
Nature are now merchandised 
in the general market hair col- 
or section as well as in the tra- 
ditional ethnic hair section of 
many chain drug stores.

Thomas directs Peoples’ ethnic focus 


efore Peoples Drug 

Stores promoted Eric 

Thomas, assistant 
H&BA buyer, to ethnic prod- 
ucts buyer, the 850-unit chain 
never had a buyer exclusively 
for ethnic products. 

In the years before Thom- 
as’s promotion this past 
spring, ethnic had been one of 
several categories overseen 
by the Peoples H&BA buyer. 

But because the Alexan- 
dria, Va.-based chain has so 
many stores in highly ethnic 
neighborhoods, the ethnic 
products department has 
grown to be especially valu- 
able to the chain. Thomas’s 
boss, cosmetics vp Vicki Wil- 
liams, describes ethnic as “a 
very important category for 
the chain, an area for growth 
and opportunity.” 

Thomas has been with Peo- 
ples for 10 years. He joined 
the company in 1978 as a mer- 
chandise manager coordina- 
tor, and before that was a 
sales rep for Harris Beauty 
Supply, a major distributor of 
ethnic products. 

“Ethnic is already a ver 
strong category for us.” 
Thomas says. “The category 
overall is flat, and there is tre- 
mendous competition in this 
area, but even so, our sales are 
up. I think we can generate 
even more growth, and I 
wouldn’t be surprised if, at 
some point, we could double or 
even triple our current sales.” 

Thomas says that “advertis- 
ing is the key to getting ethnic 
to grow. You have to get the 
word out to the people,” he 
says, “so the people will know 
the t pe of mix you have. 

We re going to be making a 
statement that Peoples has 
the products people want and 
at the most competitive 
prices. We have very heavy 
ethnic demographics in our 
Washington, D. C. and mid- 
Atlantic stores, but I’m talk- 
ing corporately when I talk 
about ethnic. All our divisions 
will be getting behind it.”

ranging from four to 12 feet,
