By James Frederick 

CINCINNATI — Fighting to maintain its in- 
dependence in the face of a possible takeover bid 
from the Haft family, Kroger Co. is considering a 
restructuring plan that would strip the company 
of all non-core operations and load it with debt in 
exchange for a substantial cash payout to share- 
holders. 

The plan, announced Sept. 13, involves the 
declaration of a special dividend of approximate- 
ly $40 on each common share of Kroger stock. 
The dividend would also include a junior subordi- 
nated deferred-interest 20-year debenture with 
an expected trading value of about $8 for each 
common share. 

The rumors surrounding the proposed re- 
structuring and possible takeover e the Hafts 
drove the price of Kroger’s stock up more than 
$10 Sept. 18, to $50.25. 

Meanwhile, Moody’s Investors Service said it 
was reviewing Kroger’s securities ratings for 
possible downgrading, since the proposed reca 
italization would raise its already high debt level. 


Kroger’s move followed quickly on the heels of 
an announcement by the Federal Trade Commis- 
sion that the Haft family had received federal 
clearance to accumulate a stake in the giant food 
and drug retailer. Through spokesman Stanley

ORLANDO — Phar-Mor has shaken up this central-Flori- 
da market more in one year than Drug Emporium has in eight, 
through sharper pricing than people had ever seen here. 
“Customers come in and amaze me! They'll gt a Phar- 
Mor price on a prescription that’s maybe $15 below my 
cost,” said Linda Smith, pharmacy manager at a 4-month- 
old Publix supermarket with pharmacy located in a develop- 
ing neighborhood. “We just can’t go that low.” _ 
ing a recent visit to this market, it was evident that 
drug chains and competirg pharmacies will go to great

growth over the next few years has an all-star roster of re-

~ NEWS IN BRIEF 


Judge blocks American-Lucky merger 


LOS ANGELES — Although Federal Trade Commis- 
sion approval has already been granted, a federal judge 
has temporarily blocked the merger of American Stores’ 
Alpha Beta division and Lucky Stores. 

ee Angeles Federal District Judge David Kenyon grant- 
ed a temporary restraining order in ag i to an antitrust 
lawsuit filed by California Attorney General John Van de 
Kamp. The suit claims the $2.5 billion merger will stifle com- 
petition in California and raise consumer prices. 

The ruling requests that Lucky and Alpha Beta continue 
to operate separately at least until the next scheduled hear- 
ing. (At press time, the next court date was set for Sept. 16.) 
Kenyon’s ruling does not sitions the company from selling 
Lucky’s Kash ’n Karry Florida stores, Arizona locations or 
the 37 stores to be sold under the FTC’s order. 

Lucky ceo John Lillie said the merger would “bring an 
estimated $50 million in savings to consumers per year.” 

American Stores intends for Lucky to operate all of the 
combined 567-store grocery chain under Lucky’s every- 
day-low pricing policy. Under this operating structure, 
analyst John Resecott with First Manhattan in New York 


said consumers would indeed save money. He noted that 
Alpha Beta “hasn’t been pricing competitively.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, September 26, 1988 


Store Automation 


Automation takes the drug store industry by storm 


By Susan Ball 
rug stores are plugging into 
the electronic age with a speed 
and gusto matched only by the 

rate at which the technology is surging 
into new areas. 

Even smaller chains and indepen- 
dents are entering the world of auto- 
mation; with pharmacy computers al- 
most as common in drug stores now as 
freezers are in supermarkets, more 
and more drug store operators are 
looking to point-of-sale (POS) sys- 
tems, scanning and beyond: to such ca- 
pabilities as electronic credit-card au- 
thorization and_ third-party 
processing, and, looming on the hori- 
zon, electronic funds transfer. 

For leaders in drug store automa- 
tion, such as Pay Less NW, Rite Aid 
and Walgreens, the commitment to 
chainwide automation has alread 
been made and is being implemented. 
A few, such as Pay Less NW, Osco and 
Thrifty, have POS systems in place in 
all their stores; others are steadily pro- 
gressing toward that goal. Still others, 
such as Rite Aid, are pausing in their 
push toward chainwide systems while 
they assimilate acquisitions. 

A major challenge for these leaders 
surrounds the human factor: how to 
bring their people on-line in terms of 
understanding and acceptance of the 
technology, and how to use the mass of 
new information available to the best 
advantage in running their stores. 

“The major chains are studying and 
making the transition,” said Ted 
Rosner, manager of operations at the 
ag division of Hook-SupeRx. 
“The impact [of automation] is phe- 
nomenal and affordable.” 


Must do it gradually 


The technology is necessary, 
Rosner said, “in order to handle our fu- 
ture; but if you don’t do it gradually, it 
becomes a bottleneck rather than a 
bocn.” 

SupeRx, which has POS chainwide, 
pluggable to scanning, has introduced 
more sophisticated capabilities one 
phase at a time; “otherwise, you lose 
people,” Rosner said. “Once our people 
get used to daily and weekly balancing 
with POS, we'll take them to scanning, 
and then to the next phases.” 

For Pay Less NW, which has had 
POS for about five years and has in- 
stalled scanning in 70 of its 255 stores, 
the challenge now is to “utilize the in- 
formation more fully,” said James 
Baer, vp-electronic data processing. 

The processing of the masses of data 
gathered by POS and scanning sys- 
tems requires a major investment of 
time as well as money, and many drug 
chains, and even supermarkets, are a 
long way from utilizing the data to the 


fullest, even if they have the costly 
central data-processing units neces- 
sary to do so. 

But while automation leaders are 
facing the problem of how to put the 
data to maximum use in ye nigr, 
their stores, many chains are sti 
struggling with testing systems, figur- 
ing out how to protect investments in 
existing equipment as they upgrade, 
and working out a timetable for install- 
ing equipment chainwide. 

or example, Wayne Cammack, the 
new vp-manager of information servic- 
es, at Shoppers Drug Mart in Canada, 
said SDM put all systems development 
on hold last winter, in order to take 
stock of the marketplace, their inter- 
nal information systems and the com- 
pany’s direction for future growth. 


Standardization of systems 


The chain is now moving toward 
standardization of systems. It has cho- 
sen one vendor for implementation of 

harmacy computerization chainwide 
about half of its 600 store have phar- 
macy computers) and one store-level 
accounting system and is in the process 
of evaluating POS vendors. Eight 
stores already have one type of POS 
equipment, and from those, “we’ve 
learned a lot about installation, how to 
operate them, how to gain the maxi- 
mum benefits,” said Cammack. 

The very definition of POS is hard to 
pin down. It can simply mean electron- 
ic cash registers, and it can mean much 
more: functions such as automated 
pricing, time and attendance, elec- 
tronic mail, movement tracking, pro- 
ductivity tracking and security report- 
ing, to name a few. 

ystems can be tailored to individual 
chains’ needs. At Fay’s, for example, 
POS currently consists of electronic 
cash registers that have promotional 
price lookup—vital to this highly pro- 
motional chain. 

With promotional price lookup, a 
chain can post signs telling customers 
the sale price that will be entered at 
checkout, eliminating re-stickering 
each item for the sale, and then stick- 
ering again when it’s over. 

“It’s a tremendous savings of labor, 
aggravation and dollars. It allows you 
to capture the data so that you know 
how each item did vis-a-vis the ad,” 
said one manager information services 
specialist at another chain. “That alone 
can pay for a system.” 

Determining whether POS is cost- 
effective “can be fast or can take a year 
to analyze,” said John Frazzini, gener- 
al manager of Stores Automated Sys- 
tems Inc. (SASD). 

“The information gathered becomes 
valuable very fast with more than one 
store,” he continued. 


MINNEAPOLIS — Thrifty e 
White, based here, is testing elec- 
tronic credit card autl srization in 
two of its stores, both located in 
Jamestown, N.D. 

Like many other chains, the 59- 
store chain sees the magnetic-stripe 
card verification system as a way to 
achieve quicker authorization on 
MasterCard, Visa and other card 
transactions and to make funds 
available more quickly for Thrifty- 
e@White to put to other uses. 

“More people are using credit 
cards now, and it was getting bur- 
densome to process them the old 
way,” said Henry C. Beinert, presi- 
dent of White Drug Enterprises. 


Thrifty @ White tests electronic credit card 
authorization in two Jamestown, N.D. units 


“The transaction takes a very 
short time, and there is no dialing of 
numbers or writing the proper au- 
thorization number, which cuts 
— employee mistakes,” Beinert 
said. 

The chain chose the Envoy Co. 
for the test, partly because it also of- 
fers the option of electronic process- 
ing of third-party claims, a feature 
the chain may add eventually. 

In evaluating the test, Beinert 
said the chain will be looking at how 
well employees adapt to the proce- 
dure, how fast the cash actually can 
be moved back into the main ac- 
count and whether it saves time and 
money at store level.

Five years ago, it might have cost 
about $150,000 to equip a 15-lane store 
with POS terminals and one control de- 
vice in the back. Today, for $200,000, 
such a store could have two control- 
lers, enough disk space to put all items 
on file, and terminals with scanners, 
according to one estimate. In other 
words, with a relatively small increase 
in investment, chains can get a bigger, 
better, faster system. 

There have been rapid changes in 
POS technology since the first genera- 
tion was introduced in the 70s. The 
equipment has become more flexible, 
easier to program and easier to oper- 
ate. And where older systems had a 
fixed number of capabilities, systems 
now are designed to integrate added 
features, so retailers can w with 
the system they have. A chain might 
not initially choose to handle credit- 
card authorization electronically, for 
example, but can add that function lat- 
er. “The features are available,” said 
Frazzini. “Whether you want to take 
advantage of them now depends on 
your needs.” 

When SupeRx, for example, bought 
a POS system in 1984, the vendor 
Tech America, provided ROM-based 
(read-only memory) registers but 
agreed to later convert them to RAM- 
based, or host-programmable, so that 
down- and uploading is done centrally 
through the corporate mainframe. 
Scanning can be added when the chain 
chooses, “We bought tomorrow’s tech- 
nology,” said Rosner. 

SupeRx’s system includes daily and 
weekly balancing, daily cashier re- 
porting, video rentals, lottery func- 
tions, departmental movement report- 
ing and gross pe reporting. 

n what might seem a minor feature, 
the chain’s POS system also has al- 
lowed it to comply with new federal 
regulations on deposit of checks with- 
out modifying the equipment. 


Now that SupeRx is 100 percent 
POS-equipped, the company is moving 
to continue already scheduled updat- 
ing of the recently-acquired Brooks di- 
vision with POS, after which the Hook 
division is scheduled to be converted. 

Some chains have gone beyond basic 
POS and scanning capabilities. Pay 
Less NW, for example, already offers 
such services as electronic credit-card 
authorization and electronic funds 
transfer (EFT). 

While electronic credit-card autho- 
rization systems are already being in- 
stalled or tested at several chains, 
electronic funds transfer is at the cut- 
ting edge of paperless transactions at 
the register and may be the wave of the 
future for drug chains. EFT, using 
automatic teller bank cards or “debit 
cards,” speeds up checkouts, a major 
plus for consumers. The EFT transac- 
tion can take as little as 10 seconds. 


Another benefit 


Another benefit to customers is that 
it streamlines the identification pro- 
cess. The customer enters a secret per- 
sonal identification number, or “PIN” 
number, in the POS system, and if the 
bank approves the transaction, it is 
complete. Shoppers also save money 
on buying paper checks. 

For retailers, the faster transaction 
and convenience afforded by EFT 
translates into increased sales and re- 
duced labor costs, plus better security. 

Representing automation on a truly 
large scale is the Carrefour Hypermar- 
ket in cheesey pt which has adopted 
the Grocery Management System 
(GMS), from ICL North America. The 
installation contains the largest single 
scanning site of POS terminals in the 
country—61 front scanning lanes, plus 
six other POS terminals throughout 
the store. It also includes networked 
microcomputer-based retail control-

Scanning, once considered 
“the expensive toy of retail 
food stores,” in one drug store 
executive’s words, is becom- 
ing accessible to drug chains. 
ust a few years ago, most 
drug chain execs weren’t even 
thinking of scanning. But sev- 
eral factors have changed 
their minds: the cost has come 
down, enough product lines in 
drug stores are now UPC-cod- 
ed to make it feasible, technol- 
ogy has improved and the 
equipment is more compact. 
Moreover, “the fact that it’s 
a proven technology [from 
over a decade of use by many 
supermarkets] is very impor- 
tant,” said Wayne Cammack, 


vp-manager of information 
services (MIS) at Shoppers 
Drug Mart. 

7 ig stores don’t save 
money because scanning is 
faster. Although it allows im- 

rovement in customer satis- 
action by checking them out 
faster, you still have to man 
the cash register for any num- 
ber of customers. Scanning al- 
lows you to keep up with cus- 
tomers with the same amount 
of labor,” said John Frazzini, 
y Serpents manager of Stores 

utomated Systems (SASI). 

But scanning’s advantages 
for drug stores include: 

@ It cuts down on price-mark- 
ing products, which saves la- 


bor and increases reliability. 
@ It affords cashier account- 
ability through polling draw- 
ers and cash reporting. 
@ It provides a more precise 
picture of what is being sold at 
checkout, capturing more in- 
formation more accurately 
than by manual key-in.

a MIS executive at Perry 
Drug Stores, tells one story 
from his Perry days to illus- 
trate the value of POS with 
scanning [all numbers used 
are “ballpark” rather than 
real, as Perry’s actual sales 
numbers or percentages are 
confidential]:

ere’s no question that

Mart, headquartered in Medi-

few months, his stores have 
seen about a 15 percent unit 
growth m hair care sales and 
about a 10 percent increase in 
dollar sales. 

Boodjeh says the growth is 
coming from Drug Mart’s ex- 
panding support of the econo- 
my brand shampoos, condi- 
tioners, and styling aids. 
“They’ve taken over from the 
premium-priced brands that 
we no longer carry exclusive- 
ly,” he says. 

Boodjeh says that these 
days he’d just as soon not car- 
ry some of the premium 
brands like Ivory, Head & 
Shoulders or Prell, because “I 
can’t make any money on 
them. Everybody is giving 
them away. 

“But because of the way 
we're able to buy the economy 
brands, which is often by the 


onomy 


brands 


truckload, we’re able to price 
very competitively yet still 
keep our margins. That’s why 
our dollar sales and our profit 
dollars are increasing on these 
lines. 

‘“‘We’re selling 10 of the 
economy brands for every one 
of the premiums, and since 
we're buying truckloads ver- 
sus small lots, our margins are 
better.” 

Boodjeh says that some of 
his best sellers right now are 
White Rain, Aqua Net and 
L’Oréal’s Ultra Rich, all of 
which he retails for under a $1, 
usually 99 cents. 

In styling aids, which is the 
strongest growth segment in 
hair care right now, sales in 
Boodjeh’s stores are up about 
15 percent in dollars and 20 
percent in units. His best sell- 
ers are still the economy 
brands: White Rain and Aqua 
Net, especially. 

Because price is important to 
Drug Mart customers, Boodjeh 
reports that most brands that 


boost sales 
10% for Discount Drug Mart 


offer consumer values such as 
rebates or low prices do well in 
his stores. He says White Rain, 
which has been doing some 
heavy rebating in recent 
months, has “taken over the 
market in my stores.” 

Salon Selectives, one of last 
year’s major line launches, is 
continuing to do well in Drug

Nielsen: Hair care sales up 7% 


Nielsen Marketing Services reports that hair care sales in 
retail drug stores are up nearly 7 percent, to $1.45 billion. 

Most of the growth is coming from the hair fixatives category, 
including gels, mousses, spritzes and sprays. The category is up 
nearly 14 percent, to $196 million, for the year ending June 30. 

The hair color segment is up 11 percent, to $290 million. 

Mousse is still down in drug stores. Nielsen estimates that 
mousse sales declined almost 13 percent to $52 million for the 12- 
month period that ended last June. 

Mousse is still a good categorv for drug stores, but it is losin 
sales because many consumers are switching from mousse sty]- 
ing aids to go's, spritzes and sprays. 

uring this past year, drug stores continued to strengthen 
their market share of hair color sales. The drug store industr 
gained half a share point to end the year with 54.1 percent of all 
mass market retail hair color sales. 

They also strengthened their position in perms, ending the 
period with a 49.6 percent share, up .7 over last year. Food 
stores continued to be the dominant source of purchase for after- 
shampoos or conditioners, but drug stores picked up .2 in this 
category for the 12-month May-June neni j 

Food stores are also domi- 
nant in shampoo sales, ending 
the year with nearly 51 percent 
of all mass market retail sales.

from last year. Mass merchan-

Western Region : 


Arizona — Mike Henry, 
head pharmacist of Arrow 
United Pharmacy, has been 
elected president of the Ari- 
zona Pharmacy Association. 


California — The California 
Pharmacists Association has 
held its first two AIDS 
spokespersons training ses- 
sions. The sessions were the 
first in a program designed 
to train one person from 
each of the association’s 38 
local affiliates to be a source 
of AIDS information. 

“Our goal,” said Gail Loh- 
mann, marketing assistant 
for the association, “is to 
have one pharmacist at ev- 
ery pharmacy who is trained 
in AIDS education.” 


Iowa — The Iowa legisla- 
ture has taken further action 
to limit physician dispensing. 
The legislation requires phy- 
sicians who dispense pre- 
scription drugs other than 
samples to register with 
their examining board. The 
bill also requires the practi- 
tioners to provide their pa- 


tients 
with free- 
dom of choice 
in the selection of 
a pharmacy. 


North Dakota — The North 
Dakota Pharmaceutical As- 
sociation will be developing 
protocols to deal with the 
newly passed legislation re- 
= out-of-state mail or- 

er pharmacies to be li- 
censed by the state board. 

William Grosz, executive 

secretary of the association 
and the board, said the asso- 
ciation is looking into how to 
enforce the new rule and 
will be sending information 
to out-of-state mail order 
houses operating in the 
state.

Antihypertensives under new scrutiny from health pros 


NEW YORK — Three ma- 
jor groups of antihypertensive 
medications are being closely 
scrutinized as results of na- 
tionwide research into effec- 
tive methods of controlling 
high blood pressure are dis- 
seminated among physicians 
who treat the estimated 58-60 
million Americans suffering 
from the disorder. 

The current research is be- 
ms focused primarily on ACE 
inhibitors, beta blockers- and 
calcium antagonists. The phy- 
sicians are also taking a closer 
look at non-pharmacologic 
methods of treating hyperten- 
sion. 

A study published in the 
Journal of the American Med- 
ical Association (JAMA) indi- 
cated that beta blockers, used 
as initial antihypertensive 
treatment, were associated 
with “significantly lower” 
five-year mortality “because 
of fewer deaths from coronary 
heart disease and stroke” than 
were thiazide diuretics, 
which, at one time, was the 
first-line treatment of hyper- 
tension. The effect was partic- 
ularly pronounced in smokers. 
John Wikstrand, M.D., 
Ph.D., the Swedish physician 
who directed the study, said it 
showed beta blockers the 
“only therapy effective in pri- 
mary prevention.” 

In its fourth Joint National 
Committee report, the Na- 
tional High Blood Pressure 
Education Program added 
ACE inhibitors and calcium 
antagonists to its list of initial 
therapy for hypertension 
which already included thia- 
zide-type diuretics and beta 
blockers. Published in the Ar- 
chives of Internal Medicine, 


the report represent- 
ed the consensus of 32 
organizations’ of 
health care providers, 
including the Ameri- 
can Medical Associa- 
tion, the American

duce drug dosage. To control 
hypertension, as well as to re- 
duce other cardiovascular risk 
factors, the report stresses the 
importance of weight reduc- 
tion, restriction of alcohol con- 
sumption, regular aerobic ex- 
ercise, tobacco avoidance, and 
the restriction of sodium con- 
sumption. It also mentions the 
benefits of biofeedback and re- 
laxation therapies, as well as 
the potential importance of in- 
creased potassium calcium in- 
take and the modification of di- 
etary fat consumption. 

“since the goal of therapy is 
to control blood pressure with 
the fewest drugs at their low- 
est dose, sound patient man- 
agement should include at- 
tempts to decrease the dosage 
or number of antihyperten- 
sive drugs while maintaining 
nonpharmacologic modal- 
ities,” said the report. To 
achieve this, the committee 


added a “step-down” portion 
to its step care therapy chart. 
The report also mentioned 
non-compliance as a factor in 
treating rtension. 

“Poor adherence to long- 
term treatment, both non- 

harmacologic and pharmaco- 
ogic, has been identified as 
the major reason for inade- 
quate control of high blood 
pressure,” said the report. 

The report further advo- 
cates collaboration between 
physicians and other health 
care providers, including 
pharmacists, as a means to- 
ward improving long-term ad- 
herence. 

Maude Babington, 
Pharm.D., the American 
Pharmaceutical Association’s 
director of professional af- 
fairs, has three suggestions 
for pharmacists interested in 
such collaboration. All are 
predicated on the belief that 


compliance is most likely if pa- 
tients are prescribed the 
smallest possible number of 
different medications taken at 
the lowest possible frequency, 
and all require pharmacists to 
know their antihypertensive 
medication: | 
@ Ifyou receive a prescription 
for medication that must be 
taken, say, four times a day, 
but are aware of how to reduce 
the dosage to, perhaps, two 
times a day, call the physician 
and suggest the switch. 
e If a physician prescribes 
drug A which must be taken 
three times a day, but you 
know drug B is similar but 
only needs to be taken once a 
“, call and suggest a change. 
e If a doctor has written a 
prescription for two different 
drugs, as is often the case with 
antihypertensive medication, 
but you are aware that a com- 
bination drug exists, consider 
asking the physician about it. 
“These are good areas for 
the pharmacist and the physt- 
cian to collaborate on behalf of 
the patient,” said Dr. Babing- 
ton, especially since “some- 
times patients tend to tell 
pharmacists things they 


-wouldn’t tell their physician. 


It is possible that pharma- 
cists might be the first to learn 
about impotence associated 
with antihypertensive medi- 
cation, a common side effect of 
thiazide and loop diuretics, 
beta blockers, and centrally- 
and peripherally-acting ad- 
renergic inhibitors. Another 
side effect Dr. Babington 
thinks would be particularly 
likely to be discovered in the 
pharmacy is nasal congestion, 
which is often associated with 
rauwolfia akyloids.

store opening pace 


YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — At a pace worthy of Olympic 
gold, Phar-Mor is —— 20 stores this fail, with four 
stores set for Houston, six for Florida, and the rest stretch- 
ing from Appleton, Wis. in the Central states to Hickory, 
N.C. in the Southeast. 

The first two stores in its latest surge of openings were | 
both launched Sept. 28 in Houston, a new market for this 
deep discount pacesetter. 

Between now and Dec. 7, Phar-Mor will open two more 
units in Houston; six in Florida, where it already has 22; three 
in the Chicago area; and one store each in Terre Haute, Ind.; 
Hickory, N.C.; Rockford, Ill.; Shreveport, La.; Appleton, 
Wis.; and Pittsburgh and Altoona, Pa. 

Louisana and Texas represent new penetrations for the 


chain. 
In Florida, the new units will open in Ft. Walton Beach, 
est Palm Beach and Or- 


ae Ri Brandon, Lake Worth, 
ando. 

Including the 26 new stores already unveiled this year 
that will make 46 stores opened by year’s end, comp 
with 32 last year. Phar-Mor will reach the 1988 finish line 
with a total of 114 stores and plans to open 50 next year, said 
James Teichman, senior 3 

Ranging in size from 45,000 to 64,000 square feet, the 
stores will have computerized pharmacies and will retain 
the typical Phar-Mor format, Teichman said. 

Almost all of the 20 units are newly constructed, primari- 
ly co-anchoring with one or two other retailers in large 
shopping centers.

Schwarz named exec. vp at Dart Drug 


LANDOVER, Md. — Jeff Fantle, Dart Drug’s presi- 
dent and chief operations officer, announced recently that 
James Schwarz has been named as executive vp, corpo- 
rate secretary and general counsel. 

Schwarz, a George Washington University law gradu- 
ate, served at Peoples Drug in the same capacity for the 
past 15 years. 


Wander seals Maple Village buy 


FARMINGTON, Mich. — Former Perry Drug Stores ex- 
ecutive vp Alvin Wander is back in the chain drug business, 
following completion of his purchase of Maple Village Phar- 
macies in early September. Wander bought the seven-store 
chain from founders Harvey and Alvin Rubin for an undis- 
closed sum, and has renamed the chain Maple Drugs. 

Maple stores operate in southeastern Michigan from 
Ann Arbor to Detroit, and range in size from 5,000 square 
feet to 7,500 square feet. 

Former Perry merchandise manager Pat Teeley is serv- 
ing as head of advertising, erdhanadising and marketing, 
and Wander has retained Sheldon Rich as director of phar- 
macy operations. 


Lucky-Alpha merger held up in court 


LOS ANGELES — The Lucky Stores-Alpha Beia 
merger is still on hold while a U.S. District Court reviews 
an antitrust lawsuit brought against the grocery chains by 
John Van de Kamp, California's attorney general. 

At presstime, Federal District Judge David Kenyon 
was examining additional materials submitted recently by 
the parties involved. During this process, Kenyon has 
maintained the temporary restraining order, which pre- 
vents the two grocery chains from combining operations. 
No date has been set for his decision. 

The attorney general’s office seeks to prevent the merg- 
er on antitrust grounds, claiming that the combined opera- 
tion will hold too great a market share in California and 
lead to higher prices. 

On a similar matter, negotiations with the attorney gener- 
al’s office and Vons—surrounding its acquisition of the 
Southern California Safeway stores—are nearing a close, ac- 
cording to Bill Davila, Vons president and chief operations 
officer. He declined to give details of the negotiation. 


Perry takes seniors to the zoo 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores sponsored a 
free day at the Detroit Zoo recently for over 3,000 senior 
citizens from the Detroit area to observe the seventh an- 
nual Isabella Fiesselmann Day. 

The day commemorates Fiesselmann, 92, who wrote a 
letter to the zoo in 1981, longing to see it. The zoo granted 
her wish. Ever since her death in 1983, Isabella Fiessel- 
mann Day at the zoo is an annual event. ee 

Perry gives each senior citizen a “goodie” bag ne 
sample-sized Perry brand products, discount coupons an 
health record booklets, and raffles off a color television. 


Fred Meyer opens unique specialty store 

SEATTLE — Replacing one of the company’s few drug 
stores locations, Fred ear te opened a new 32,000-square- 
foot specialty store here this summer, that while no longer 
a drug store, still includes a agen 

The change was prompted by a major remodeling of the 
property, which took several years. During this time, 

red Meyer was able to continue running just the pharma- 
cy business, operating out of both a trailer in the parking 
lot and in a temporary site. 

The new store includes six of the company’s 11 depart- 
ments, which all operate on a vertical self-sufficient struc- 
ture: general merchandise, pharmacy, nutrition, soft lines 
a sports apparel), fine jewelry, and photo and 
electronics. 

According to company spokesman Rob Boley, the new 
store is about the same size as the previous location. How- 
ever, the category mix is now greatly expanded from the 
past assortment and better targets the urban market. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, October 10, 1988 


Texas stores brace for Gilbert, 


but are spared hurricane’s fury 


By Pamela Krein 

BROWNSVILLE, Tex. — Texas area dru 
stores had readied for the worst of Hurricane Gil- 
bert’s fury, but the storm’s path hit south of the 
state and spared the region from the devastation 
witnessed in Mexico, the Yucatan and Jamaica. 

Billed as the worst hurricane to ever hit the 
Western Hemisphere, Gilbert had cities all along 
the Texas coast preparing for monumental dam- 
age. Playing a part in the preparations, the ar- 
ea’s drug stores were often sold out of such storm 
necessities as batteries, kerosene lamps, mask- 
me Sor candles and distilled water. 

tailers from Texas’s Gulf Coast told Drug 
Store News they also filled a higher than average 
number of script orders, since many customers 
fled these cities with their essentials, not know- 
ing when they would be able to return to their 
homes. 

At Medico Discount Drug in Brownsville, 
store manager Vidal Hernandez said total sales 
ran three times higher than normal the day be- 
fore the storm hit. Sales were up for obvious 
storm-related items like batteries, but Hernan- 
dez said the store also sold a lot of games, as cus- 
tomers sought ways to wait out the storm. 

Hernandez said the store stocked up on sta- 
ee boarded windows and closed on the day Gil- 

rt was expected to hit. 

While Hernandez said the area experienced 
heavy rain, wind and minor power outages, his 
store and merchandise were not damaged. 

Perfecto’s Pharmacy in Brownsville also re- 


mained unharmed by the storm, according to 
manager Persecto ia. “People who were 
prepared didn’t have any damage,” he said. 

arcia said his store took precautionary mea- 
sures, such as securing medicines and its com- 
ui system. He brought items like insulin 

ome the day of the storm, Garcia said, to assure 

~— could be kept cold in case of a power outage. 

or Felix Maldonado, owner of Maldonado 
Pharmacy in Brownsville, the only damage he 
had was some spoiled insulin. While Maldonado 
said he remembered to place dry ice in the store’s 
refrigerator compartment, he forget to place dr 
ice in the freezer, resulting in some pi et ala 
ucts when power outages occurred. 

Although Gilbert’s intensity decreased as it 
proses’ through Texas, several areas were 

aced with ensuing tornadoes. San Antonio 
alone sighted some 30 twisters. Even here, 
damage was limited. 

Reveo and Walgreen, which both have nu- 
merous stores in San Antonio, said their stores 
remained undamaged by the storm, although 
some closed briefly. 

Mary Ellen Kari, Walgreen’s spokesperson, 
said the chain rushed extra merchandise to 
these stores, and made sure that technical 
backup was available via generators. 

Similar plans were in place at Revco, which 
sent regional personnel to the area on a 24-hour 
call basis in case of storm damage, company 
spokeswoman Kathleen Obert id Drug tore 

ews.

Twice each year we 
issue a report identi-

cus 1s on million-dollar

Some of the numbers may 
be understated, since there 
may be line extensions that 
could be regarded as new 
products. What’s more, there 
are many products introduced 
regionally or recently that 

have not been counted be- 
cause they have not reached 
the million-dollar level. 

In the 52 H&BA categories 
tracked by SAMI for which we 
have two full years or more of 
data, there were 918 brands 
with annual volume exceeding 
$1 million. Of these brands, 
298—or 32.5 percent—were 
introduced during the ’80s. 
Ten of these new brands cur- 
rently enjoy annual volume of 
more than $25 million. Anoth- 
er 22 new brands now gener- 
ate between $10 million and 
$25 million. And fifty brands 
introduced during the ’80s 
have achieved sales ranging 
between $5 million and $10 
million. 

Interestingly, we find that 
new brands turn up more fre- 

uently on the million-dollar 
list as the sales parameters de- 
cline. For example, new 
brands comprise 34.4 percent 
of those generating $2.5 mil- 
lion to $5 million and 40.1 per- 
cent of those ranging from $1 
million to $2.5 million. 

During the 1980s, the big- 
gest year for the introduction 
of million-dollar brands was 
1985, when 55 were launched. 
Forty-four were launched in 
both 1984 and 1987, and 40 
first appeared during 1986. 
The low points were reached 
in 1980 and’81 when 24 and 19, 
respectively, were intro- 
duced. | 

Because new products have 
a relatively short life span in a 
number of categories—partic- 
ularly hair care needs—there 
are many new products first 
marketed in the early ’80s that 
have either disappeared from 
drug store shelves or now 
command annual volume of 


less than $1 million. 

Of the new million-dollar 
products of the ’80s, 3.4 per- 
cent are in the $25 million vol- 
ume group. In contrast, all 
$25 million-plus brands com- 
prise 5.4 percent of all million- 
dollar brands.

ume in the year under scruti-

more than 40 percent of annual 
category volume.

hey arrive in mid-Octo-

open their condos and

home to the likes of Ohio,

Permanent residents call

migrations to Sunbelt ha-

on local trade. 

One newspaper, the News/ 
Sun-Sentinel in Fort Lau- 
derdale, Fla., even publishes 
a Snowbird edition, to keep 
them up to date on their 
winter homes during their 
summer absence. (See box

Sunday circulation of the Mi- 
ami Herald, which rises

come wintertime. 


deep

ercent of the customers in

and eat it, too: Snowbirds 
from Ohio are already famil- 
iar with Drug Emporium or 
Phar-Mor back home, so 
when one opens up in, say, 
Orlando, they are likely to 
flock to it. 


Phar-Mor reinforces its everyday low-price image with overhead signs that are impossible to miss and 
tell a message that appeals to shoppers on fixed incomes.

with the same chains in the 
North and South, especially 
drug stores, because they’ve 
built trust in one at home,” 
and that carries over, said 
Jo Bowman, a display adver- 
tising account executive with 
the News/Sun-Sentinel.

drug store operators in some 
Florida and Southwest areas

during the winter, with Jan- 
uary and February busier 
than for their Northern 
counterparts, they don’t 
overtly go after the snow- 
bird trade. For example, 
they generally don’t adver-

Introduction 
1988 Nielsen Review of Retail Drug Store Trends 


1988 is proving to be a banner 
year for drug stores. So far this 
year, retail drug store sales in- 
creased 8%, well ahead of 1987. 

Total retail sales were up 5% in 
1987 and they’re up 7% for the first 
half of 1988. 

The information compiled by 
Nielsen Marketing Research and 
presented in this publication shows 
that: 
® Consumers still have money to 
spend and that is one of the major 
reasons that the U.S. economy con- 
tinues to perform well. 

@ Economic growth during the re- 
mainder of 1988 and the first half of 
1989 will be moderate. 

@ Chain drug outlets now account 
for 62.1% of all U.S. retail drug 
store sales. 

@ Drug store sales of toiletry and 
remedial items are increasing at a 
rate that is twice their growth in 
food stores. 

© 86% of all chain drug outlets now 
have computerized pharmacy oper- 
ations. 

@ Alcoholic beverages are now sold 
in 64% of all chain drug stores. 

@ Chain drug store executives are 
predicting that the use of cable TV 
and other electronic media as adver- 
tising mediums will be greatly ex- 
panded during the next five years. 
@ More than 8 out of 10 key chain 
drug executives feel that within the 
next five years, the utilization of 
UPC scanner checkout systems in 
their stores, will equal the utiliza- 
tion within food chains.

CHAPTER I: 


The Economic Environment 


The U.S. ‘economy is expanding 
at a pace that exceeds the projec- 
tions of analysts in the aftermath of 
the 1987 October financial crisis. 
Whatever influence the stock mar- 
ket crash had on real economic ac- 
tivity is behind us. The dark clouds 
on the horizon continue to be the 
federal budget and trade deficits. 

The economy’s strength over the 
past several months has been at- 
tributed to robust consumer and 
business spending accompanied by 
healthy export growth. Total U.S. 
retail sales increased 5% in 1987 to 
$1.5 trillion. During the first half of 
1988, sales are running 7% greater 
than last year and are expected to 
continue at that rate for the remain- 
der of this year. 

Economic growth during the re- 
mainder of 1988 and the first half of 
1989 should be moderate.

Total U.S. drug store sales in- 
creased an average of 6% across the 
U.S. in 1987. 

Much of that strength can be 
found at opposite ends of the coun- 
try: on the east coast (New England 
at +10% and Metro New York at 
+ 10%) and in the west, Southern 
California at +11%, and Boise/ 


Salt Lake/Phoenix at + 11%). 
There are no areas reporting 
sales decreases although sales in 
Dallas/Houston (+ 1%) are slow. 
Total drug store sales per capita 
is highest again this year in North- 
ern California (160), Chicago (123) 
and Southern California (118). 
These are areas where drug stores 


have been particularly successful in 
presenting to consumers a wide va- 
riety of non-traditional merchan- 
dise and services.

Drug chain dollar sales of the 66 
categories in the Nielsen HBA In- 
dex increased by 11% during the 
first part of this year, while inde- 
pendent drug store HBA sales in- 
creased at a 4% rate. 

Some categories are turning in 
outstanding performances: skin 
care, oral hygiene and external 
medicines are doing well in both 
chains and independent stores. An- 


Drug Store News 


algesics/digestive remedies and col- 
or cosmetics product groups are do- 
ing well in chain drug stores, as are 
selected sundries and men’s prod- 
ucts in independents. 

The total dollar volume of the 
Nielsen HBA Index categories now 
represents 24.8% of chain drug total 
sales volume and 12.5% of total in- 
dependent volume. 


A total of 62 of the 66 categories 
tracked in the Nielsen HBA index 
registered sales increases during 
the first half of 1988. This was an in- 
crease of 21 categories over those 
that showed such growth last year. 

A total of 14 categories fell in the 
“very hot” group and 11 categories 
in the “hotter” group. 

Very few categories this year are 
suffering sales declines.

A total of 9 of the 25 selected HBA 
categories surveyed in chain drug 
stores were allotted more shelf 
space than they had in 1987. Of 
these 9, hair fixatives was the big- 
gest gainer with an additional 9 feet 
of shelf space. Paper products cate- 
gories and cold and sinus remedies 
also got healthy space increases. 

While 9 product categories went 
up, 11 selected categories were allo- 
cated less shelf space in chain drug 
outlets including hair preparations, 
vitamins and shampoos. 


Independent drug stores gave ad- 
ditional space to 21 of 25 categories. 
Hair fixatives gained the most of 
any category. Only 3 categories lost 
shelf space, with each only losing 1 
foot. 

9 HBA categories received addi- 
tional shelf space from chain food 
stores while mass merchandisers in- 
creased the shelf space of 13 catego- 
ries.

CHAPTER VI: 


Drug Store Merchandising 


The most popular “extra” in drug 
chains across the country is film 
processing, 98% of all drug chains 
offer film processing to their cus- 
tomers. Penetration of the service 
is virtually complete in all areas of 
the country except New York. 

At the same time, pharmacy com- 
puterization is rapidly becoming an 
essential in drug chains, 86% of all 
chains now have pharmacy comput- 
ers, up from 71% last year. In the 
Nielsen East Central, Metro Chica- 
go, Southwest, Metro L.A., and Pa- 
cific regions, over 90% of all drug 


chains have pharmacy computer 
systems. 

Alcoholic beverages are now sold 
in 64% of all chain drug stores and 
are especially prominent in the Met- 
ro Chicago, Metro L.A. and Pacific 
regions. 

Being open 24 hours is offered in 
only 7% of drug chains in the U.S. 
Metro Chicago, West Central and 
the East Central are the only re- 
gions in which this extra is in more 
than 10% of the stores. 

Other merchandising strategies 
that are popular in specific areas of

Melville’s muscle powers 
growth of Freddy’s chain 


OCHESTER, N.Y. — 

Freddy’s, the off-price 

weapon in Melville 
Corp.’s retail arsenal, is draw- 
ing on Melville’s financial mus- 
cle to boost its market pene- 
tration in upstate New York, 
central and southern Virginia, 
and Florida. 

The deep discount drug 
chain has added six stores in 
the past year to boost its store 
count to 18 units, and will open 
“a number” of stores next 


year, according to chain presi- © 


dent and founder Fred Silver- 
stein. The first of those will be 
a Freddy’s in Florida’s Dade 
County next February, he 
said. 

Freddy’s now operates six 
units in the upstate New York 
cities of Rochester, Buffalo, 
Syracuse and Niagara Falls; 
nine units in Florida, includ- 
ing five in Broward County, 
three in the Tampa/Clear- 
water area and one in Orlando; 
and three units in Virginia. 

Although Silverstein would 
not discuss specific expansion 
objectives, he said the finan- 
cial backing of its parent com- 
pany has enabled Freddy’s to 
accelerate its growth. The off 
price chain came under Mel- 
ville’s sg, “Ap wing five 
years ago, but operates com- 
paen independently of the 

olding company’s CVS chain 

drug division, Silverstein told 
Drug Store News. 

Last spring, Freddy’s 


opened up new market oppor- 
tunities with the purchase of 
three former Pathmark Super 
Drug stores from F & M Dis- 
tributors. The stores, in Rich- 
mond, Hampton and Virginia 
Beach, Va., give the chain a 
base for growth in the mid-At- 
lantic region, midway be- 
tween its upstate New York 
and Florida market bases. 

“Our expansion next year 
will generally be targeted to 
upstate New York and Flori- 
da, and we will be building on 
our presence in Virginia,” Sil- 
verstein said. ‘‘We had 
planned to move into Virginia 
anyway, so it was fortunate 
that the F & M stores became 
available.” 

Silverstein said Freddy’s 
continues to operate stores 
averaging about 27,000 
square feet (17,000 selling), 
with the main focus on drug 
store basics at discounts of 30 
percent to 50 percent or more. 

“The emphasis is still on 
brand-name items, most 
heavily in the areas of H&BA, 
cosmetics, stationery/home 
office/school supplies, phar- 
macy, greeting cards and can- 
dy and snacks,” he said. “The 
basic concept hasn’t changed 
much since our association 
with Melville, but it’s always 
being refined.” 

Except at grand opening 
events, the chain also contin- 
ues to rely on word-of-mouth 
for advertising. —J. F.

Long Hot Summer Sparks Beverage 


Sales In Non Food Store: 
Gatorade was “Outstanding” 


chains, sales suffered because people didn’t 
want to stir, let alone shop. 

But at least nonfood retailers report there was 
one bright spot in the almost constant 90 degree 
weather: beverages. 

According to most buyers for nonfood chains, all 
beverages did well this past season, but some bev- 
erages, in the words of many buyers, were “out- 
standing.” 

Just about every buyer F'm talked to in August 
reported that their sales of Gatorade were “phe- 
nomenal” this past season. 

Buyers say all their flavors are selling well this 
year, but their two newest flavors, Citrus Cooler 
and Lemonade, are doing phenomenally well. 

“Gatorade had a great year with us last year, but 
this year it’s even stronger,” said one buyer for a 
mid-west drug chain. “It’s incredible. It seems 
like everyone who steps outdoors has been drink- 
ing it. It’s partly because it’s the only brand in its 
category. It has about a 98% market share, but 
you also can’t turn on a sporting event anywhere 
without seeing some athlete drinking Gatorade.” 

A new juice/bottled water drink, Stroh’s Sun 
Dance, also sold well this past quarter, helped by 
an ry greg advertising —_—— from Stroh’s, 
and by the fact that many nor chains jumped 
on Sun Dance, almost from its first launch day. 

According to brokers who handle Sun Dance, 
Stroh’s did something very unusual for a manufac- 
turer launching a new grocery item: they intro- 
duced it to the nonfood trade at the same time they 
introduced it to the food trade and many nonfood 
chains were actually quicker than the food chains 
to promote and feature Sun Dance. 

ccording to the sales reps who sell Sun Dance 
into the stores, about 25% to 30% of Sun Dance’s 
Mig right now is coming through the nonfood 
trade. 

Nonfood chains usually like to work on ads six to 
eight months down the line, but sources say that 

al-Mart took two weeks from the time their buy- 
ers first saw the Sun Dance presentation to the 
time they ordered the item. 

“Their management saw the advertising 
Stroh’s was putting behind it. They liked the 
uniqueness of the product, and they just turned on 
a dime. They dropped other items they had 
planned to promote and they just made space for 
it. It’s been one of their hottest items this year,” 
said a well placed source. | 

In Washington, D.C., the People’s operated 
chain of Bud’s Discount Drug stores had a mid- 
summer massive display of Sun Dance in the back 
of their stores next to Coke and Pepsi. 

At a time when the food chains were primarily 
selling the beverage at a full mark-up with retails 
averaging about $2.99, Bud’s set up bulk displays 
and promoted the item at $1.99. One store actually 
had 100 cases on display one week-end.

Liquor Sales Continue Flat 


Coolers are still experiencing moderate growth, but beer, wine and hard liquor, 
in both sales and consumption, are all flat or down. Consumers, in a moderate 
mood, are seeking healthier beverages. 


leoholic beverage sales re- 
A mained slow in 1988. Wine 

and the darker liquors like 
scotch, bourbon and rye continued 
to experience consumption de- 
clines and flat sales. 

White spirits enjoyed somewhat 
better growth, but nothing that 
can be described as dramatic. 

According to buyers and indus- 
try experts, diet or health posi- 
tioned drinks including light bev- 
erages were still in this year, and 
flavors such as peach, raspberry 
and coconut, were still popular. 

But generally in 1987 and con- 
tinuing through 1988, the story is 
that individual brands managed to 
generate growth, but, with a few 
exceptions, most categories did 
not.

Bright Spot in Beverage Consumption 


I mpact magazine, a leading beverage industry publication, believes that 

total per capita beverage consumption is destined to rise over time. 
Impact bases its theory partly on the fact that The Physician’s Hand- 

book has reported that daily liquid consumption increases as people grow 


older. 


The Physician’s Handbook reports that infants — 11 to 33 liquid 
ounces daily; children require 33 to 60 ounces daily, an 


83 ounces daily. 


Impact says the fact that the U.S. adult population is growing, combined 
with the availability of a much broader selection of beverages and with in- 
creased purchasing power, should promote total per-capita consumption 


growth.

Outlook For Tomorrow’s Alcohol Market 


\ K T hat will be the nation’s strongest selling beverages from now through 


In its 1988 Review and Forecast edition of Beverage Trends in America, 
Impact magazine signals out soft drinks, coolers and fruit juice/drinks as 
the growth areas for beverages from now through the year 2000. 

Impact predicts that the overall bevera 
year through 1990, reaching 47.8 billion gallons in 1995 and 51.5 gallons by 


e market will expand 1.4% a 


By 1990, Impact expects that alcoholic beverage volume will be win- 
nowed down to just over 6.7 billion gallons, where Impact thinks the mar- 
ket will remain through the year 2000 and beyond. 

Their market experts feel that alcohol’s ae of beverage consumption 
will dwindle from 14.1% in 1990 to 18% in 2000. 

Impact says that beer volume will probably erode at a modest but steady 
pace over the coming years, fo to just over 6.7 billion gallons by 1990, 


Impact thinks wine wil dip te to about 445 gallons by 1990, but should re- 
cover to maybe 459 million gallons by 2000. 

Spirit consumption will probably slide more dramatically, going down to 
about 385 million gallons by 1990 and to 357 million by 2000. 

Coolers, which were at 187 million gallons in 1987, one climb as high as 
316 million gallons by 2000. By the turn of the century, Impact thinks cool- 
ers may account for 4.3% of all alcoholic consumption.

Methodology of SPAR study 


At the request of Drug Store News, SPAR Marketing 
Services, an Eden Prairie, Minn.-based company that spe- 
cializes in in-store data collection, audited the fragrance 
departments of 415 chain drug stores in the top 20 metro 
markets. 

The survey was done on Thursday, April 21, and it was 
designed to determine the following: 

@ How much extra display space did the average chain 
eo give fragrances at Mother’s Day? 

® at were the most popular types of displays for mer- 
chandising fragrances: islands, endcaps, counter displays 
or expanded shelf allocations? 

@ What percent of chain drug stores merchandised their 
i ea under glass at Mother’s Day? 

@ How are some of the major brands displayed at Moth- 
er’s Day? How much expanded space are they given in the 
average chain drug store, and where are they generally 
displayed? 

@ What were some of the most productive brands at Moth- 
er’s Day, i.e., the brands that generated the highest sales 
within the space allocations they were given? 

@ When did the average chain drug store put up its fra- 
grance displays for Mother’s Day, and how many stores 
supported those displays with point-of-purchase aids? and 
@ How did the chains with the strongest cosmetics/fra- 
grance programs treat the fragrance category at Christ- 
mas? How did Walgreens, Longs and CVS merchandise 
select brands? 

We shared the data that SPAR collected for us with 
merchandisers and buyers for eight of the industry’s top 
drug chains.

chains in the top 10, one president of a small regional chain

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 10, 1988 


Retailers analyze fragrance 
space allocations in stores 


the most popular fra- 

grances at Mother’s Day 
among those we tracked were 
Chantilly, Vanderbilt, Charlie 
and Forever Krystle. These 
were the fragrances that got 
the most display space as mea- 
sured in total linear feet. 

Interestingly, paaget | 
and Forever Krystle got al- 
most as much display space at 
Mother’s Day as they had at 
Christmas. 

Most drug stores gave the 
brands we tracked substan- 
tially less off-shelf display 
space at Mother’s Day com- 
pared to Christmas, but Chan- 
tilly’s off-shelf display alloca- 
tiens were only down by 14 
percent and Krystle’s were 
only down by 20 percent. 

Vanderbilt and Caharlie’s 
Mother’s Day display space 
were down from Christmas by 
37 percent and 39 percent, re- 
spectively. 

The only two fragrances to 
get more display space in the 
stores at Mother’s Day than at 
Christmas were Deborah’s 
ScentSational Scents, which 
are alternative designer fra- 

rances, and the newest scent 
rom Charles of the Ritz, Xia 
Xiang. 

Some of the retailers who 
helped evaluate the SPAR 
findings reasoned that Xia 
Xiang was given expanded 
space at Mother’s Day be- 
cause the brand did exception- 
ally well at Christmas even 
with relatively limited distri- 
bution. 

Retailers felt the allocations 
for Chantilly, Vanderbilt and 
Charlie were justified because 
of their popularity, but they 
thought that Lady Stetson, 
because it is such a strong sell- 
er, deserved more total feet 
than the brand had been given 
at Mother’s Day. 

However, our retailers also 
pointed out that merchandis- 
ers have to consider more than 
market share when they allo- 
cate off-shelf display space to 
— particular fragrance. 
“Chantilly had four or five pro- 
motional programs available 
for the Mother’s Day period,” 
one buyer recalled, “while 
Jungle Gardenia just had one, 
and Vanderbilt had about one 
or two. 

“When I look at promotional 
opportunities for fragrances, I 
have to look at the programs 
because my customers want to 
see something special. They 
want a value, and to get an in- 
cremental sale at an event like 
Mother’s Day, I need a good 
program because I don’t have 
a captive audience at this holi- 
day. People aren’t coming into 
my stores looking to buy a fra- 
grance as they do at Christ- 
mas.” 

Another buyer for one of the 
major deep discount dru 
chains said that it made eat 
marketing sense that Chantil- 
ly was so prominently dis- 
— during the Mother’s 

ay sales period. 

“Chantilly’s allocations 
make sense because the brand 
has been around so long,” she 
said. “It’s more of a traditional 
fragrance. Many women can 


F or drug store retailers, 


remember their grandmoth- 
ers using Chantilly. It’s not 
geared to as young a market as 
say Vanderbilt or Lady Stet- 
son.” 

There were two alternative 
designer scents among the 
fragrances tracked: Primo and 
Deborah’s ScentSational 
Scents. 

Primo was in nearly 80 per- 
cent of all the stores audited 
and it was given a generous al- 
location of space, 662 total lin- 
ear feet. However, that was 
down 48 percent from Primo’s 
allocations at Christmas, 
which our sources said made 
sense. 

“Many shoppers don’t buy 
the ADF's to give as gifts,” one 
buyer pointed out. “They are 
more commonly a self pur- 
chase.” 

ScentSational Scents was 
given more space in the stores 
that displayed it than it had 
been given at Christmas, but 
the line was in a much smaller 
number of total stores than 
the other brands we audited. 

Several buyers, in fact, said 
they were cutting back on 
space for alternative designer 
fragrances. “The category is 
not as strong as it once was,” 
said the buyer for a major mid- 
western chain. ‘We’ve cut 
back and right now I’m only 
carrying a few select SKUs.” 

Not too surprisingly, men’s 
brands were not given much 
display space in April. 

ovan Musk got the most 
display space in mid-April, 
oe it could be because the 
stores were hoping to pick up 
early Father’s Day sales, and 
also because Beecham has 
been sending out attractive 
pre-packs of Jovan Musk to 
complement stepped-up ad- 
vertising for the brand. 

The original Pierre Cardin 
fragrance got the second high- 
est space allocation in mid- 
April, which was surprising at 
first, until several buyers ex- 

lained that the Cardin brand 
as been doing much better 
under Shulton’s management. 

Several sources said Shul- 
ton has been putting more 
“creativity” behind the brand, 
and its marketing hasn’t been 
as “stodgy” as it has been in 
earlier years. 

The same was true for Adi- 
das. Several buyers say Adi- 
das sales have been picking 
up, and one source said the 
brand’s sales in her deep dis- 
count drug stores were “very 
strong. 

“It’s because of the interest 
in the Olympics, I think,” she 
said. “They have just done an 
excellent job of advertising 
Adidas and tying it into the 
Olympics.” 

However, sources also felt 
that some men’s fragrances, 

articularly Night Spice and 
ron, didn’t seem to have got- 
ten enough space based on 
their relatively stron 
launches and their genera 
success at Christmas. 

Our sources thought the al- 
locations for some of the other 
leading brands, Chaps, Stet- 
son and English Leather Co- 
logne, however, were “right 
on target.”

A summary of key findings from the SPAR study: 


@ The majority of all chain drug stores Mother’s Da 
oe displays (74.4 percent) were up by April 
16, 1988. 


@ 18 percent of the stores in our survey said they 
were not planning a Mother’s Day display. However, 
some of these stores could or did have other promo- 
tional displays for fragrances. 


@ The total linear footage or the “everyday allot- 
ment” for the fragrance sections we measured for 
our Mother’s Day audit was 32,324 linear feet. In 
preparation for the Mother’s Day holiday, the stores 


we measured added another 9,502 linear feet for pro- 
motional display. This was a 29 percent increase in 
space for fragrances at Mother’s Day, compared to a 
79 percent increase at Christmas. 


@ The percent of stores displaying fragrances de- 
creased substantially from Chretien to Mother’s 
Day. For women’s fragrances, there were 47 percent 
fewer stores displaying fragrances at Mother’s Day, 
and there were 66 percent fewer stores displaying 
men’s fragrances. 


@ Among the women’s fragrances we selectively 


measured, Xia Xiang had the largest increase in both 
the number of stores carrying it and in regular shelf 
space expansion. It also had the smallest decrease in 


the numbers of stores displaying it. 


@ At Mother’s Day, Chantilly had the best share of 
shelf space for women’s fragrances. Vanderbilt came 
in second. Last Christmas, their roles were re- 
versed. At Mother’s Day, Chantilly took first place 
because it had the largest share of promotional dis- 
plays. At Mother’s Day, 6.4 percent of all displays 
—— - Chantilly, compared to 3.2 percent for Van- 
erbilt.

Wal-Mart puts Dot deep discount chain on the block 


By David Vaczek 

BENTONVILLE, Ark. — Wal- 
Mart is saying “period” to Dot. 

The giant discounter has offered to 
sell its 14-store Dot deep discount drug 
chain to at least two national dru 
chains recently, market sources tol 
Drug Store News. 

Phar-Mor, Drug Emporium, and 
F&M Distributors, the Midwest- 
based low-priced drug leaders, are 
seen as likely buyers. 

A Wal-Mart spokesperson, unable 
to discuss any possible sale, said Wal- 
Mart plans no new Dots through 1989. 
The company had projected earlier it 
might add as many as nine Dots this 
year. 

Two were added this year in the 
same sort of heartland metro markets 
Dot has favored since opening its first 


store in Des Moines, Iowa, in 1983. 
There are now five Dots in Kansas 
City, three in St. Louis, three in Des 
Moines, two in Wichita, Kan., and one 
in Lincoln, Neb. 

Although some stores approach the 
$5 million annual sales level, Dot has 
largely suffered from a faulty location 
strategy that favors inexpensive, 
weak metro area sites, ——— to 
drug industry sources in Kansas City 
and St. Louis. 

“They’ve tried to be mini-Wal- 
Marts,” said one Kansas City insider. 
Sited poorly in the metro area, Dot’s 
KC stores found they couldn’t pull cus- 
tomers from a wide enough radius. 
Wal-Mart’s discount stores count on 
dominating a 10- to 15-mile radius in 
their small town markets, the source 
contended.

Genovese opening 1st deep discounter 


CARLE PLACE, N. Y. — Genovese Drug Stores will 
open its first deep discount store here Oct. 26, across from 
the iant Roosevelt Field shopping mall and within blocks 
of a hack Bottom unit. 

The store, named Great American Drug Store, will be 
15,000 square feet, said division head Paul Genovese, 
which is larger than conventional Genovese stores, but 


smaller than many deep discounters across the country. 


Ansell recalis two lots of Lifestyles 


DOTHAN, Ala. — Ansell Inc. is voluntarily recalling 
two lots of its 12-pack Lifestyles Extra Strength condoms 
with Nonoxynol-9, after Hawaii’s Department of Health 
advised the company that a few condoms had weak spots in 
the reservoir end. The recall, the first in the company’s 
history, is confined to lot numbers 6087254-C68E and 
6087223-C57E, code number 2112. Retailers and distribu- 
tors are advised to return the coded product to Ansell, 
1500 Industrial Rd., Dept. A, Dothan, Ala. 36302. 


Longs appoints Renner its gmm 


WALNUT CREEK, Calif. — Longs Drug Stores has 
promoted Barry Renner to general merchandise manag- 
er, replacing Dale Bystrom, who joined Osco this summer. 
Renner has been with Longs since 1959, and during the 
last 17 years has held managerial positions at six Central 
California stores. 


Bill’s moves HQ to Benicia 


BENICIA, Calif. — Bill’s Drugs recently moved its 
headquarters here from Lafayette, where the chain had 
been run since its inception in 1959. 


Revco fills two marketing slots 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Reveo D.S. has appointed Guy 
L. Shirk director of advertising and promoted Brent L. 
Rodgers to director of special programs. Shirk, 44, previ- 
ously vp and management supervisor at Hesselbart & Mit- 
ten of f (maa will . responsible for Revco’s image, event 
and product advertising and media, photographic and 
ae operations. 

Rodgers, 30, who joined Revco in 1976, moved up from 
supervisor of product presentation. His new responsibil- 
ities will include integration of advertising and marketing 
efforts into existing programs, such as in-store vendor 
promos and grand opening events. 


Vons’ headquarters moving 


ARCADIA, Calif. — Vons announced it will move its 
headquarters here from El] Monte. Vons has purchased, 
for an undisclosed amount, a 240,000-square-foot three- 
level May Co. department store retail site. 

Vons spokeswoman Mary McAboy said the chain is cur- 
rently operating out of three somewhat overcrowded El 
Monte locations, and with the addition of Safeway stores, 
the crowding problem has intensified. 7 

Two of the current locations are owned. One includes a 
distribution center, and the third site is leased. She said 
Vons will continue to operate the DC and keep the compa- 
ny-owned sites. Some employees will move to the new site 
this month; the rest in January. 


Company that IDs new products formed 


NORWALK, Conn. — Group EFO Ltd., a consulting 
company that helps consumer product companies create 
and identify new peeage opened here recently, accord- 
ing ig Edward F. Ogiba, the company’s founder and presi- 

ent. 
_ “Identifying a truly innovative product is what market- 
ing and the new product business is all about today,” 
Ogiba, most recently managing director of Product Initia- 
tives, said. “More than 80 percent. . . of all new products 
fail because. . . they do not create a point of difference for 
consumers.”

no further discussions with 
Kroger. “We can only con-

60 years ago 

NEW YORK, 1928— A good rule to remem- 
ber, when —— on trade, is: “If a customer 
seems exceptionally gruff, it may be just a false 
front to cover up an unusually tender heart.” 

Or it may be a sense of humor expressing it- 
self in a queer way. Ifa man can hand you a hot 
one and you toss it back to him in the right 
way, then he’ll warm up to you. Usually you'll 
find his bark is worse than his bite. 


50 years ago 

WASHINGTON, D.C., 1938 — Thomas N. 
Beavers of Peoples Drug Stores, Washington, 
said at the National Association of Chain 
Stores’ annual convention that his company ad- 
vises managers to join service clubs such as Ro- 
tary, Kiwanis, and so on, as well as the chamber 
of commerce. He spoke of a plan of using the 
store windows at intervals to show the wide 


range of of local manufacturers—a plan 
that has been effective in small cities. 
40 years 


VANPORT, Ore., 1948 — When disastrous 
floods struck the Northwest at the end of May 
and early in June, the drug chains got into ac- 
tion quickly to give aid. The chain drug stores 
in and on the i of the flooded area were 
closed for the Memorial Day holiday when 
pir eink Ore., was overwhelmed. They 
quickly reopened and sent their stocks of first 
aid i where they were needed. 

Rexall Drug in Los Angeles, 1,500 miles to 
the south, rushed nearly a ton of emergency 
drugs to an airfield to be flown to the survi- 


place.” They can feel far more proud of the de- 
served title of “the nation’s first aid stations.” 


30 years ago 

NEW YORK, N.Y., 1958 — Overheard in 
the stores. “I keep a supply of paper bags at 
the feminine hygiene counter for shy custom- 
ers, and it’s helped our volume. But here’s the 
funny thing: most of those bags are being used 
by men, whose wives asked them to pick up a 
box of sanitary napkins. If I didn’t have those 
bags there, a lot of men would refuse to do it.” 


20 years ago 

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., 1968 — Hook’s an- 
tique drug store, which has been attracting 
considerable attention on its site on the Indi- 
ana State Fair grounds in Indianapolis, is vir- 
tually complete now with the addition of an 
antique soda fountain ap us. Dating from 
1875, the ornate marble box sports three spig- 
ots and s knobs, and there’s plenty of 
room for ice inside. Jim Rogers, Hook’s public 
relations director and ‘ er” of the an- 
tique store, paid $250, and he indicated that it 
is actually worth about $2,000. 


10 years ago 

ELEARWATER, Fla., 1978 — Less than 
three years after entering the highly competive 
Denver market, Jack erd Corporation has 
called it quits and is pulling out. It is the second 
major drug chain to leave Denver; the first was 
Pay Less , which abandoned this market a 
year ago. Stewart Turley, chairman and presi- 
dent of JEC, announced that the 865-store 
chain had closed its nine Denver area siores at 
the end of last month.

~Wacky weather plays havoc 


with sun care 


EW YORK — ing on loca- 

tion, sun care sales in chain drug 

stores this past season have been er- 
ratic. Some chains report growth as high as 20 
percent to 25 percent while others say the cate- 
gory has been flat or only up moderately. 

In some sections of the country, buyers say 
the weather is to blame for flat sales or just 
moderate growth. It’s been rainy or unpleas- 
ant and people haven’t had much need for tan- 
ning or protection products.

Wholesalers: Is there life after price-cutting? 


The days of volume for volume’s sake may be drawing to a close, 
as players eye new product mixes and picking methods to shore up profits 


By Elizabeth Parks 
epending on who you 
talk to, the drug 
wholesale industry is 

either entering a new stage of 
sophistication and restraint 
concerning strategies that im- 
pact profits, or it is not. 

About half the drug whole- 
salers Drug Store News inter- 
viewed for this special report 
thought that at least the major 
drug companies in 1987 and 
1988 were starting to show 
some restraint in some mar- 
kets regarding cutthroat price 
competition. 

owever, just as many 

sources thought the opposite 
was true. They believed that 
while everyone in the industry 
is giving “lip service” to the 
need to adopt strategies that 
will enhance gross margins, 
the reality is that companies 
are still going after volume for 
the sake of volume, or market 
share at any cost, and that this 
is why the industry’s average 
gross margin was down anoth- 
ay mt of a percentage point in 


Theoretically, wholesalers 
were in complete agreement 
over the need to attack the 
ay margin erosion issue. 

ost felt it was simply dan- 
gerous for the industry to ig- 
nore the margin issue and 
hope it could continue to store 
up profits by improving pro- 
ductivity and efficiency. 

Many sources said it was not 
enough to talk about success- 
fully stabilizing margins, that 
the industry’s real challenge 
was to get gross margins to go 
7 Several even said they felt 
the industry deserved to oper- 
ate with margins in the 7 - 
ble-digit range, “for all the 
services we provide to our cus- 
tomers.” 

Wholesalers also felt it was 
especially important to devel- 
op more of the value-added 
services to attract customers 
without resorting to offering 
“the lowest prices in town.” 

Most of the major compa- 
nies said they were trying to 
improve margins by —— 
ing marketing services for in- 
dependents, chains and 


hospitals. 

More wholesalers were also 
expanding their product mix 
to try to enhance margins, 
adding more H&BAs, OTCs 
and sundry lines to their mix 
so they could either enhance 
their standing as, or evolve 
into, full-line wholesalers. 

A few were experimenting 
with rack jobber programs, 
both as a way to grow margins 
and as a way to achieve incre- 
mental volume by improved 
servicing of new and existing 
customers. ag ~s try- 
ing to improve their buying 
and also enhance services by 
adopting or expanding catalo

s bought on deal. 

In the product mix arena, 
home health care was still per- 
ceived as a growth area, and 
so were generic drugs and me- 
dical/surgical supplies. 

Drug chains, food chains, 
mass merchandise chains, 
nursing homes and physicians 
were seen as growth areas 
with plenty of potential for

Owens & Minor had a fairly

rofits in the drug wholesaling 
usiinen were flat, primarily

corrected that problem b 
merging that division wit 
O&M’s medical surgical sales 
division. 

“Our core business is profit- 
able, but Miami was a loser. 
Now that it’s merged with me- 
dical/surgical, it’s not that 
much of a loser.” 

Minor says his company is 
continuing to try to reduce ex- 


penses. He says it has been 
able to improve productivity 
by increasing sales per em- 
ployee through automation. 

“I don’t how much room is 
left to reduce operating costs 
in the industry,” he says. “But 
you won't see the dramatic im- 
provements you've seen ir the 
past.” 

Minor says he sees two ma- 
jor factors working against 
the industry as companies try 
to improve overall margins 
and profitability. The first is 
the growing share of low mar- 
gin business that is going 
through hospitals. 

Minor says that about 55 
percent of his business now is 
with hospitals so O&M has 
managed to “go through that 

hase of learning to deal with 
ower margins.” 

He said the other problem is 
that retail customers have 
formed buying groups and are 
continuing to put pressure on 
wholesalers for lower margins 
and lower prices. 

“So it’s a double squeeze go- 
ing on and I don’t know when 
it will stop.” 

Owens & Minor is trying to 
add more services like plano- 
graming to help its retail cus- 
tomers, and the company is 
slowly expanding its se. He 
mix to include more front end 
items.

ALENCIA, Calif. — 
Bergen Brunswig, the 
nation’s second largest 
drug wholesaler, recently re- 
leased an interim report on its 
uniquely designed state-of- 
the-art distribution center, 
which opened last March here. 
Bergen’s president Phil En- 
gle says Valencia could gener- 
ate cost savings for Bergen 
and will probably become the 
rototype for all of Bergen’s 
uture high volume ware- 
houses. 

The report described the fa- 
cility as follows: 

The 208,100-square-foot 
building has space for offices 
and administration and expan- 
sion space above the office 
area. 

Additionally, the design of 
the warehouse will accommo- 
date a future mezzanine area. 
Fully expanded, the total 
a+ gh available is nearly 
300,000 square feet. 

The computer room has spe- 
cial acoustical treatment and 
secured access and fire sup- 
pression equipment, in addi- 
tion to a magnetic synthesizer 
that monitors electrical pow- 
er. 

Receiving doors are 
po re with dock levelers. 
Shipping docks have double 
roller conveyors that handle 
totes for each delivery run. 

Warehouse lighting is com- 
puter controlled with an ener- 
By management system. The 
office heating and air condi- 
tioning system is linked to an 
automatic setback system. 
Overall, the facility employs a 
five-layer, cable-linked com- 
puter architecture to control 
automation and business re- 
quirements. 

The Automated Picking 
System (APS) is designed to 
store and dispense the fastest 
moving prescription drugs 
and over-the-counter prod- 
ucts. A demanding series of 
capability and acceptance 
tests continues. Current esti- 
mates indicate that the fast- 
moving items represent 50 
percent of Valencia’s total 
sales volume. The remainin 
50 percent of the volume will 
be picked manually.

uter-controlled conveyors 
or picking and replenishment 
are provided by the Automat- 
ed Material Handling System 
(AMHS). Operating together, 
the APS and AMHS have or- 
der picking and replenishment 
capacity far greater than any 
current Bergen Brunswig dis- 
tribution center. Custom de- 
signed tote boxes are used 
throughout the system. 

Flow rack and static shelv- 
ing can store additional non- 
prescription product lines and 
additional lines of prescription 
medicine. Pallet-size racks 
provide bulk storage for some

share of total drug wholesaler 
sales went down two points 
from 1986 to 45.6 percent. In 
1984, independents had ac- 
counted for a whopping 53.5 
percent of all drug wholesaler 
customer sales. 

Sales to chain drug stores 
also went down one point in 
1987 to 22.7 percent. 

Most wholesalers agree 
that this shift does have some 
impact on the continued ero- 
sion of gross margins. Hospi- 
tals are very price conscious, 
and they usually give their 
business to the lowest bidder. 
This means that many whole- 
salers have had to sacrifice 
pe margin profitability to 

uild their base of business 
with this clientele. 

So far, too, hospitals have 
not been as interested in retail- 
ers in obtaining “value added 
services” from their wholesal- 
ers. Wholesalers have been 
able to create an entirely new 
category of higher margin busi- 
ness by developing value-add- 
ed programs for their retail cus- 
tomers, but hospitals until now 
have been more interested in 
buying product at the lowest 
possible price. 

Many wholesalers think this 
trend will change as hospitals 
come to realize how wholesal- 
ers can produce management 
services that will make them 
more profitable, but until that 
change comes, wholesalers 
will have to contend with deal- 
ing with a lower margin cus- 
tomer base that is growing 
dramatically in importance to 
them. 

In 1987, the average drug 
wholesaler gross margin 
slipped to 7.6 percent, down 
from 8.1 percent in 1986. 

Whoiesalers were able to 
hold the line on operating prof- 
its, however, because they 
were able to again lower oper- 
ating expenses to 5.3 percent 


in 1987, down from 6.0 percent 
in 1986. 

As a result, operating prof- 
its were up by one-tenth of a 
percentage point to 2.3 per- 
cent in 1987. 

Profitability was also 


helped by a tax rate reduction: 
the effective tax rate went 
down from 48.0 percent to 38.0 
percent, but as NWDA points 
out, that was a “one time shot 
in the arm” that won't recur in 
1988. 

Pharmaceutical sales con- 
tinued to increase as a percent 
of the average wholesaler’s 
sales mix. They went to 78.8 
percent of all sales in 1987, 
compared to 76.4 percent in 
1986. and 71.7 percent in 1984.
